title: Arms and Artefacts
text: Arms and Artefacts The objects of the Obligatory Quest: swords above fireplaces, hats required by forms, benches in eleven pieces, and one crate, stencilled on all six faces, which you should not have opened. The full catalogue is in preparation.

title: Bestiary
text: Bestiary The creatures of the road, as reported by the people they were rude to. I have not met any of them myself and do not intend to. I have relied, for the classification, on Wren Halloway, who has, and who will tell you what they are whether you have asked or not. The full catalogue is in preparation.

title: A Glossary of Cliches
text: A Glossary of Cliches An adventuring convention is a thing that happens on every quest because it happened on the first one, and nobody has thought to stop it. The Forty-Eighth walked into very nearly all of them. This volume lists them, with where he walked into each, and who was still annoyed about it. The glossary is in preparation.

title: History
text: History The history of the world, so far as anyone has written it down, is very largely the history of one document. Everything before the Prophecy of Thistlewick belongs to the elves, who will tell you about it if you ask and who have never been asked. Everything since belongs to the Prophecy, which has been asked a great deal and has answered, every time, in clauses. This volume holds the articles that are about time rather than about a person or a place. Article What it covers The Prophecy of Thistlewick The document itself: its signing, its clauses, and what it turned out to be. The Chosen Ones All forty-eight of them, so far as they are known, with what became of each. The Obligatory Quest The quest of the Forty-Eighth, from the bed to the throne room, and after. Two Reckonings Why the Tower is two thousand years old and four thousand eight hundred, and both are true. Timeline Every date I could pin, in order.

title: The Chosen Ones
text: The Chosen Ones For the document that chose them, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . For the last of them, see Bram Thistle . The Chosen Ones of Thistlewick Number Forty-eight First In the first century of the Third Age Last Bram Thistle, Third Age 2000 Chosen by The Prophecy Committee, in session, with or without the candidate Equipment A sword (one). Companions, up to three. Potions, three, from the parish fund Success rate Forty-seven out of forty-seven, according to the Committee Commemorated The Wall of the Forty-Seven, Prophecy Hall; the Obelisk, the Obligatory Tower; the memorial, Nether Sopping Next There isn't a forty-nine The Chosen Ones are the forty-eight people whom the village of Thistlewick sent north, under the Prophecy , to put down the Dark Lord in the Obligatory Tower . It worked forty-seven times. Thistlewick will tell you so. Ask it what happened the other times, and it will tell you that it worked forty-seven times. "Everyone tells you it's an honour," the father of the Forty-Seventh told the Forty-Eighth, on the morning he left. "Nobody tells you it's a rota." How a Chosen One is chosen By the Prophecy Committee , in session, at a moment it finds convenient (see Two Reckonings). The candidate does not need to be present, and the last one was not: the minutes of the meeting at which Bram Thistle was chosen list, under apologies for absence, his name and one goat. He was asleep. The goat has not been found. The Chosen One is then summoned to Prophecy Hall , where Elder Wispel unrolls the Prophecy until it reaches the far wall and gives the charge: take companions, up to three; go north; kill the Dark Lord; come home. "In that order, ideally." The Chosen One receives a copy of the Prophecy in triplicate, five hundred crowns and three potions from the parish fund, and a sword. Every one of them did the sword. What happened next was, for forty-seven of them, the same. They went north. They climbed the Tower. They found the Dark Lord, Grimspite the Inevitable , reading, and he put his bookmark in and said, "So, you have come at last," which he meant the first time. They fought him, and they won, and before they reached the stairs clause twelve renewed him. They came home and Thistlewick said that it had worked. "Forty-seven of us," Halbert Quy told the Forty-Eighth. "We all did the sword. Not one of us ever asked the man why he doesn't stop." And forty-seven went before, and every one took up the sword, and not one asked him what it was for, and that is all the old record. From the notebooks of P. Quill, by permission Miss Quill has asked me to point out that "record" is stressed on the second syllable here, for the rhyme, and that this is allowed. I have pointed it out. What became of them They came home, and they were awkward. A Chosen One who has come back knows what is at the top of the Tower, and says so at meetings, and asks why the Committee is already drafting the next one. Somewhere about the Ninth, Thistlewick wrote clause nineteen, and from then on a returning hero received a pension, a cottage, and such distance from the village as was mutually agreeable, which was forty miles, to Nether Sopping . That is where they are, those of them who are anywhere. Most of them drink in the Slain Wyvern . Thistlewick does not write. The forty-eight The Committee keeps a souvenir book, The Forty-Seven, with a portrait, a date and a pressed flower on every page. The flowers are all turnip flowers. I have seen it, across a table, and was not permitted to copy the dates, which are Committee property. So I have printed below only what I could get from somebody who was there, and where nobody was, I have left the space. No. Set out Name What is known 1 The first century of the Age Not recorded Shown in the stained glass of Prophecy Hall, slaying the Dark Lord. The glazier has given the Dark Lord a very patient expression, like a man waiting for a bus he has been told is coming. 2-8 A century apart Not recorded The Committee found a hundred years convenient, at first. 9 About the year 900 Not recorded Came home, and was awkward. Clause nineteen was written somewhere about him. 10-38 Closer and closer together, always in a round year Not recorded The Committee began to find shorter periods convenient. Nobody in Thistlewick has remarked on it. 39 About 1930 Not recorded The cousin of a regular in the Gilded Turnip , who will tell you so. 40 Before 1940 Not recorded 41 1940 Halloran Vance Came back from the marshes with nothing and a whole town waiting on the quay for a monster. So he brought them one: two days, with wire, and a goose. It has been a wyvern over the mantel of the Slain Wyvern for sixty years. He was a good man, and he needed it to be a wyvern. 42 The 1940s or 1950s Not recorded He and his wife drink in the Slain Wyvern, and come every year for the anniversary. 43 The 1940s or 1950s Not recorded 44 1960 Ambrose Fitch Pensioned to Nether Sopping and ignored for forty years, watering a pot with a dead thing in it every morning. Died about 1999. Thistlewick cut THISTLEWICK REMEMBERS over the door of his mound; somebody has chalked under it that Thistlewick did not write once. He asked for a bench. He has one now. 45 1970 Halbert Quy Declined Grimspite's tea, because he thought it was a trick, and has thought about it ever since. Asked at the next meeting why there was always a next one. The cottage was ready by the Friday. He is next door to Fitch's. 46 1980 Not given Got as far as the Gloamwood , said the woods were enough, and sat down on a log, where he still is. His party said: fair. Two of them, Nabb and Tolly, write to him every month, and he reads every letter, and that is his answer. 47 1990 Not given The Old Man's boy. Came off the ledge at Olde Evermore and landed on his feet, for five point nine, the best score since the First Age. He did not come home to Thistlewick. 48 2000 Bram Thistle A turnip farmer, chosen asleep. Asked the question. See The Obligatory Quest. Forty-seven, or forty-six. Grimspite says he said "so, you have come at last" forty-seven times and was renewed forty-seven times, and the Obelisk in his tower lists forty-seven RENEWED. The Forty-Sixth says he got as far as the woods. Miss Hoyle of Upper Clanging, who counts for a living, counts forty-six that went up that road. I have all three numbers, and I have not been able to make them into one. I set them down here side by side, which is what an encyclopedia is for. Monuments The Wall of the Forty-Seven, in Prophecy Hall: forty-seven portraits. Forty-six of them are looking at the viewer. One of them is looking at the door. I have asked which, and why, and was told that it was a very old portrait. At the end of them there is now a forty-eighth frame, new and empty, with a card pinned in it: PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. The sitter is not at the coast. He is at home, two fields away, and has been for two years. Nobody has changed the card. A second card, the Quills', is tucked into the corner to make room. The Obelisk, in the Obligatory Tower: forty-seven entries, each a date and a name and the word RENEWED. There is room for a forty-eighth. It will not be needed. The memorial at Nether Sopping: a hundred and eighty-one names. It lists everybody who went north with them - healers, hired swords, cousins, a cook, somebody listed only as "the lad who carried the rope" - and not only the Chosen Ones, which is the difference between Nether Sopping and Thistlewick in one stone. The end of the list When the Forty-Eighth had read the Prophecy through and it had stopped being binding, Grimspite signed him a receipt and sent him home with a message. "Grow your turnips. There isn't a forty-nine. Say that to them, when you get in. Say: there isn't a forty-nine." He said it. The Committee minuted it. It has not, so far as I can tell, been believed, but it has been true for two years, which is the longest anything has been true in Prophecy Hall. See also The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Obligatory Quest Two Reckonings Nether Sopping

title: The Obligatory Quest
text: The Obligatory Quest This article is about the quest of the Forty-Eighth, in the year 2000. For the forty-seven before it, which went the same way as each other, see The Chosen Ones . For the man, see Bram Thistle . The Obligatory Quest The Forty-Eighth, after the event Date Third Age 2000, the last of the winter Chosen One Bram Thistle, No. 48 Companions Up to three at any one time (that is the clause); eleven in all, at one time or another Objective Go north. Kill the Dark Lord. Come home. In that order, ideally Outcome The Dark Lord retired. The Prophecy read in full, and no longer binding. The Chosen One home Cliches encountered Very nearly all of them Receipt Yes The Obligatory Quest of the year 2000 was the forty-eighth expedition sent north by the village of Thistlewick under the Prophecy , and the last. It set out like all the others, and went where all the others went, and differed from them in one respect, which is that when it arrived the Chosen One asked the Dark Lord a question and then stayed for the answer. I have told the whole of it in Volume Two, from first-hand accounts, at length. What follows is the short version. It is still not short. The choosing Bram Thistle was a turnip farmer, and was asleep when the Prophecy Committee chose him. The minutes give his name under apologies for absence, with one goat. He woke chosen, took down a sword he did not seem entirely comfortable holding, and went to Prophecy Hall , where Elder Wispel unrolled the Prophecy to the far wall and told him it had worked forty-seven times. He asked what had happened the other times. He was told that it had worked forty-seven times. He was given five hundred crowns and three potions from the parish fund, and the Prophecy, which was, regrettably, free. A neighbour in the lane, a farmer, asked who was doing the west field. Nobody had an answer to that either. The company The clause allows a Chosen One three companions, and Bram, over the course of the Quest, went through rather more than three, though never more than three at once. In the order in which people generally list them, which is not the order in which anybody joined, they were: Merribell , Thistlewick's healer; Hob Grumnir , its blacksmith; Zephyrine Vance , a hedge mage, with a history at the Collegium Arcanum; Nix , in acquisitions; Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III , a knight errant who could not find the north gate; Piper Quill , a bard, who was writing it all down; Corvin Ash , a doomed rival, from a corner of the Slain Wyvern; Wren Halloway , a cataloguer, from another corner; Roland Fairweather , a guest star, from a table near the door, who had somewhere to be; and Spare Cotterill , the ninth of the Cotterills of Upper Clanging, aged nine, who joined after a discussion with his mother. Which three of them were with him at the top of the Tower is a matter on which I have taken evidence from all of them, and every one of them has told me, kindly and firmly, that it was them. I have not adjudicated. I have noted that Roland Fairweather is the only one who does not claim it, because he left at the door, as he always does. See his article for why. The road north The north gate of Thistlewick turns back a Chosen One who goes alone, and is where it has always been, whatever Sir Aldric tells you. Beyond it is the Gloamwood , where the Thing In The Woods, about which Thistlewick had argued for two hundred years - is it a bear? several bears? a bear-shaped hole in the idea of a wood? - stopped being in the woods. Thistlewick will never believe it. Bram has not told them anyway. In the Gloamwood, on a log, the party met the Forty-Sixth, who had got as far as the woods in 1980, decided the woods were enough, and sat down. He asked whether the Forty-Seventh had come back. He has a sack of letters beside him from two members of his old party, who write every month. The south, which nobody does Then the Forty-Eighth did the thing that no Chosen One before him had thought to do. He went south. Forty miles south is Nether Sopping , where clause nineteen sends the heroes who come back, and in Nether Sopping is the Slain Wyvern , where they drink, and in the Slain Wyvern is a table by the fire, and at the table, at the time, was I. I asked him to do what I could not: to go round the room and be told. Six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end. He did. He found forty-seven of them in a tavern, and sat down, and listened, and in the course of it he found out that the wyvern over the mantel is a goose. My history was finished on the strength of it. He paid the fee later, as I shall come to. He did a good deal else in the south, and all of it is in Volume Two: he registered with the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) , on the strength of a character reference, a hat and the mat, and both of its bounty cards came off the board while he was there; he got oil up to the Lighthouse of Saint Bother , which is lit again, and can be seen from the crossroads, which is the whole of what it is for; he went down into the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth , where Ambrose Fitch was waiting to fight him, because that is what is done, and stopped when asked, which is not, and asked for a bench; and Bram built him one, facing the sea; and he walked to the cottage of Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, who told him the only thing he had come home with that was worth the trip. Ask him why. The north North and west of the road is Upper Clanging , where the Hoyle Works had been trying for two hundred years to fly to the Tower. With the Forty-Eighth's help Miss Ott Hoyle 's two hundredth attempt reached it. The attempt log reads REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. Clause seven requires a Chosen One to go on foot, and he did, from the grass beside the door, which was as far as the airship would set down. Attempt Eighty-Four, who had been repairing herself out of the wrecks either side of her since she came down in 1860, was stopped, and is being rebuilt. ITEM 1 came off its crag for the first time since 1802. Hob Grumnir met Bryd Ollerenshaw, and they went for a drink, and are still arguing about rivets. The Tower The door of the Obligatory Tower was barred. There is a key under the mat, labelled SPARE - DO NOT LOSE AGAIN, which is the most honest thing in the building. Nix did not need it. ("Bar's on the inside. Classic.") Inside is a plaque that says the building was established approximately four thousand eight hundred years ago, under the same management; an Obelisk with forty-seven RENEWED on it; and a cupboard of hooks with the companions' trades on brass labels, one of them reading GUEST and always empty. The party climbed it. At the top there is a throne, and there was a Dark Lord on it, and he was reading. The top "Forty-eight," said Grimspite the Inevitable . "Right on time. Sit down. No? Fine. Standing is traditional." He had said "so, you have come at last" forty-seven times, he told them, and meant it the first time. Then the Forty-Eighth asked him why he did not stop. "Ah. The clever one. They're rarer than you'd think." He could not stop, and he showed them why: the sentence carved forty-seven times into the wall behind them, THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN, which is clause twelve, and which is not a threat but a renewal notice. When Bram told him who had sent him with the question, he asked him to go back and tell Halbert that the tea was just tea, and to listen to all of it, because he would like, once, for somebody to have listened to the whole of it. Bram listened. Then they fought, because the Dark Lord does not stop until he is stopped, and at the end of it Grimspite went down on one knee and said: "...Thank you." The Prophecy came down from the ceiling to renew him, and found instead a party of the correct size, at the correct place, on the correct date, and appointed it. Grimspite told Bram not to kill it but to read it, out loud, all of it. He read it, and it came apart in the middle of a sentence, and Grimspite the Inevitable stood up and waited to be renewed and was not. "Four thousand eight hundred years," he said, "and it was an admin problem." He signed a receipt for one Dark Lord, renewable, in case anyone asked whose fault this was, and gave it to Bram, and sent him home. "Grow your turnips. There isn't a forty-nine." The account An account of the Quest was drawn up afterwards, and is kept on a lectern in Prophecy Hall, as amended. It lists everything, in order: who came back, how many cliches were walked into and turnips eaten, what was lit and built and flown and rebuilt, and which verses the Committee struck. Of my own work it says this: There is a song about it now. Hosea Bellwether wrote it from first-hand accounts and it is, therefore, complete. It is not remotely accurate. It is not a song. It is four hundred pages and a pamphlet, and none of it rhymes, and I would refer whoever drew up the account to Miss Quill, who writes the songs. The rest of the sentence I accept. That is what Volume Three is for. Miss Quill's ballad was finished on the road, in the Gilded Turnip, after an afternoon on which the whole party tried to find her a rhyme for turnip. There is none. She moved the turnip down a line, in nine seconds, and everybody who had spent the afternoon on it was furious. The last verse, as she fixed it: 'And so he came home to the fields, and hung his sword above the grate, and sat down with a turnip, which was worth the journey, and the wait.' P. Quill, the ballad, last verse Of the official account of the Forty-Eighth there are, depending on whom you ask, one or two, and I have been asked by everybody named Quill not to say which is the right one. I have not. The morning after The next morning there were still turnips. There was also a letter on the mat, in the Committee's envelope: clause nineteen, a quarter's pension, and the key to a cottage at Nether Sopping. We trust Friday will suit. At the top of the Tower, Grimspite was in his chair with a kettle, and the book at the bookmark. The Committee struck clause twelve from its records and wrote in its place SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. Bram walked south. He told Halbert Quy what Grimspite had said, all of it, in order, including the part about the tea. It took most of an afternoon. Then he came into the Wyvern and told me, and that was the fee, and I filled the last page. Six months later, after a very long meeting, the Committee struck clause nineteen as well. Afterwards The Quest is over, but it did not quite stop, and some of what came after is as much a part of it as the throne room. Bram has been in and out of the cottage clause nineteen gave him, which was Ambrose Fitch 's. Roland Fairweather came back. Sir Dunstable lent Bram a lamp, and the party went down the Stair behind the Door into the Mountain at Hithermost , which I have written up under the Stair , and found something at the bottom of it that the Guild had a card for. In the spring, which he had asked about every morning, Spare Cotterill went home to Upper Clanging for the birth of the tenth Cotterill. And every year, on the day, Bram walks up to the top of the Tower, and the kettle is on. Bram reads this article every time he comes south, and every time he corrects something in it, and every time it is the same thing, which is that he did not do any of it on his own. I have let it stand. He has asked me to add that it was a very long walk. It was. See also The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones Timeline Bram Thistle Grimspite the Inevitable

title: The Prophecy of Thistlewick
text: The Prophecy of Thistlewick For the people it chose, see The Chosen Ones . For the last occasion on which it chose anybody, see The Obligatory Quest . The Prophecy of Thistlewick Kind A prophecy, according to the title. A contract, according to everything underneath it Signed Third Age 1, three times by everybody Length Unrolled in Prophecy Hall, it reaches the far wall Copies The Committee's own; one issued to each Chosen One, in triplicate; a fair copy in the Forbidden Archive at Olde Evermore Clauses known Two, four, seven, eleven, twelve, fourteen, nineteen, thirty-one Marginalia One horse Read in full Twice that I know of. The second time was fatal Status Not binding, since the year 2000. Still kept The Prophecy of Thistlewick is a document of very great length, kept by the Prophecy Committee in Prophecy Hall , which for very nearly two thousand years told the village of Thistlewick that every hundred years the Dark Lord would rise in the Obligatory Tower and that somebody had better go. It was right every time. That should have been the first clue. It was never a prophecy. It is an employment contract, with numbered clauses, and the post it filled was the Dark Lord's. That was not understood until the year 2000, and then only because a turnip farmer did the one thing nobody in Thistlewick had ever done with it, which was to read it. The signing The Prophecy was signed in the first year of the Third Age, and Thistlewick has always held that the Age began with it. The elves of Olde Evermore , who were there, say the Age began with a great many things and that the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. I have not been able to get either party to say more, and I record both. What is agreed is that the signing was ever so long. I have that from an eyewitness: Mirabel , the oracle of Olde Evermore, who attended as a child of about two thousand and was bored. Everybody had to sign it three times. So she drew a horse on it. The Forbidden Archive at Olde Evermore keeps a fair copy made at the signing by a copyist who copied everything, and I can confirm that "everything" includes the margins. The horse is in the margin beside clause twelve. It is a good horse. I have nothing further to say about it, and when I asked the copyist whether he had anything further to say about it, he went on copying. Nobody has told me where the original is, or who held the pen for the other side. What it says The Prophecy has never been printed entire, and I have not attempted it here; Volume Two is large enough. These are the clauses I have been able to establish, from the copy, from the people they were done to, and in one case from a leaflet. Clause two: a hundred years "A hundred years" is a defined term. It means "such period as the Committee shall find convenient." This is the most important sentence in the document, and for two thousand years nobody noticed it. It was found by Miss Pargeter of Frostwick , who keeps the winter there under a contract of her own and reads contracts the way other people read weather. She went all the way through the Forty-Eighth's copy, which nobody had ever done, and turned back to clause two. The consequences are in Two Reckonings, which is a separate article because it needed one. Clause four I do not know what clause four says. It appears on the back of the Committee's leaflet, So You've Been Chosen, which is one page long and says CONGRATULATIONS!, and then, in very much smaller print, CLAUSE FOUR APPLIES. I have asked every Chosen One I could reach what clause four was. All of them said that it applied. The companions clause Elder Wispel gives the charge to every Chosen One, and includes this: take companions, up to three. "That is the clause," he says, "not my preference." I have not been able to find its number. The Tower has a cupboard on its fourth floor with ten hooks in it, each with a small brass label: CHOSEN ONE, HEALER, SMITH, MAGE, SPECIALIST, KNIGHT, MUSICIAN, and two added later in a cheaper brass, RIVAL and CATALOGUER. The tenth reads GUEST, and is always empty. So the clause is at least well provided for. Clause seven: on foot The Chosen One goes on foot. Grimspite himself explained why, when he was asked: "Because a thing that flies over and drops something is not a story. It is a Tuesday." The town of Upper Clanging has spent two hundred years building ships that fly to the Tower, and kept the ones that did not in the Long Field . Grimspite was of the view that Miss Hoyle would never get one off the ground in sight of his tower, and that it had nothing whatever to do with her spars. Her two hundredth attempt landed beside the Tower that same year, with a Chosen One aboard. As far as I know nobody has mentioned this to him, and I do not intend to be the first, in an encyclopedia or out of one. Clause eleven: fit to travel A Chosen One is certified fit before departure. It had been done forty-seven times. The Forty-Eighth's certificate was blank, because the Committee chose him while he was asleep, and nobody had examined a man who was asleep. Merribell found the blank on a pad of works fitness forms in Upper Clanging and did it properly, on the road, with stamped scales borrowed from the fish stall at Nether Sopping, the light of a lit lighthouse, and a witness. He is certified fit to travel. He had, by then, travelled. Clause twelve: the renewal THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN. For two thousand years Thistlewick read this as a warning. It is not a warning. As Councillor Fenn of the Committee told his colleagues for years, to no effect: "That's not a warning. That's a subscription." Grimspite put it more shortly, and he had more right to: "It isn't a threat. It's a renewal notice." Every time a Chosen One beat the Dark Lord, clause twelve renewed him, "before you reach the stairs". It renewed him forty-seven times. The sentence is carved forty-seven times into the wall behind his throne, and on the Obelisk in the Tower there is a list of forty-seven dates and names, each ending in the word RENEWED, with room left at the bottom for a forty-eighth. In the copy issued to the Forty-Eighth, clause twelve has been underlined by somebody worried. The Committee struck it in 2000, nem. con., and in its place wrote a note: SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. Clause fourteen: the first meeting The first meeting shall not go well. I have this from Merrow Halgate , whose party of twenty - the best-equipped that ever went north - fought the Dark Lord at the bridge and lost, as the clause required, and as was written down in advance. He has made his peace with losing. He has not made his peace with the paperwork. Clause nineteen: the Resettlement Clause A returning Chosen One shall receive a pension, a cottage, and such distance from the village as is mutually agreeable. It was added later, somewhere about the Ninth, when Thistlewick found that a hero who comes home is awkward: he knows what is at the top of the Tower, and he asks at meetings why the Committee is already drafting the next one. Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, asked exactly that - "if it works every hundred years, why is there always a next one?" - and the cottage was ready by the Friday. The mutually agreeable distance turned out to be forty miles, which is how I come to be writing this in Nether Sopping , among most of the people in it. "They're not cruel," Mr Quy told the Forty-Eighth. "They're embarrassed." It was applied to the Forty-Eighth the morning after he got home, by letter, on the mat: his pension, one quarter, in advance, with no mention of the next one, and the key to a cottage at Nether Sopping. We trust Friday will suit. Six months later, after a very long meeting, the Committee struck clause nineteen as well. Forty miles south, a man in a garden read the notice twice and then went indoors. The meeting was eleven hours. I have read the minutes. They are, for the most part, about the biscuits. Clause thirty-one: mechanism THE DARK LORD SHALL NOT BE CONCLUDED BY MECHANISM. This is why ITEM 1, which had stood unticked in the Hoyle Works ' stores book since 1802, did nothing whatever when it was finally set down in front of the throne, except make smoke and knock Grimspite's bookmark on to the floor. "Ordnance is not provided for," he said. "Nothing is provided for. That is what a renewal notice is." How it ended The Forty-Eighth beat Grimspite, as forty-seven had before him. Clause twelve unrolled - the Prophecy itself, the width of the room, moving like something with an opinion - to renew him, and then, instead of renewing him, it turned to the party. It had found a party of the correct size, at the correct place, on the correct date. THE CHOSEN ONE SHALL BE CHOSEN. A NEW DARK LORD SHALL BE APPOINTED. THE ROLE IS VACANT. CONGRATULATIONS. "Yes," said Grimspite. "That's how I got the job." It was Grimspite who told the Forty-Eighth what to do. Not to kill it: to read it, out loud, all of it, because a contract that has been read in full has never once survived the experience. He read it. It came apart in the middle of a sentence. It did not burn or explode. It simply stopped being binding, which for a contract is the same as dying. "Four thousand eight hundred years," said Grimspite, "and it was an admin problem." The Committee keeps it still, rolled, in Prophecy Hall, with two clauses struck. It is not binding on anybody. The Committee consults it anyway, at every meeting, out of habit, and minutes that it has been consulted. Why the role was vacant this time. Grimspite said clause twelve had renewed him forty-seven times before anybody reached the stairs. On the forty-eighth it declared the post vacant instead. Nobody has told me why, and I have three theories from three tables in the Wyvern, which I give without preference: that it was because he said thank you, which in forty-seven fights he had never said; that it was because the Forty-Eighth was still in the room, listening, which in forty-seven fights none of them had been; and that the clause had always said so and nobody had read that far down. Grimspite, asked by letter, replied that it was a very good question and that he had a kettle on. See also The Chosen Ones The Obligatory Quest Two Reckonings Timeline The Prophecy Committee

title: Timeline
text: Timeline All years are years of the Third Age, counted the way the sun does. Where the Prophecy counts otherwise, see Two Reckonings . This is every date I have been able to pin, in order. A date I have from a headstone, a ledger or a plaque is given plainly. A date I have from somebody's memory is given as "about". Where I have nothing, I have left a gap, which in a timeline is more honest than it looks. Several of these dates have been corrected by post, from the top of the Obligatory Tower, in a very beautiful hand. I have accepted all of the corrections. I have not been told the date of the correspondent's birth, and I have not printed one. Before the Third Age When What The First Age Olde Evermore is where it is. Thalion begins judging every arrival off the ledge, out of six. The Second Age Mirabel is born, about two thousand one hundred and thirteen years before the Prophecy. Elder Lirien and Elder Faelan marry. Calder begins fishing for the one fish in the pond. Before the year 1 The Dark Lord's engagement is held at the castle on the cloud, the Former Premises, so that no hero could ever reach it. None ever does. What began the Third Age is not known to me. It was not the Prophecy. The first nineteen centuries Year What 1 The Prophecy of Thistlewick is signed, three times by everybody. A horse is drawn in the margin. The engagement moves to the Obligatory Tower, which has a door at the bottom, and the first hero to arrive gets the job. The caretaker of the Former Premises is retained. 100s-900s The first nine Chosen Ones, a real century apart. About 900 About the Ninth: Thistlewick finds a returning hero awkward, and writes clause nineteen. 900s-1930s The Tenth to the Fortieth, closer and closer together, always in a round year. 1400 The Collegium Arcanum is founded, by the Founder, in one afternoon. 1500 The First Dean's portrait is hung, pending the Hanging Committee. 1702 Weeping Bottom is founded by Mother Ursula Pym, for the sea air. Her Rule of Life is four lines long, and one of them is about socks. 1749 The Sky Anvil falls into Meech's top field. His great-great-grandfather makes it a gatepost. 1750 Pilgrims build a shrine round the gatepost. 1788 Great Dunnage seals its Counting House, "when the key was lost". J. Pocklington, Clerk to the Corporation, leaves behind the Door one chair and a note: WE SPENT IT. 1794 Sump: wasps in the well. The Water Committee is wound up. Cursed 1794. 1795 Sump: a general sense that things used to be better. The parish drafts Standing Orders for the Lifting of the Curse, and does not use them. About 1800 Nether Sopping begins throwing things down the Pit. 1802 The Hoyle Works begins its stores book. ITEM 1 is written into it. Bond No. 40, one cabbage, very large, "for the show", goes into the Bonded Warehouse at Great Dunnage. 1804 The Hoyle Works takes its first apprentice. 1811 Dame Honoria Pemberton-Gore's portrait is painted. 1840 Rollo, a dog, is painted. 1841 The clock at Upper Clanging goes four minutes fast. 1860 Attempt Eighty-Four comes down in the Long Field. 1890 Mabel Thistle, Bram's great-grandmother, is born. She grows a turnip as big as a chair. The twentieth century Year What About 1900 Attempt 112 comes down on her rock. 1902 Elspeth Moore is born. She will win the Thistlewick turnip show forty-one years running. The forty-second was fixed. 1908 A crate of ship's biscuit is stencilled for the store at Saint Bother's. 1909 The shipping stops. The Lighthouse of Saint Bother is kept lit for the ones coming home. 1919 Beatrice Grumnir is born. About 1930 The Thirty-Ninth sets out. Mr Ottershaw of Fenmarch Hall begins the animals. 1931 Mrs Pardew's gran makes her last jar of gooseberry jam at Sump, and labels it BETTER. 1940 The Forty-First, Halloran Vance, comes home from the marshes with nothing, and makes a wyvern out of a goose and wire in two days. Upper Clanging, which sets its watches by its clock, begins to be four minutes early for everything. 1940s-1950s The Forty-Second and the Forty-Third. 1941 Abel Thrush begins carrying the post between Little Gore, Fenmarch and Sump, every day, for fifty years. 1949 Corvin Ash's grandfather makes the black sword and cuts its name into his doorstep at Ashcombe, with MIND THE STEP under it for visitors. 1959 Wick, of Wick & Barrow, outfitters, of Nether Sopping, goes north, in the spring. His peg is still on the wall. 1960 The Forty-Fourth, Ambrose Fitch. Beatrice Grumnir makes a sword at the Thistlewick forge and sells it to a man going south. Perce Stagg breaks Frostwick's winter. The Adventurers' Guild is founded, provisionally. The Gloamwood Society is founded, to prove the Thing In The Woods is not there. 1969 Gideon Markup prices the Sword of Ultimate Ending. 1970 The Forty-Fifth, Halbert Quy, declines the tea. Tobias Frayne's first revival of eleven. Sir Aldric, sixteen, is due to keep his vigil, and keeps it in the wrong chapel. Mr Tinder, the parish's last fire person, retires, and the Cinder Fen is not burnt again for thirty years. Mr Cobley begins fishing for Old Tom. 1971 Edith Pellow sees the Thing In The Woods, and counts nine heads. 1972 K and M marry, and carve it into the driftwood on the beach at Nether Sopping. STILL is cut under it later. 1974 Walt Ashbury begins at the Eight Hours, Restwell. 1977 Roland Fairweather, aged eleven, is page to Dame Florence Ickworth against the Wyrm of Ickworth. 1978 Roland Fairweather is told that his prophecy is nearly ready. 1979 Mabel Thistle dies. 1980 The Forty-Sixth sits down in the Gloamwood. 1986 Sir Hamo Tench comes to Weeping Bottom for the sea air. 1987 Bryd Ollerenshaw wins BEST IN HALL at the Smiths' Hall in Great Dunnage. Hob Grumnir does not enter, having a cold. The Committee begins meaning to water the plant in Prophecy Hall. 1989 A year of beginnings and endings. Corvin Ash, nineteen, sits down in the corner of the Slain Wyvern, and Ashcombe floods in his absence. Nix, fifteen, puts her gran's coat into bond until it fits, and starts the ledger. Attempt 199 is lost in sight of the Tower. Zephyrine Vance's incident at the Collegium, with the Dean, a duck and an unsanctioned quantity of fire. Beatrice Grumnir dies. 1990 The Forty-Seventh, the Old Man's boy, comes off the ledge at Olde Evermore and lands on his feet. 1991 Sir Aldric goes out errant, with an invitation to deliver to Little Gore. Abel Thrush dies, in the spring. 1992 Sir Aldric talks to the Wrong Dragon about Horace until dark. 1993 Maud Penhallow, nine, becomes Roland Fairweather's understudy. 1994 Elspeth Moore dies. Sir Aldric reaches Thistlewick and cannot find the north gate. That winter his horse walks into a yard at Great Dunnage on her own, saddled. 1996 Mr Pilbeam rescues Princess Rosamund from the eagle. Merribell leaves the Sisterhouse at Weeping Bottom, because it has begun holding symposia. 1997 Much Pottering twins with Upper Clanging. Effie Gotobed and Spare Cotterill, both six, become pen pals. About 1999 Ambrose Fitch dies, in his cottage at Nether Sopping. The masons come within a fortnight. The year 2000 When What The last of the winter The Forty-Eighth, Bram Thistle, is chosen in his sleep. The Obligatory Quest, from the bed to the throne room. The Prophecy is read in full and stops being binding. Grimspite retires. The next morning There are still turnips. The letter on the mat: clause nineteen, a quarter's pension, a key. We trust Friday will suit. Clause twelve is struck, and SEE BRAM written in its place. Spring Washer, the tenth Cotterill, is born at Upper Clanging at six in the morning, on the hooter. Clevis Cotterill's book pays twenty to one. That year Bram walks to Nether Sopping and tells Halbert Quy everything Grimspite said, including the part about the tea. My history is completed, and the last page filled. Autumn Clause nineteen is struck, after a meeting of eleven hours. Winter The forty-eighth frame on the Wall of the Forty-Seven still reads PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. Since When What 2001 Merribell addresses the Healers' Table, for eleven minutes, on water. It is the shortest address in the Table's history, and is minuted as the most useful. 2001 The Gloamwood Society's annual walk, three hundred and twelve strong. Nothing is found. The Society minutes it with satisfaction. 2001 Ott Hoyle lays the keel of the Two Hundred and First. 2001 Corvin Ash is asked back to the Flood Dinner at Ashcombe, and goes, and is early. 9 June 2001 Sir Aldric finds the north gate of Thistlewick, unaided. He has not found it since. 2001 Hob Grumnir and Bryd Ollerenshaw judge the Smiths' Hall prize together, and disagree for nine hours. Harvest 2001 Bram's first full crop since the Quest, and the best in the parish. The Committee asks whether it was prophesied. It was not. 21 March 2002 The first day of spring, which Spare Cotterill has confirmed by letter. I sign this volume. See also Two Reckonings The Chosen Ones The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Obligatory Quest

title: Two Reckonings
text: Two Reckonings For every date in order, see Timeline . For the clause responsible, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick, clause two . The two reckonings The calendar Kept by The elves, and everybody who is not the Prophecy Counts The way the sun does The year Third Age 2002, at the time of writing The Tower About two thousand years old The contract Kept by The Prophecy, and everybody who works for it Counts Whatever the Committee finds convenient A century Lately, about ten years The Tower Approximately four thousand eight hundred years old There are two reckonings of time in the world, and the history of the Obligatory Quest is written in both of them at once, usually in the same sentence. The calendar is the elves' Third Age, in which this is the year 2002. The contract is the Prophecy's, in which a hundred years is whatever the Committee says it is. By the one, the Obligatory Tower is about two thousand years old. By the other it is four thousand eight hundred. Both are correct, and it took a woman in Frostwick with her gloves on to find out why. The calendar The years in this book, and in most books, are years of the Third Age, which is the elves' count. Olde Evermore counts in Ages, and has been where it is since the First; Mirabel has been making her prophecy about biscuits since the Second. The Hoyle Works' stores book was begun in 1802, Weeping Bottom was founded in 1702, the Collegium Arcanum in 1400, and the Forty-Eighth set out in 2000. Those are all the same kind of year, a year of the sun, and they add up. Thistlewick signed the Prophecy in the first year of the Third Age, and has said ever since that the Age began with it. It did not. What did begin it, I do not know, and Elder Faelan would only tell me that the Age began with a great many things and the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. I have not been able to find out what the others were. I suspect that nobody has ever asked, and I suspect that is the reason. The contract The Prophecy counts in years of its own. Its clause two defines a hundred years as such period as the Committee shall find convenient, and every figure that comes from the Prophecy's side of things - from the Tower, from the Dark Lord, from the people who are paid to look after him - is a figure of that kind. These are some of them: What Says Means The Dark Lord rises Every hundred years Whenever the Committee found it convenient. Latterly, every ten The plaque in the Tower Est. approx. 4,800 years ago, UNDER THE SAME MANAGEMENT Forty-eight Committee centuries, give or take the first few Grimspite's tenure Four thousand eight hundred years, this job The same The Contingency Cache, fourth floor RESTOCKED EVERY CENTURY Every Chosen One. Nobody has ever opened it. It is six feet from the stairs The wayshrine's visitors' book The last entry, "Feeling good about this one!", is dated a hundred years ago The Forty-Seventh's, 1990 The Former Premises Two thousand years of Dark Lords, and nineteen thousand two hundred quarterly reports Contract years again: four a year, for four thousand eight hundred The calendar and the contract ran together at first, while the Committee still found a hundred years convenient, for the first nine Chosen Ones or so. Then it began finding shorter periods convenient, and then shorter still, and always in a round year. By the end the Forty-First went in 1940 and the last five went ten years apart, which is how the Forty-Fifth, a man who set out three centuries before the Forty-Eighth, is in his seventies and potting things on his kitchen table forty miles from here. Who notices It depends, very largely, on how far you live from the Committee. I have made something of a study of it, from a table in the Slain Wyvern, which is forty miles away and is where the people who noticed were sent. In Thistlewick nobody notices. The village holds both reckonings at once, comfortably, like a man with a pie in each hand. The Old Man's boy was the Forty-Seventh. A regular in the Gilded Turnip will tell you his cousin was the Thirty-Ninth. They went a hundred years apart. Nobody in the village is over a hundred. I have put all of this to nobody in Thistlewick, because I like it there and should like to go back. In Nether Sopping, everybody noticed, which is why they are in Nether Sopping. Halbert Quy asked at a meeting why, if it worked every hundred years, there was always a next one, and the cottage was ready by the Friday. Down here we talk in plain years, sixty and forty and thirty, and we do not make a point of it. We do not have to. Upper Clanging believes the text. The Hoyle Works read "every hundred years" two hundred years ago and made an engineering programme of it, and has not counted since, because the document had done the counting for it. Noticing grows with distance, I find, but it is not guaranteed by it, and engineers who take a document literally are their own case. In Frostwick, far to the north, there is one person who reads contracts, Miss Pargeter , who keeps the winter there under a contract of her own - nine years, renewed on time. She read the Prophecy through, all the way, and found clause two, and read it out. She does not do the arithmetic for you, and does not see why she should. The elves simply tell you. Elder Faelan told the Forty-Eighth that the Forty-Seventh came off the ledge ten years ago, a lovely boy, and that the Committee will have told him it was a hundred. "It counts the way the Prophecy does. We count the way the sun does." And the Prophecy's own people do not notice either, because to them there is nothing to notice. The Tower is four thousand eight hundred years old. They have the paperwork. I wrote to Grimspite, after the Quest, to ask whether he had ever thought it strange that his Tower should be four thousand eight hundred years old in a world where the oldest dated thing in the Collegium is six hundred. He wrote back, in a very beautiful hand, that the Tower was four thousand eight hundred years old, that he had been there for all of it and would know, and that he had the paperwork, if I should like to see it. He has also corrected three of my dates in Volume Two, all of them correctly. I asked him, in the same letter, how old he was. He replied that he had held the post for four thousand eight hundred years, and that how old he had been when he took it was his own affair, and that he hoped I was keeping well. Reading the two together The rule I have used in this book is the one the world uses without meaning to. A date is a calendar year unless it comes from the Prophecy, the Tower or the Former Premises, and "N years ago" means two thousand less N, counted from the Quest. A span the Prophecy gives is in contract years, and should not be added to anything. Where the two disagree I have printed both. Where they agree, which is mostly in the first nine centuries, I have been grateful. See also Timeline The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones Frostwick Olde Evermore

title: The Thistle-pedia
text: The Thistle-pedia Being Volume Three of A Complete And Accurate History Of The Obligatory Quest , arranged alphabetically so that people will stop coming to my table to ask me things. The compiler, at work. The hand at the temple is thought. The ink on it is also thought, after a fashion. My name is Hosea Bellwether , and I am the historian of the Obligatory Quest. I am not the only historian of the Obligatory Quest - the Prophecy Committee of Thistlewick keeps minutes, and the minutes are very thorough about biscuits - but I am the only one who has ever gone and asked the people it happened to. I do my asking from a table of my own by the fire in the Slain Wyvern , in Nether Sopping , where the book lives. It needs a table of its own. You will understand why when you try to lift it. This is the third volume. Volume One was a pamphlet, and there is still a copy upstairs in the Wyvern for any guest who finds themselves short of something to read and long on time. Volume Two is downstairs and is the size of a door; it has been mistaken for one, twice, by people coming in out of the rain. This volume is the same history again, cut up into articles and put in order, with pictures, so that you may look up a turnip farmer, a goose or a clause of a contract without having to read the four hundred pages in between. The compiler I should say at the outset that I have never been on a quest. That is the qualification. Everybody else in the Slain Wyvern has been on one, and not one of them would tell a historian about it - they told me about the weather, and their knees, and what Thistlewick charges for a pint. So for a long while my great work was complete , in the sense that it had a beginning and an end and a great many chapters in the middle, and it was not accurate , in the sense that nobody in it had been consulted. Then, in the year 2000, a young man from Thistlewick came in out of the wet with a sword he did not seem entirely comfortable holding, and stood about. I wrote him down at once. Chapter Three Hundred and Twelve: The Forty-Eighth arrives, and stands about. It remains, I think, the most accurate sentence in the history, and he read it over my shoulder and did not dispute it. His name was Bram Thistle . He was the forty-eighth Chosen One of the Prophecy of Thistlewick , a turnip farmer by trade, and the Prophecy Committee had chosen him while he was asleep. I asked him to do the one thing I could not: to go round the room and be told . Six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end. He did. Nobody does. They get two and go and look at a dungeon. He got six, and came back, and I paid him handsomely for a man with ink on both hands, and I wrote him into the history in small type at the bottom of page four hundred and one. The footnote says that he listened. Nobody else has one. Then I told him to go north, and that I would leave the last page blank until I heard how it went, and that coming back to tell me was the fee. He came back. He paid. This book is what he paid for. That was two years ago, near enough, and in the two years since I have gone round again and asked everybody what became of them afterwards, which is a question nobody in the Slain Wyvern had ever been asked either. Their answers are at the end of their articles. The world, briefly It is a small world and a long one, and most of it is weather. * Thistlewick * is a village in the middle of it which believes, sincerely and on paper, that it is the middle of it. Every hundred years - or every hundred years as the Committee reckons them, which is a separate subject and has its own article - the Dark Lord rises in the Obligatory Tower to the north, and Thistlewick sends a Chosen One to put him down. It has worked forty-seven times. Thistlewick is extremely proud of this, and has never once asked why there is always a next time. * Nether Sopping *, where I am writing this, is a wet fishing town on the south coast, forty miles from Thistlewick and the better part of a world away. It is where Thistlewick's Chosen Ones go when they come back, under clause nineteen , which gives a returning hero a pension, a cottage and "such distance from the village as is mutually agreeable". The distance turns out to be forty miles, and the agreement turns out to be Thistlewick's. As a consequence every adventurer in the world who has finished adventuring has pooled down here, in one tavern, with their old companions, their old grudges and a stuffed wyvern over the mantel which is a goose. The north belongs to Upper Clanging , a town of engineers who have been trying for two hundred years to build a ship that flies to the Tower, and to the Long Field , where they keep the ones that did not. Further north still there is snow, and Frostwick , and a chapter house that has filed everything. The west has Great Dunnage , a city of guilds, and in the south-west the elves of Olde Evermore , who have been here longer than the calendar and are very nice about it. The east has a magical college and a village that was flooded in somebody's absence, and the south-east a great house whose portraits watch you. And above all of it, on a cloud, there is a castle that nobody has ever reached, with a caretaker in it, who has been waiting. There are, besides, a great many standing stones, wells, signposts, hermits, chests and old men who know things. I have tried to give each of them their due. Some of them have asked me not to. What happened What happened, to put it as shortly as I am able - and I am not, by temperament, able - is that the Forty-Eighth went north, as forty-seven had before him, and climbed the Tower, and met the Dark Lord, and found that the Dark Lord did not want to be there either. Grimspite the Inevitable had held the post for four thousand eight hundred years, by the Prophecy's own count, under a contract that renewed itself every time a hero beat him. He had been beaten forty-seven times, and every time it had counted as a renewal. The Prophecy, you see, was never a prophecy. It was an employment contract, and it had a clause twelve, and when the Forty-Eighth beat him the contract itself unrolled to enforce it. The Forty-Eighth beat that as well. You may read about it under The Obligatory Quest , and about clause twelve under The Prophecy of Thistlewick . Thistlewick struck clause twelve from its records afterwards and wrote in its place a note reading SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. Six months later, after a very long meeting, it struck clause nineteen as well. He did not go alone. He went with friends - a healer, a smith, a hedge mage, a shopkeeper, a knight, a bard, a brooding man, a naturalist, a guest star and, in the end, a boy from a boiler - though never with all of them at once, and which three of them climbed the last stair with him depends on whom you ask, and everybody I asked says it was them. I have given all of them articles. I have not adjudicated. A historian who adjudicates between a blacksmith and a knight about who was standing nearest the Dark Lord does not remain a historian for long. He becomes a footnote, in somebody else's book, in small type. How to use this book The volumes are these: Volume What is in it History The Prophecy and its clauses; the forty-eight Chosen Ones; the Quest of the Forty-Eighth; the two calendars and why they disagree; a timeline. People The Forty-Eighth and his companions; the Dark Lord; and the people of the towns, villages and holes in the ground. Places Every settlement, ruin, tower and tavern I have been able to visit, write to or hear about. Institutions The Prophecy Committee, the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional), the Hoyle Works, the Collegium Arcanum and other bodies with minutes. Bestiary The creatures of the road, with notes on which of them are what they say they are. Arms and Artefacts Swords, hats, benches and one crate, stencilled on all six faces. A Glossary of Cliches The well-worn conventions of the adventuring life, as the Forty-Eighth walked into very nearly all of them. Words in a different colour lead to other articles. Words in red lead to articles I have promised and not yet written; I am told this is normal in an encyclopedia and I find it a great comfort. The box at the top of the page will search the whole work, which is more than I can do with Volume Two. A word on accuracy Everything in this book is complete. Not all of it is accurate. Where my sources agree, I have said so. Where they disagree I have given both sides, or all eleven, and said which I believe and why, and you may believe the other. Where they cannot both be true - Merrow Halgate's account of the bridge and Councillor Dree's account of the chair, for instance, cannot both be true on a Tuesday - I have printed both, because that is what complete means. Where nobody knows, I have said that nobody knows, and then, being human, I have usually guessed, and marked the guess as mine. I have been asked by the Prophecy Committee to make clear that this work is not authorised by the Prophecy Committee. It is not. I have also been asked by the elves of Olde Evermore to make clear that the Third Age did not begin with the Prophecy. I asked them what it did begin with, and Elder Faelan said that it began with a great many things, and that the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. I have left it there. So, I think, should you. Acknowledgements To the regulars of the Slain Wyvern, who told me nothing for years and then told the Forty-Eighth everything in a fortnight. To Dorcas Thrupp, for the table. To the goose. To Piper Quill, who was also writing it all down, and whose version has more rhymes in it and fewer footnotes, and whom I consider a colleague and, in the matter of scansion, a rival. And to Bram Thistle, Chosen One Number Forty-Eight, who came back and told me how it went - all of it, in order, including the part about the tea - and so paid the fee. H. B. The Slain Wyvern, Nether Sopping The twenty-first of March, Third Age 2002, which Spare Cotterill has confirmed by letter is spring

title: Institutions
text: Institutions An institution is a group of people who have agreed to keep minutes. The world has a great many of them, and the minutes are where most of my evidence comes from, which is to say that my evidence is very thorough about biscuits. Institution Seat The Prophecy Committee Prophecy Hall, Thistlewick The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Nether Sopping The Hoyle Works Upper Clanging The Collegium Arcanum the east, since 1400

title: Bram Thistle
text: Bram Thistle For the expedition, see The Obligatory Quest . For the forty-seven before him, see The Chosen Ones . For the small brown thing in the turnip field named after him, see Bramus agricola . Bram Thistle Sat for, under protest Known as The Forty-Eighth; Chosen One No. 48; Bram Of Thistlewick , two fields from Prophecy Hall Trade Turnips Chosen Third Age 2000, in his sleep, by the Prophecy Committee, nobody objecting Equipment One hoe. One sword, off the wall Good at Everything, slightly Bad at Nothing, impressively Luck Statistically indefensible (see Bramus agricola ) Holds A receipt for one Dark Lord, renewable Status At home. SEE BRAM Bram Thistle is a turnip farmer of Thistlewick , and was the forty-eighth and last of the Chosen Ones . He was asleep when he was chosen, and so did not object, which the Prophecy Committee took as consent. He went north, as forty-seven had, and beat the Dark Lord, as forty-seven had, and then did the one thing none of them had done, which was to ask the Dark Lord a question and stay for the whole of the answer. He would like it known that he did none of it on his own. I have known him for two years and that is the only correction he has ever made to anything I have written about him, and he makes it every time. Early life The Thistles have farmed the same ground outside Thistlewick for as long as anybody has written anything down, which in Thistlewick is not long. His great-grandmother, Mabel Thistle, grew a turnip as big as a chair, and the family still speaks of it in the tone other families keep for a war. He lives with his mother, who keeps the house, irons his good shirt on a Tuesday, and on the morning of the Quest told him there were eleven people outside and one of them had a scroll. I record, because one version of events in circulation says otherwise, that his mother is alive, well, and has read that version. She asked me to put in that she makes a good pie. She does. There was a sword on the wall above the grate. It had been there, his mother said, a hundred years, waiting for exactly this, "and frankly it has been unbearable about it." I have tried to date the sword and cannot. A hundred years is what Thistlewick says about anything that has been anywhere for a while, and in Thistlewick that is not a measurement (see Two Reckonings ). It is back on the wall now, and is, I am told, quieter. The choosing The minutes of the meeting give his name under apologies for absence, with one goat. He was not consulted, because he was asleep, and he was not woken, because the Committee did not think it would make a difference, and it did not. Elder Wispel gave him the charge in Prophecy Hall , the parish gave him five hundred crowns and three potions, and a neighbour in the lane asked him who was going to do the west field. His own account of that morning, which I have had from him several times, is that he did not know what else to do, so he went. I have put this to forty-seven people who did the same and they all recognised it at once. The Quest The whole of it is under The Obligatory Quest, and the longer version is Volume Two. What distinguishes him from the forty-seven is not what he did - they all went north and did the sword - but the things he did that were not on the way: He went south. Nobody does. He came into the Slain Wyvern , sat down with a room full of people the Committee would rather he had not met, and listened to six of them to the end. I paid him for it, and he found out the wyvern is a goose. He asked. Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, told him what to ask at the top, and he asked it. He listened to the answer. All of it. Grimspite had been waiting four thousand eight hundred contract years for somebody to. He read the document. Out loud, in full, in the middle of a fight, because somebody he had just beaten told him to. It is the only recorded case of a Chosen One reading the Prophecy, and it was fatal to the Prophecy. He also, on the way, helped fly a ship, light a lighthouse, build a bench, stop a wreck, examine a goose, register with a Guild, name a beetle (it is not a beetle; I have been corrected), find a rhyme that does not exist, and walk into, by the account's own count, very nearly every cliche there is. He was certified fit to travel at about the point at which he had finished travelling. The account in Prophecy Hall also records how many turnips he ate on the road. I have the figure. He has asked me not to print it, on the grounds that it is nobody's business, and I agree. The question of companions The clause allowed him three at a time and he had eleven, in one combination or another, and so whatever you have heard about who was at the top of the Tower with him, somebody else has heard something different, and both of you heard it from the person concerned. Bram's own answer, when I asked him, was "all of them", which is not possible under the clause, and which he says is true anyway. The articles on each of them are listed below, and each says what they told me. Character He is not clever, and does not claim to be, and is the only person I have met who has had the whole Prophecy explained to him and understood it. He is polite to everybody, including the people who were about to kill him. He has a quantity of confidence that has never once been audited, and has never needed to be. He is, it must be said, very lucky; Miss Halloway has described his luck in print as "statistically indefensible", and he took it as a compliment, after some thought, because it was accurate. He does not like being written about. He comes south anyway, about once a month, to correct me. Afterwards The next morning there were still turnips. There was also a letter on the mat: clause nineteen, one quarter's pension, and the key to Ambrose Fitch 's old cottage at Nether Sopping , with the Committee's trust that Friday would suit. Friday did not suit. He stayed at home and farmed, and six months later the Committee struck clause nineteen, after a meeting of eleven hours. He kept the key. He uses the cottage when he comes south, which is about monthly, and every time he is in it he waters the pot on the sill, which has had something dead in it since Mr Fitch's day. Nothing has grown. I check. The Committee struck clause twelve as well, and wrote in its place SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to see him yet. The Committee has twice minuted that it might. It has also offered him a seat, which he declined, because it meets in planting time. His harvest of 2001 was the best in the parish. The Committee asked whether it had been prophesied. It had not. Once a year, on the day, he walks up to the top of the Obligatory Tower . The kettle is on. In Prophecy Hall, at the end of the Wall of the Forty-Seven, the forty-eighth frame is still empty, and the card in it still says PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. He is not at the coast. He is two fields away. Nobody has changed the card, and he has asked me not to tell them. See also The Obligatory Quest The Chosen Ones Grimspite the Inevitable Thistlewick

title: Corvin Ash
text: Corvin Ash For the village he is from, see Ashcombe . For the one under the lake, see Old Ashcombe . They are both Ashcombe. Corvin Ash Don't ask about the scar Known as The Brooding One; the Doomed Rival Of Ashcombe ; for eleven years, the corner of the Slain Wyvern Trade Rival of a great hero, according to a fortune-teller, for twopence Age Thirty-two Good at Dark damage, and more of it the worse things get Bad at Defence; luck; being told the school is very good Sword Black. Called Mind The Step Scarf Knitted by his mother. The wrong colour. Worn League table Second, the Sable Hart Destiny None whatsoever (Mother Selvidge, three readings) Corvin Ash sat in the corner of the Slain Wyvern from the age of nineteen, waiting for a destiny, for eleven years, which is longer than most careers. His village was destroyed by flooding, in his absence, and everyone was fine, and they moved eight miles inland, and there is a school now, and it is very good, and he could not make anybody understand. "...Leave," he told the Forty-Eighth. "This road ends in ash." Then he told him about the flood, and the school, and asked him not to look pleased, and went to get his coat. I sat across the room from him for most of those eleven years, at the table by the fire, and I want to put it on record at the start that he is not nothing, and never was. He is a genuinely dangerous man with a black sword who sat still for a decade because somebody once told him he was important. The sitting still was the only part of it that was ever a waste. Ashcombe He was born at Ashcombe , in a valley that is now a lake. In 1989, when he was nineteen and away from home, the water came up, and the village was flooded, and nobody was hurt, and the whole of it moved eight miles inland (eight miles by the road; the lake says less) and built itself again. He took the name Ash when it went under, as a memorial, after thinking about the gesture for some weeks. The village also kept the name, because it was its name and it was still using it, and so the new Ashcombe is Ashcombe too, and has a post office. You cannot mourn a place that is answering its correspondence. The new Ashcombe is proud of the flood. It has a plaque about it, which is upbeat, and a Drainage Museum, and an annual dinner. The fortune At a fair, the same year, a fortune-teller called Mother Selvidge told him, for twopence, that he was the rival of a great hero. He organised his entire adult life around it. He went and sat in the corner of the Slain Wyvern, which is where a great hero's rival goes, and waited for the hero, and the drinks there were, he points out, somewhat cheaper. On the Quest The hero came in at last, in 2000, and asked him along, and he said "If fate demands it", twice, the second time more loudly, so that it would be clear that fate had. He did dark damage, more of it the worse things went, which on the Quest was often. Ashcombe, new. He went home. Everyone was delighted to see him. His mother is fine, and has a new kitchen. His childhood bedroom was rebuilt, larger, with better light, and is a study. He was invited to speak at the Flood Dinner, and did, and it went well. He gave the village its name back. His mother knitted him a scarf in the wrong colour, and he wears it. Ashcombe, old. The lake is drawn down one week a year for the sluices, and if you are there that week you can walk into the old street. The party was. There is a pub sign, a doorstep, and, in a strongbox in what was the schoolroom, his own school report, which the schoolmistress had kept because she kept everybody's. It says that he will go far, if he ever gets up. On the doorstep, cut in by his grandfather in 1949, is the name of the black sword, which his grandfather made, as a doorstop: MIND THE STEP. That is its name. I am told by everybody who was there that this was the one moment in his story that was allowed to be simply sad, and that it lasted until somebody read out the report. The Sable Hart. There is an inn on the moor where doomed rivals brood professionally. Every corner is taken. There is a waiting list for the darkest, kept fairly, on a rota, and a newsletter. Corvin had been a member for years and had never attended, because attending would be admitting there was a category. There is a league table. He was low on it. He is second now, behind a scar. He has a chair in the middle of the room, in the light. He attends. Mother Selvidge. She is still working the fairs, and did not remember him, and read him again for twopence, and got a long life, a useful trade, and no destiny whatsoever. He asked her to do it again, and she did, and got the same. On the third reading she put the cards down and told him, kindly and without mystery, that she says the rival thing to about four young men a year, because it is the reading that makes them stand up straight, and that it has never once been wrong, in the sense that they all went and did something. She has read him three times. She has never once been wrong. The appraisal. He took the sword to Miss Fettle at the Smiths' Hall in Great Dunnage, expecting a curse. There is no curse. It is a very good sword in poor condition, and she was enthusiastic about the tang. He asked how much a curse would cost. It is not expensive. There is a form. He has the form, if he wants one. Afterwards He was asked back to the Flood Dinner in 2001, and went, and was early. He is up. He has the scarf, the chair at the Sable Hart, the form, which he has not filled in, and a long life and a useful trade still to come. He does not sit in the corner of the Slain Wyvern any more. When he comes in, which he does, he sits at a table in the middle, and on one occasion he sat at mine, and asked how the history was going, and listened to the end of the answer. He has asked me to remove the line about the drinks being cheaper. I have checked it, and they are, and I have left it in. See also Ashcombe The Sable Hart Mother Selvidge The Obligatory Quest

title: Grimspite the Inevitable
text: Grimspite the Inevitable For the contract, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . For the building, see The Obligatory Tower . For the forty-eight people who came up the stairs, see The Chosen Ones . Grimspite the Inevitable At the bookmark Known as The Dark Lord; Grimspite the Inevitable; latterly, Grimspite Of The top of the Obligatory Tower Post Dark Lord, under the Prophecy of Thistlewick, renewable Held Four thousand eight hundred years, by the contract Renewed Forty-seven times Appointed The same way the post was nearly filled in 2000 Age His own affair Hand Very beautiful Status Retired, 2000. Receipt issued Kettle On Grimspite the Inevitable was for four thousand eight hundred years, by the Prophecy's own count, the Dark Lord of the Obligatory Tower , against whom the village of Thistlewick sent forty-eight Chosen Ones. He did not want the job. It was an employment contract, and he could not get out of it, and every time a Chosen One beat him it renewed him before they reached the stairs. The forty-eighth asked him why he did not stop, and listened to the answer, and read the contract, and Grimspite has been retired since. He reads. He was reading when every one of the forty-eight came up the stairs, and he put the bookmark in every time. He is very tired and very polite, and he writes to me. The post The post of Dark Lord was held, before the Prophecy, at the castle on the cloud that its caretaker now calls the Former Premises , which no hero could ever reach. Grimspite has never been there. "I've read the file. The drains were a disgrace, and the east wing faced the wrong way." He holds, or held, the post at the Tower, under clause twelve of the Prophecy. Every hundred years, by the Committee's reckoning of a hundred years, a Chosen One came up the stairs, and he said, "So, you have come at last." He said it forty-seven times. "And I meant it the first time." They fought him and they won, and clause twelve renewed him. It is carved forty-seven times into the wall behind his throne: THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN. "It isn't a threat. It's a renewal notice." How he came to hold it in the first place he told the Forty-Eighth in four words, at the moment when the Prophecy had just declared the post vacant and congratulated the party on it. "That's how I got the job." I have not been able to find out any more than that, and I have tried, and I have been told by letter that he hopes I am keeping well. The forty-seven All forty-seven did the sword. Not one of them asked. Clause fourteen says the first meeting shall not go well, and it never did: Merrow Halgate's party of twenty fought him at the bridge and lost, as was written down in advance, and he tells me that halfway through, Grimspite stopped, and apologised, and then carried on. Nobody ever believes him about that part. I do. One of them, Halbert Quy, the Forty-Fifth, was offered a cup of tea, and declined it, because he thought it was a trick, and has thought about it ever since. Grimspite has wondered too. None of them died, at the top. "Forty-seven of them, and they all won. Do you know how that looks, to the forty-eighth?" He has four skeletons up there, in plaster, for the look of the thing. One of them has an extra foot, because there was a foot over and it seemed a shame. The forty-eighth "Forty-eight," he said. "Right on time. Sit down. No? Fine. Standing is traditional." The Forty-Eighth asked him why he did not stop. He said: "Ah. The clever one. They're rarer than you'd think. I can't." He showed them the wall. He asked who had told Bram to ask, and when he heard it was Halbert he asked him to go back and tell Halbert that the tea had just been tea, and to listen to all of it, because he would like, once, for somebody to have listened to the whole of it. Bram did. He answered the other questions he was brought. Clause seven requires a Chosen One to go on foot, "because a thing that flies over and drops something is not a story. It is a Tuesday." He was of the view that Miss Hoyle of Upper Clanging would never get one off the ground in sight of his tower. Asked, on her behalf, what the Tower is made of, he said that nobody had ever asked him that, that he did not know, and that he had leaned on that wall every day for four thousand years and never once wondered. "Tell her the work was good." When ITEM 1 was set down in front of his throne, it smoked, and knocked the bookmark on to the floor, and did nothing else, because of clause thirty-one. He looked at it for some time. "That is the first new thing in four thousand eight hundred years, and I would like a moment with it. Whoever made that has never once been told that it was any good." Then they fought, because that is the part they were for, and at the end of it he went down on one knee and said, "...Thank you." The rest is under The Obligatory Quest. It was his idea to read the thing. "Four thousand eight hundred years, and it was an admin problem." He signed the Forty-Eighth a receipt for one Dark Lord, renewable, and sent him home with a message: "There isn't a forty-nine." The top of the Tower The room at the top is furnished in the traditional manner, and he will tell you about every piece of it, which nobody did before the ending because nobody stayed. The tablet over the door was a present from the Prophecy, in the year one, and was the only joke it ever made. The two statues are of an aunt, who sat for both and would not stop talking, and did not like either of them, "and you don't throw away an aunt". One mirror is late, because of the altitude. The other shows where you would rather be, and he has put his name down for a bungalow. There are two seeing-orbs, which are very old and very heavy and show only each other. Afterwards He is retired. He stays in the Tower, in his chair, with a kettle and the book at the bookmark. He is still on the same book. The forty-eighth carving will not be needed. He receives visitors and has about one a month, most of them people who would like to see the chair. Bram comes up once a year, on the day, and the kettle is on. Halbert Quy, told all of it, said no to the tea as well. "It's all right. The kettle's always on now." Mr Quy sends his regards up the hill. He writes to me, in a very beautiful hand, about my dates. He has corrected three of them in Volume Two, all of them correctly. I asked him how old he is. He said he had held the post for four thousand eight hundred years, and that how old he had been when he took it was his own affair. I have sent him this article for his corrections. He returned it with none, and a note: that it was very fair, that the east wing still faced the wrong way, and that if I should ever be passing there was a kettle. I have not yet been passing. I am a historian, and I do not climb things. But I have begun to think about it. See also The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones Bram Thistle Halbert Quy The Obligatory Tower

title: Hob Grumnir
text: Hob Grumnir For the hammer, see below; she does not have an article, and has said she would not want one. Hob Grumnir Listening to Beatrice Known as Grumnir the Smith Of The forge, Thistlewick Trade Blacksmith, third of that forge Trained by His aunt, Beatrice Grumnir, from the age of nine Hammers Several. Two named. One talks back Good at Taking a hit; giving one, very large, once Bad at Speed, magic, being subtle Pricing "Take it" Invoicing A shelf Rival Bryd Ollerenshaw, of Upper Clanging Hob Grumnir is the blacksmith of Thistlewick , third of that forge, and an enormous man who talks to his hammers. Two of the hammers have names. One of them, he insists, talks back. She is called Beatrice , and she joined the Forty-Eighth's company on the same morning he did, because, as he explained, "Beatrice comes. I come with Beatrice. That's the arrangement and it's not up for discussion, mainly because she'd win." The forge Hob learned the trade from his aunt, Beatrice Grumnir, who was born in 1919, kept the Thistlewick forge for most of the century, and died in 1989. By every account in the village she was right about everything and never once said anything anybody wanted to hear. Her headstone is in the churchyard. It now has a good gate in front of it.
