He has made a very great many things and owns almost none of them, because when somebody needs a thing he makes it and says "take it", and the record of what is owed is a shelf. Half the village has something of his. When he asked for a few things back, for a competition, every one of them was glad to see him and none of them would give it up, and each of them had a better reason than the last, and he said that was fair. Beatrice Beatrice is a hammer. I want to be precise about this, because I am a historian. She is a forging hammer of the ordinary kind, well used and well kept, and she is right about everything. She told him the Forty-Seventh had come in for a sword, and got a good one, and it had not helped. She told him a sword is no good on its own, and that somebody has to swing it who knows what breaks. When the company was full she said that was a shame; "Beatrice says a lot of things." She said nothing for a fortnight once, which Hob said was not sulking, because hammers do not sulk; it was her being professional about it. I asked in the village about Beatrice, and everybody I asked told me the same thing, which is that Beatrice was always right. Nobody in Thistlewick has ever said anything more than that, and nor shall I. On the Quest The Assize of Hammers. The Worshipful Company of Smiths at Great Dunnage judges work every three years, and Hob had never entered, having nothing he owned to enter. In 2000 he entered Beatrice, who is not his work. She was disqualified under clause one. The Wardens' notes, which I have seen, say that she is right about everything. He was entirely satisfied. The gate. Beatrice went quiet, and he admitted at last that the last thing she had told him to do, eleven years before, was make a marker, and that he had never been able to get the words right. He made three markers, each one magnificent, and rejected all three ("It's right. It's not her."), and then made the churchyard a gate with a good latch, because the old one stuck and she would have hated the fuss. Beatrice began talking again on the walk home, and said the latch wants a spring. The Sky Anvil. A thing fell out of the sky into Elias Meech's top field in 1749 and has been a gatepost since. Mr Meech would not sell it, it being a very good gatepost, but he would swap it for a gate, and Hob had lately become good at gates. The star-iron made exactly one sword. Hob has not said who it is for. The anvil. His own anvil was stolen, once, by two apprentice bandits on the six-week syllabus. They got it eleven feet, in the dark. He was angry for nine seconds and then impressed. Their apology is framed in the smithy, next to nothing he made. The sword at the door. Roland Fairweather's sword, which Roland left at the tower door, has a maker's mark on it. Hob looked at it for some time. "That's my aunt's. She made this here. On this. Forty years back, near enough. Sold it to a man going south." And then: "She did good work." Beatrice, on that occasion, said nothing at all. He later put a Thistlewick haft on it, so that it would swing for a Thistlewick hand. "Still hers. Handle's mine." Bryd Ollerenshaw Bryd Ollerenshaw , of Ollerenshaw's at Upper Clanging, was apprenticed alongside him, and they have been rivals ever since. She won Best in Hall at the Smiths' Hall in 1987, the year he did not enter, having a cold. They met again in 2000, and went for a drink, and are still arguing about rivets. Later the same year they made the tube plate for the Two Hundred's refit at Ollerenshaw's, in one heat, by four hands, which neither of them has mentioned since. Miss Hoyle says it will do. One of the Cotterill children says they do this every time. I record that they are rivals. Both of them have read this sentence and both of them asked me to leave it exactly as it is. Afterwards He is at the forge. The churchyard gate swings well, and the latch has a spring now. He still has not said who the star-iron sword is for. I have a theory, and I am not allowed to print it. In 2001 he and Bryd Ollerenshaw sat as joint judges of the Smiths' Hall prize at Great Dunnage, and disagreed for nine hours. The prize was awarded. Neither of them will say to whom. I read this article to him at the forge. He listened to all of it and said it was fair. Then he said that Beatrice says I have spelled Ollerenshaw right and the rest of it is soft. I have let it stand. See also Bryd Ollerenshaw The Worshipful Company of Smiths Roland Fairweather The Sky Anvil

title: Hosea Bellwether
text: Hosea Bellwether This article is about the compiler of this volume, and was written by him, against his judgement, on the advice of everybody else. For his work, see the front page . Hosea Bellwether With ink hands Known as The historian at the table by the fire Of Nether Sopping , the Slain Wyvern , the table by the fire Trade Historian Work A Complete And Accurate History Of The Obligatory Quest , three volumes Complete Going well Accurate The problem Quests undertaken None Things climbed None Footnotes awarded One Hosea Bellwether is a historian of Nether Sopping , and the compiler of A Complete And Accurate History Of The Obligatory Quest , of which this is the third volume. Complete is going well. Accurate is the problem. He has never been on a quest, and has written about little else. I did not want to write this article. An encyclopedia that leaves its compiler out is, I was told by everyone I asked, inaccurate, and they were right, and I have done it, in the third person where I could bear to and the first where I could not. Nether Sopping He is a Nether Sopping man, which is to say that he counts in plain years, sixty and forty and thirty, and that he lives forty miles from Thistlewick , among the people Thistlewick sent there. Clause nineteen of the Prophecy sends a returning Chosen One to a cottage at a mutually agreeable distance, and the distance has been Nether Sopping for most of a century, and Nether Sopping is consequently the only place in the world where everybody in the bar has been to the top of the Obligatory Tower except the historian. I have sat at the table by the fire in the Slain Wyvern for most of my working life, under the goose, as it now is, with ink on my hands, listening. I have had a great many stories. I have had very few of them to the end. Volume Two Volume Two, the history proper, was compiled at that table, from first-hand accounts. Everybody in the room had been on one, and not one of them would tell a historian. They told the Forty-Eighth. He was going north; he was in it. So I asked him to do the thing I could not, and go round the room and be told: six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end, and then come back. I paid, handsomely, for a man with ink hands. Nobody does it. They get two and go and look at a dungeon. He did all six. They came from Ysolde Marrow, Hulda Bole, Nabb, Merrow Halgate, Councillor Dree, and the young lady with the tiara, who is going to work it out any day now, and it will be marvellous. With those, the history was complete. It is not accurate, because Merrow's bridge and Dree's chair cannot both be true on a Tuesday, but it is complete. It runs to four hundred pages and a pamphlet. At the bottom of page four hundred and one, in small type, there is a footnote that says the Forty-Eighth listened. Nobody else has one of those. I left the last page blank, until I heard how it went, and told him that hearing it was the fee. He came back, after the Tower and after Halbert Quy, and told me, and I filled it. The account in Prophecy Hall says that I wrote a song. I did not. I have dealt with this elsewhere, and calmly. Volume Three This is Volume Three. It is the encyclopedia: every person, place, institution, creature, artefact and cliche of the Quest, in order, with the cross-references the history could not hold. It is signed on the twenty-first of March, Third Age 2002, which is two years after the Quest and the first day of spring, as Spare Cotterill has confirmed by letter. I have not written all of it. Where somebody knew a thing better than I did, I asked them to write it, and printed what they sent me whole, with my notes in the margin: the Bestiary is Miss Halloway's, the technical articles are Miss Hoyle's, the songs are Miss Quill's, and there are letters from the top of the Tower which have been the greatest pleasure of the work. Method I believe what I am told, and then I write down who told me. Where two accounts disagree I print both. Where the Committee's account and the calendar disagree I print both, and say which is which (see Two Reckonings ). Where a matter is none of my business I have tried to say so, and to leave it there, and I have not always managed the second part. Where I do not know a thing I have said so, which in a history is more honest than it looks and in an encyclopedia is rarer than it should be. Afterwards The last page of Volume Two is filled. Volume Three is this. Bram Thistle comes south about once a month, to correct me, and is always right, and always about the same thing. Miss Quill and I meet at the Wyvern to disagree. Spare Cotterill writes. Grimspite writes. I have had a kind letter from Miss Pargeter of Frostwick, pointing out a clause. I am told that I am in Miss Quill's notebooks, at some length, in the third person. I have asked to see the verses and been told that I may when they are finished, and that she has been finishing them since the Quest, and that they will scan. It has been suggested to me, more than once and by a dark lord, that a historian of the Obligatory Quest ought one day to climb the Obligatory Tower. I have said that I do not climb things. I have also, this winter, bought a pair of boots. See also The front page The Obligatory Quest The Slain Wyvern Piper Quill

title: People
text: People A great many people have been on the Obligatory Quest, and a great many more have stood beside the road while it went past. This volume holds the ones who did something about it - which in practice means the ones who talked to me, or to the Forty-Eighth, which is the same thing at one remove. The Forty-Eighth and his company Bram Thistle Merribell Hob Grumnir Zephyrine Vance Nix Sir Aldric Piper Quill Corvin Ash Wren Halloway Roland Fairweather Spare Cotterill The other party to the contract Grimspite the Inevitable , the Dark Lord, retired Everybody else The people of the towns are being written up a town at a time, and are listed here as each town is done. Hosea Bellwether , the compiler, who was persuaded that leaving himself out would be inaccurate

title: Merribell
text: Merribell For her order, see The Order of Whatever Works . For the meeting she spoke at, see The Healers' Table . Sister Merribell She would like to know when you last drank water Known as Sister Merribell; the Sister of Whatever Works Of Thistlewick , at the chapel Trade Village healer; field medic Order The Order of Whatever Works, the only member for eleven miles Trained The Sisterhouse at Weeping Bottom , until it began holding symposia Age Twenty-eight Good at Healing, reviving, Light Bad at Hitting things Carries The basin Patients lost None Merribell is the healer of Thistlewick , a Sister of the Order of Whatever Works , and the first person to join the Forty-Eighth, on the grounds that he had not had a glass of water since Tuesday. Her order holds that theology is a distraction from the actual problem, which is usually that you have not had any water today. She has never lost a patient. "Sit down. When did you last drink water?" is how she meets everybody, and it was how she met Bram. He gave an answer. "That wasn't the question," she said. "Water. When." The Order The Order of Whatever Works has a founding document, which is a pamphlet, and a Rule of Life four lines long, one of them about socks. It does not have a doctrine and does not want one. Merribell trained at the mother house at Weeping Bottom , a wet valley chosen by a founder who believed the damp was good for the chest, and left at twenty-two, in 1996, because the Sisterhouse had begun holding symposia. She keeps the most complete medical record in the county: every ailment of every soul in Thistlewick, dated, in a good hand. The Prophecy Committee has never once asked to see it, preferring the Prophecy. Manner She is a professional, and professionals have a vocabulary. She says the anatomical words the way other people say "elbow", plainly and at the volume needed to be heard over a fight, and the party learned early to look at the ceiling. "Where does it hurt? Be specific. 'Down there' is four separate systems and I will guess wrong." When Bram said ankle, she said, "Oh, thank goodness." She carries a basin. She brought it unasked. "Nobody has ever won an argument with me about hydration and I am not starting a losing streak on a Thursday." On the Quest Of all the things done on the road, three were hers, and the Prophecy's own account records each of them. Fit to travel. Clause eleven of the Prophecy requires a Chosen One to be certified fit before departure. It had been done forty-seven times. The Forty-Eighth's form was blank, because he had been asleep. She found the form on a pad at Upper Clanging and did it properly: stamped scales from the fish stall at Nether Sopping, the light of the lighthouse at Saint Bother's, lit, a clean surface, and a witness, from among the company. It is, the account says, the first properly documented attempt in four thousand years. I have interviewed several of the witnesses and they all looked at the ceiling. The Sisterhouse. The mother house had split between the Order of Whatever Works and the Order of What Ought To Work, which wins every argument and loses patients, and the two agreed to settle it the way this world settles things, with a ward and a queue. Merribell asked the patients whether they had eaten. Whatever Works won on points, nineteen to one, in an afternoon. Sister Bewick, of the other order, has since been examined on Whatever Works' doctrine, and passed. It is four lines long. The curse of Sump. The village of Sump had been cursed since 1794, with headaches, poor sleep and a general sense that things used to be better. She diagnosed it in nine seconds. There were wasps in the well and nobody had had any water for two hundred years. The curse was lifted by the Water Committee, one member, with a glass of water, and the minutes record an item three. She also called on Tobias Frayne , who had been revived by passing adventurers eleven times, and declined to make it twelve. "There is nothing wrong with you, Mr Frayne. That's the trouble." She prescribed having the parish to tea, through the door, on purpose. He has not died since. The Healers' Table Every surviving party medic within forty miles meets once a year in the back room of the Slain Wyvern, under the chair of Mrs Ysolde Marrow , to compare the worst thing they ever had to improvise. Merribell was invited in the year of the Quest, the youngest at the Table by thirty-eight years, and asked to speak, and had nothing. "I've never lost anybody," she told them. "I know what that means. It isn't a virtue. It's an average." The room did not console her and did not laugh. Mrs Marrow told her to write it down, all of it, now, while she still thinks it is boring. She said, "Yes, Mrs Marrow." I was in the bar, and the door was not quite shut, and I have written down only what she has since said I may. Merribell has read this article and has one correction, which is that I should drink more water. I have noted it. Afterwards She spoke at the Healers' Table in 2001, as the account said she would. She spoke for eleven minutes, which is the shortest address in the Table's history, and the Table minuted it as the most useful. The subject was water. She is still Thistlewick's healer, still the only member of her order for eleven miles, and still has not lost anybody. She is writing it down. See also The Order of Whatever Works Weeping Bottom Ysolde Marrow The Obligatory Quest

title: Nix
text: Nix For the shop, see Nix's Emporium . For the provenance of particular items, see the notes in Arms and Artefacts , which are hers. Nix She did not take it Known as Nix; Acquisitions Of The back room of the general store, Thistlewick Trade Locating things, ahead of schedule On behalf of The party of the second part Ledger kept since 1989, at fifteen Age Twenty-eight. The parcel said not to open it until twenty-six Good at Speed, not being hit, several small hits, finding things in other people's pockets Bad at Taking a hit Opened The Obligatory Tower, without the key; the Counting House at Great Dunnage, without the form Coat Fits Nix runs the back room of the general store in Thistlewick . She does not steal things. She locates them, ahead of schedule, on behalf of a client who has not yet been identified. "Everyone asks eventually," she told the Forty-Eighth, before he had asked. "I like to get ahead of it. Same as everything else." She is not a thief, and the distinction is not a joke to her, and I have come round to her view of it. Every single thing in the back room was got somehow, and she can tell you how, from the ledger, by date, and the telling is always in order and is sometimes magnificent. The ledger At fifteen, in 1989, Nix worked out that "I wanted it" was not a sentence that got you anywhere in a village where everybody knows your mother, and opened a ledger instead. Every item in, every item out, every provenance, dated, in a hand that improves visibly from page to page. All of it was done on behalf of a client described in the front of the book as the party of the second part. I have been allowed to read the ledger, at the counter, with her watching. It is the most honest document in the county. The Committee's minutes are longer and the Prophecy is older, and neither of them can account for a single teaspoon. On the Quest She joined because the Tower was "a tower nobody's been inside for a hundred years, full of things nobody's counted". She had her coat on before he finished the sentence. Her terms were that three is a good number: "Small, quiet, splits four ways." The tower door. The door of the Obligatory Tower was barred. There is a key under the mat. She did not use it. "Bar's on the inside. Classic." Returned. In the front of the ledger, where the hand is worst, were eleven things she had never sold on: the longest loans she had. Bram's mother's pie dish, the Old Man's chair, the gate key, Hulda Bole's good boots, a cradle for Bessie Marsden at Upper Clanging, and six more, across three towns. "Everything's a loan, eventually. That's what the RETURNED column is for." The column had been ruled, very neatly, down eleven years of pages, and there was nothing in it. She returned all eleven in an afternoon that was not one afternoon. None of the owners had known the things were gone, every one of them was pleased to have them back, and two of them tried to pay. The ledger has a RETURNED column now, with eleven lines in it, and a double line under the last, blotted. The client. On the clean page after it, the first new entry was a parcel, brown paper, which Mrs Bole had been carrying for somebody since 1989, marked NOT TO BE OPENED UNTIL I AM TWENTY-SIX. The hand on it was Nix's own, at fifteen. Inside was a letter from the party of the second part, signed N., aged fifteen. The client, it said, wanted one thing, which was the first entry in the book, the only line in eleven years with no provenance, which was in bond at Great Dunnage , and which she had been avoiding. "Stop it." It was her gran's coat. It had gone down to her ankles. She would not wear it until it fitted, and would not sell it, so at fifteen she put it into the Bonded Warehouse, stood on a crate, and made a speech to the wharfinger, Mr Tibbs: I shall return for it when I am somebody. He wrote it in the margin. The rent came by post every quarter for eleven years, never late, no name, and she never went back, because he would have remembered the speech. He had. He unlocked the wardrobe. She put it on, and it fits. The first line of the ledger has a provenance now. Professional courtesy. Cobb Lorrimer steals things, says so, and wears a hood about it, and finds her whole vocabulary an insult. He challenged her to a contest: a list, an afternoon, and a client. She won on paperwork, having got everything on the list with permission. He has since taken a position in Nether Sopping, afternoons, signed for, in which he plays the Dark Lord for the children, and loses. The Counting House. Great Dunnage sealed its counting house in 1788, when the key was lost, and the Corporation wanted it opened by a licensed person, on Form L. She opened it in nine seconds while the Mayor was still reading the preamble. It held one chair and a note: WE SPENT IT. Form L remains blank. Half an encounter. She has a way of moving through a wood at night that halves the number of things that notice you. In 2000 the Works Band at Upper Clanging needed Mr Enoch Bagshawe, and his bassoon, brought through the Gloamwood by night without a single fight. He was brought through without one, or half of one. The Works Band has a bassoon. Afterwards The back room is open. The ledger is into its second volume, which began on the page after the coat, and its first entries are already in a better hand than the last of the old one. The party of the second part has been identified, and the book is still kept on her behalf. I asked Nix whether that made any difference. She said it made the paperwork simpler, and that she had always liked to be ahead of things, and that she had now been beaten to it once, by a girl of fifteen, and did not intend it to happen again. I have checked my pockets after every interview. Nothing has ever been missing. On one occasion there was something extra, a pencil, rather better than mine, with a note on it in a good hand: located. on behalf of the party of the second part. See also Nix's Emporium The Bonded Warehouse Cobb Lorrimer The Obligatory Quest

title: Piper Quill
text: Piper Quill For her family's work, see The Quills . For her songs, see From the Notebooks of P. Quill . Piper Quill Mid-verse Known as Piper Quill, Chronicler Of Thistlewick , usually on a table Trade Bard; chronicler, unofficial Family The Quills, official chroniclers for four generations House style Never let the truth spoil the metre Her style Writes down what actually happened Age Twenty-six Good at Making everybody else better; making everybody else worse Bad at Raw numbers Prizes Second, the Contest at the Sign of the Bell, 2000 Rhymes for turnip None Piper Quill is a bard who narrates events as they happen, in the third person, at volume, whether or not this is convenient. She is a Quill, of the family that has written the official chronicles of Thistlewick for four generations, and she is the first of them to write down what actually happened, which is why at twenty-four she was standing on a table in the Gilded Turnip instead of being paid. She went north with the Forty-Eighth and wrote all of it down. "Piper Quill. Chronicler. I do the songs. You do the sword bit. It's a good system." She is my colleague, and my rival, and she has read this article, and she says it scans in places, which from a Quill is high praise and I am going to keep it. The Quills The text under all forty-seven portraits on the Wall of the Forty-Seven in Prophecy Hall was written by somebody in her family. Her grandmother did numbers forty to forty-three, and is quoted in the Prophecy's own preamble. The house style is one line long: never let the truth spoil the metre. Piper's entire professional rebellion has been to let it. Her aunt, Ambrosine Quill, is the senior chronicler now, and is an extremely good writer. I have reason to know. On the Quest She joined in the Gilded Turnip, mid-verse: 'And lo, the Chosen One drew near, smelling faintly of turnip, and the tavern fell silent -' and immediately needed a rhyme for turnip, and said she would get one on the road. She always does. She did not, because there isn't one, and that, as it turned out, was the point. A rhyme for turnip. In the Gilded Turnip, which is named after the problem, the whole company sat down one afternoon and offered her rhymes. Hob offered burnip, without embarrassment. Zephyrine offered a slant rhyme with sherbet, which the Collegium would accept. Wren ruled everything ending in -nip inadmissible, pre-emptively, on the grounds that it is a genus. Sir Aldric offered the word for turnip in the old tongue of his house, which rhymes beautifully with nothing, in his tongue or anybody's. Corvin's scanned perfectly, and was about drowning. Merribell went looking for something anatomical, right down to the feet, and found nothing. Nix located one, ahead of schedule, on behalf of a client, and it was turnip. Bram offered a parsnip, and was told it is a different vegetable. There is no rhyme for turnip, and any competent poet would have changed the other line in the first week, which she then did, in nine seconds, moving the turnip into the middle of a line where nothing has to rhyme with it. "It was always going to be the last verse. I just had the lines the wrong way round." Everybody who had spent the afternoon on it was furious. She has asked for the nine seconds on her headstone. The verse is quoted under The Obligatory Quest. The Contest at the Sign of the Bell. A bardic competition at Great Dunnage , with categories nobody can defend and a panel of three judges, one of whom cannot hear. She lost, by one point, to a man who does birdcalls. The birdcalls are, in fairness, extraordinary; his thrush in particular. She has framed the certificate. It is the first prize a Quill has ever won for writing down what actually happened. The official account. Ambrosine had already written the official account of the Forty-Eighth before he left, because the shape is known. It is properly metred, it has a good middle, Bram is an orphan in it, Merribell dies, and there is a bit with a wolf. Piper and the Forty-Eighth went to see it. What came of that is the subject of a disagreement among the Quills that I have been asked, by all of them, not to settle, and I am not going to. There is, depending on whom you ask, one official account or two, and if there is one it has a footnote by P. Quill, and if there are two the second has a goat in it, and the goat is in the minutes. The struck verses. The Committee strikes any verse it cannot have read aloud at the fete. Of course it keeps them, in a box, in Prophecy Hall. With the party's help Piper got into the box, and has read every verse in it, and printed none. The number of them is in the account, and is larger than the Committee would like. One of them, verse forty-one, is about a cat, and she showed it to the Forty-Eighth, and only that one; I have it from him that it scans. Verse seven was struck before the Quest began, and she has never told anybody what is in it. She has not told me. The elegy On the road at Little Gore there was a card nailed to the back of the fingerpost: WANTED: AN ELEGY. For Abel Thrush, carrier, who walked the road between Little Gore, Fenmarch and Sump every day for fifty years, from 1941 until he died, in the spring of 1991, and never had one. Something with a bit of a tune. She had never met him. She asked eleven people, and every one of them described a different man, and she wrote it out of the contradictions rather than choosing between them. She did not stand on anything. She did not read it out. She pinned it to the post, under the Fenmarch arm, and stepped back. It is still there, under a little roof that somebody has made for it, and people stop and read it on their way past, and with her leave I print it whole. ABEL THRUSH, CARRIER. LITTLE GORE - FENMARCH - SUMP. He never spoke a word. He never stopped. He came in at the gate. He climbed the wall. He read no letter, and he knew them all. He carried a cow, and wept over a bird. He brought the water nobody would drink, and stopped for tea, and was at eight each day where somebody looked up to see him wave. Eleven people knew him. All are true. The road is four miles long. He walks it still. P. Quill, the fingerpost at Little Gore Mrs Vane, of Little Gore, read it twice, and said that it was him, all of him, and that every one of them was in it. Then she said they had wondered whether it might have a bit more of a tune. Piper laughed, out loud, about her own work, which nobody had heard her do before. "Next time." Afterwards She is still writing it down. The ballad is finished. The elegy is on the post. The notebooks are, I am told, into double figures, and I am also told I am in them, at some length, in the third person, and not always in the metre I would have chosen. We are colleagues. We are rivals. She says my history is complete and not accurate, and I say her songs are accurate and do not scan, and we are both right, and we meet at the Slain Wyvern about once a month to compare notes and disagree about all of them. Some of her work is printed in this volume by her permission; see From the Notebooks of P. Quill . I have asked her what is in verse seven every time we have met. She has said, every time, that it is very good. I believe her. See also Ambrosine Quill From the Notebooks of P. Quill Little Gore The Obligatory Quest

title: Roland Fairweather
text: Roland Fairweather For the door he left at, see The Obligatory Tower . For his understudy, see Maud Penhallow . Roland Fairweather Very sorry. Always very sorry Known as The Guest Star Of A table by the fire in the Slain Wyvern, between engagements Trade Being extremely good at this Since The age of eleven (the Wyrm of Ickworth, 1977) Age Thirty-six Good at Everything, genuinely Bad at Being there at the end Parties left at a door Eleven Prophecy His own, in preparation from 1978; discharged 2000, in an afternoon Review meetings attended One hundred and forty-one Sword Left at the door. Made in Thistlewick Roland Fairweather is the finest swordsman of his generation, magnificent, glowing and extremely good at everything, and for most of his life the protagonist of a much more expensive story than the one he was in. He joined the Forty-Eighth in the Slain Wyvern , carried more than his share all the way north, liked everybody, and left at the door of the Obligatory Tower , as he had warned them he would, and gave them his sword. He warned them in the first minute. "I have three things to tell you and you will only like two of them. One: I am extremely good at this. Genuinely. Embarrassingly. Two: I will come with you gladly, for nothing, and I will carry more than my share, and I will like you. Three: I cannot be there at the end." The doors He has been doing this since he was eleven, when he was page to Dame Florence Ickworth against the Wyrm of Ickworth, in 1977, and could already disarm her. He left at the wyrm's door. They had sent for him. Dame Florence and the others did the wyrm themselves. It happened at every door after that. He would turn up, help, and be called away before the last room. "It isn't cowardice. It isn't a curse. It's the shape of the thing." He tried to stay, very hard, twice. The Forty-Eighth's was the eleventh, and it happened at the tower door, in front of the whole party: "I have to be somewhere. I don't know where. I never know where. I only ever know that it is not here, and that it is now, and that I am going. ... Take it up there. It is a very good sword and it has never been in a last room. Neither have I. One of us should manage it." He is the only member of the company who does not tell me he was at the top of the Tower. He was not. The appointment What he was called away to, every time, was a review meeting. Roland Fairweather has a prophecy of his own. It is a proper one, with a lineage, a sword in a stone, a sorcerer and a Worm, and in 1978 he was told it was nearly ready. A committee of four has met about it ever since, in the snug of the Bell at Great Dunnage , under a Convenor, and at every meeting it has gone through readiness - the stone, the sword, the sorcerer, the lineage - and found it still not ready, and noted his continued availability, and thanked him for his patience. A meeting takes eleven minutes. When the party followed him to one, it was the hundred and forty-first. "Mr Fairweather. Good. We're quorate." Whenever somebody else's story came to its last door, the committee sent for him, to check that he was still available, because he was the asset, and the asset must be accounted for. I have read a set of the minutes. They are dry and they are devastating, and I have nothing to add to them. His own quest The prophecy named a thing in a place: a Worm, under Carn Drey, east of Great Dunnage, with a stone. The party went, with him, and did it. The thing had been scaled for a hero of nineteen, and he was thirty-four, and it took an afternoon, and it was over before Piper Quill had got a verse out. "That's it. That was it. Twenty-two years." He asked them, carefully, and without much hope, whether they would mind being surprised. Only a little. Everybody was. I have it from everybody who was there that it was kind, and was not sad, and should be told completely straight, and I have tried to. The sword The sword he left at the tower door has a maker's mark on it, and Hob Grumnir knew it. It was made in the Thistlewick forge in 1960 by Beatrice Grumnir, Hob's aunt, and sold to a man going south, and it had travelled, and come back. "I leave it at a door," Roland says. "Every time. And every time, somehow, it finds its way back to me." Hob put a Thistlewick haft on it. It went into the last room after all, in a Thistlewick hand. The alumni The parties he had left at their doors held a dinner, at the Slain Wyvern, organised by Dame Florence. Every one of them had finished its quest without him, and said so, warmly, and every one of them had thought of him as their Roland, and found that there were ten other tables. It was a wholly happy room. Nobody said the word. It ended in a toast: to the man who got them all to the door. The understudy Maud Penhallow had been in Fellow Blunt's yard at Great Dunnage since she was nine, learning sword, horse, lineage and how he stands, as his understudy, in case the prophecy was ready and he was unavailable. Nobody had told her about the meetings. He told her. She took it well, and thought about it, and asked a question none of the grown-ups had thought of in twenty-two years. I have it. I am not going to print it. Nobody has answered it. When the party went up the Tower, she waited at the door. "Somebody ought to see the end of one." Afterwards The prophecy is discharged. He was rehired after the ending, from his table, and went back up the Tower with the party, and was not called away, and asked what the bit after is like. "Finished? Marvellous. I've never been in the bit after. Is it nice?" Miss Penhallow came and told him how the Quest had ended, all of it, in order. Since then he has finished two further things, which he has not told me about, but which he keeps on a list, and shows people. He is still asked to leave at doors, out of habit, by committees. He mostly does not. I asked him whether he minds that he was not at the top. He said that he had been at eleven doors and the bit after, and that the Forty-Eighth had been at the top, and that between them they had very nearly the whole of one, which is more than most people get. Then he asked me how my history ended. I told him I would let him know. See also Maud Penhallow Hob Grumnir Carn Drey The Obligatory Quest

title: Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III
text: Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III For the family seat, see Fenmarch Hall . For his order, see The Order of the Errant . For his horse, see below; she is doing very well. Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III Slightly behind you at all times Known as Sir Aldric; Pemberton-Gore the Third Of Fenmarch Hall , which is small, moated and damp; latterly Thistlewick , which he was trying to leave Rank Knight Errant, At Large Arms A knight rampant regardant Age Forty-eight Good at Defence; standing in front of whoever is bleeding; encouraging everybody Bad at Damage, speed, gates Horse Duchess, a grey mare, now a partner in haulage Squire His nephew, who finds the gates North gate of Thistlewick Found unaided once, 9 June 2001 Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Third is a real knight of a real house, which is small, moated and damp, and was for six years the most loyal resident of Thistlewick , a village he was trying to leave. He arrived in 1994, meaning to go out by the north gate, and never found it, though it is nineteen paces from where he usually stood and has a sign. He is the kindest person on the Quest by a distance that is not close. "I seek only the north gate," he told the Forty-Eighth. "It moves, you see. A cunning enchantment. I shall find it." Then: "...Unless. Do you know the way?" Bram did, and Sir Aldric joined on the spot, "slightly behind you at all times", which he has been ever since. The house The Pemberton-Gores hold Fenmarch Hall, in its moat, among the marshes, eleven miles from anywhere in a direction he could not indicate. The family arms are a knight rampant regardant: a knight looking back over his shoulder, which for two centuries everybody took to be a pun about vigilance. He is the third of the name. The first and second were also lost. He rode out from Fenmarch in 1991, at thirty-seven, with a letter from his father to carry to Little Gore , four miles away, his first errand. He did not get there. He did a great deal else instead, in a great many places, most of them by accident, and kept the letter in his tabard the whole time, where it went soft at the folds. Thistlewick By 1994 he had reached Thistlewick, and in Thistlewick he stayed, not on purpose. He left many times. He also arrived many times, believing it to be another village, and the village decided, without ever discussing it, that this was fine, and that somebody should keep an eye on his laundry. He stood about in the street in a condition of readiness, which he wishes me to say was not waiting. "It greatly resembles waiting." He wrote to his father, and did not send it, because the wording proved difficult. "'Currently between quests' is accurate and reads extremely badly." He also says, and I have three witnesses, that he had narrowed the gate down to the village. On the Quest He covers whoever is bleeding without being asked, encourages everybody, and does very little damage, and everybody I have spoken to who went north with him says they would not have got there without him. In the course of the Quest he discharged, very late, nearly every obligation he had ever been given. The errand. He still had his father's letter. He insisted on leading the party to Little Gore, and proposed a route of a hundred and ten miles, by the coast, which the party let him take, and which got there. The letter was an invitation to a wedding, nine years before, which everybody had attended anyway. The bride, Mrs Hester Vane, now a mother of three, was delighted to see him, and put the letter on the mantelpiece, where it is. The vigil. A knight is confirmed by keeping vigil in a chapel. He had kept eleven, every one in the wrong chapel, two of them at the Chapter House at Coldbarrow ("It says CHAPTER HOUSE on the door. I thought it was being modest") and one in a barn, which had a weathercock. The right one was the Order's chapel at Weeping Bottom , under Sir Hamo Tench, and the party kept the twelfth with him there. The rules forbid the knight to move or speak until dawn. Things came. He did not move. He took everything. At first light he was confirmed, thirty years late, and given the shield that had been waiting over the chapel door since he was sixteen. The Sisters had taken the device on it for a pun. It is not. Regardant means looking back to see who is behind you, which is the whole of the Order of the Errant, and he had never been facing the wrong way. He had been facing his friends. The Chapter House. The Order of the Errant keeps a great map at Coldbarrow with a pin for every knight in the field. Sir Aldric had nine. Six of them were correct on different dates, and three were the same week. Chapter Clerk Mordaunt did not regard this as an embarrassment but as a data problem, formed a committee, and offered him a promotion on condition that he stay in one place for the duration of the review. He refused it beautifully. The Order promoted him anyway, to Knight Errant, At Large. He carries his own pin now. Wherever he is, the map is correct. Duchess. He had a horse, and nobody, himself included, had asked after her in six years. She is fine. One winter, in 1994, she walked in off the west road into a yard at Great Dunnage , saddled, with nobody in the saddle, and Mr Plummer took her in. She has been in steady work ever since, and is well thought of, and is now a partner in the firm, which trades as Plummer & Partner, haulage. The reunion was, I am told by everybody who saw it, very touching. She did not want to leave. He said of course, and meant it. He calls on her. Not on Tuesdays, which she plans. The Wrong Dragon. In 1992 he was sent to slay a dragon and arrived at a different one, in the rocks above the water, who is elderly, has read a great deal, and is not a dragon in the sense the commission meant. They talked about Horace until it got dark. It was established on his second visit, eight years later, that the dragon had been talking about the poet and he about his horse, whom he had only ever called Horse; both had had a lovely time. The right dragon has since been slain by somebody else, who drinks in the Slain Wyvern and is insufferable about it. The valley's last wild dragon is therefore uneaten, and a knight reads it the Odes, when he can find the way. The Fourth His nephew, Pemberton-Gore the Fourth, was ten when Sir Aldric rode out and was raised on the story of the knight who went out and never came back, which is the family's best tale and is not how Sir Aldric would put it. At nineteen he came looking, found the north gate of Thistlewick on his first attempt, and has not said so. He squires for his uncle now, three paces behind. "It's how you squire. I read it. He keeps stopping, though." Sir Aldric has been home to Fenmarch, at last. He went the long way round, and it was still a way. Afterwards He is Knight Errant, At Large, which is the only rank in the Order with no fixed address, and he holds it with great distinction. His squire finds the gates. Duchess is doing so well. On the ninth of June 2001, at about eleven in the morning, Sir Aldric found the north gate of Thistlewick on his own, without his nephew, and went out through it, and was very pleased. I have the date from three witnesses who were in the lane. He has not been able to find it since, and has said so, cheerfully, to all three of them. If there is one member of the company the reader should feel bad about having left at home, it is this one. I did not go on the Quest and I feel bad about it anyway. See also Fenmarch Hall The Order of the Errant Little Gore The Obligatory Quest

title: Spare Cotterill
text: Spare Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills . For the town, see Upper Clanging . For his letters to me, see below, and file accordingly. Spare Cotterill Can he come yet Known as Spare; the Ninth Of Upper Clanging , the ninth of the Cotterills Trade Brushing the ninety tubes of the Hoyle Works boiler, since 1997. Paid in buns Age Nine at the time of the Quest; eleven now Good at Getting in anywhere; not being hit; getting everybody up again Bad at Getting past his mother Bag Packed for two years: a jumper, a tin, a washer off Shim. There was bread Authorised by Form P-9, Application by a Minor to Accompany a Chosen One (Parish of Upper Clanging), signed after a discussion Terms Jumper on. Not in first. Write Littlest Cotterill Until the spring of 2000 Spare Cotterill is the ninth of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and was, at nine, the youngest member of the Forty-Eighth's company, and the last to join. He had had a bag packed for two years. He had asked every Chosen One who ever walked up his street whether he could come. All of them said no, until the Forty-Eighth, who said no as well, and then listened to why he should be asked again. "Are you the Chosen One? I have a bag. It is packed. It has been packed for two years. I am nine. I am nine in a useful way." Nine in a useful way The boiler of the Hoyle Works has ninety tubes in it, and they have to be brushed, and a man does not fit. Spare fits. He has been going into the boiler since he was six, and Miss Hoyle pays him in buns. He has, he says, never once been frightened. Then he said the rest of it, which I print because he has given me leave to and because it is the truest thing anybody told the Forty-Eighth on the whole of the road: "I have been frightened. Not of the dark. Of coming out and nobody being there. There is always somebody there." He was also, that winter, about to stop being the littlest. In the spring there would be ten Cotterills. He was not sad about it. "I have had nine years of being the littlest and it is a very good job. I would just like to have done one thing first." Joining It took a great deal. The party had to hear him out, all of it, and meet every Cotterill there is, on the street, in the works, at the forge, in the Safety Valve and at the Parish Rooms, because you do not take a boy out of a family you have not met. It needed the airship, because a nine-year-old does not walk to the Obligatory Tower through the Gloamwood. It needed a form, and the parish had one: Form P-9, which his sister Gudgeon, who clerks at the Parish Rooms, had never once issued and knew exactly where to find. It needed a parent's signature. It needed, in the end, a discussion with his mother, which went the way discussions go in this part of the world, and he lost it at least once, alone. He was not upset. She conceded. Her terms were these, and he has kept every one: Jumper on. You do not go in first. You write. It does not have to be long, and it does not have to be true. Shim, who is eleven and has a tin, gave him a washer. He wears it. On the Quest He does not leave at the door. That is Mr Fairweather's job. Letters home. He wrote from every town, four lines each, and handed them to the same courier, who was always already there and never explained. His mother read them out at the dinner hour at the works, and the whole shift knows about the dragon. There was no dragon. He kept a copy of every one, in pencil, in case. I have been shown the copies, and with his permission I print the first: Dear Mam, I am at the seaside. The sea is right there. I have checked. It goes out and then it comes back. I have my jumper on and I did not go in first. Nobody has hit me. There is no dragon. Love, Spare. S. Cotterill, from Nether Sopping His mother did more potatoes anyway. The Bottom Lock. His eldest brother Cotter, at the Iron Company's gate in Great Dunnage , had a job no man would fit: the bottom gate of the Dunnage cut, jammed, and a paddle to clear in a brick culvert under it. Spare went in alone, in the dark, and counted, and cleared it, and came out. Somebody was there when he came out. The pen pal. Since he was six he had been writing to Effie Gotobed of Much Pottering , through the same courier, and she had had every untrue thing he ever wrote, and what she wrote back was exactly as untrue. They met, at last. Her volcano is a bonfire. Her sea serpent is a carp. There was no volcano. They are still writing. The tenth After the Quest, he asked the party every morning, on waking, whether it was spring yet. It was not. Then one morning it was, and Bessie Marsden came for him, and the street was empty for a day, and Washer Cotterill was born at six in the morning, on the hooter. His brother Clevis had been running a book on it, and it paid twenty to one. Spare is not the littlest any more. He is a big brother. He came back to the party for a while afterwards, and was, I am told, very good at it. Afterwards He is at home for Washer, and still writing to Effie. He also writes to me. Since the Quest I have had thirty-one letters from him, every one of them four lines long, and every one of them untrue, and I have filed every one of them under Fiction, where they are the best-kept part of my files. He has given me leave to print one: Dear Mr Bellwether, I have been made Mayor of Upper Clanging. It was a close vote. The duck was against. I have my jumper on and I did not go in first. Washer has said a word. It was spring. Love, Spare. S. Cotterill, from Upper Clanging (filed under Fiction) It was also Spare who confirmed for me, by letter, that the twenty-first of March 2002 is the first day of spring, which is the date on which I have signed this volume. It is the only true thing he has ever written to me. I checked. Washer has not said a word. I have checked that too. I am told he says a great many things, and none of them is a word yet, and that his brother is working on it. See also The Cotterills Upper Clanging Much Pottering The Obligatory Quest

title: Wren Halloway
text: Wren Halloway For her work, see the Bestiary , which is hers, and which I have printed whole and not touched. For the goose, see The Goose , in the same. Wren Halloway Not to be jogged Known as W. Halloway; the Cataloguer Of A corner of the Slain Wyvern, and then outside it, and then a seat under the goose Trade Cataloguer of monsters, by what they are Carries A crossbow; seventeen specimen jars; the monograph Good at Several hits at range, poison, taking armour off things, getting two of whatever they drop Bad at Raw damage; tolerating the phrase "basically a dragon" Published The Fauna of the Valley, by What They Are , 2000 Reviewers Three, one a duck Named Bramus agricola On the wyvern A goose Wren Halloway is a cataloguer: she does not hunt monsters, she documents them, and the fighting is a step in the methodology that she resents. "You cannot measure a wing that is actively in use." She went north with the Forty-Eighth, came back with eleven type specimens and the only honest monograph on the creatures of this region, and is the author of the Bestiary in this volume, which I commissioned from her and have not altered by one word, because she would know. She met the Forty-Eighth in the Slain Wyvern, at a table of specimens, and the first thing she said to him was, "Don't jog the table. Nothing in here is dead enough to be casual about." Her terms for joining were first refusal on anything unusual, that she write the entries, and that nobody - "NOBODY" - say "it's basically a dragon". She has since drafted a clause about the phrase. The discipline Everybody else names monsters after how they died. She names them after what they are, which she calls the same job done properly. Taxonomy, for her, is a moral position. The difficulty is the previous authority. Doctor Amias Rowbotham FRS spent forty years naming some three hundred species after himself, his subscribers and his dogs, and the standard work is therefore a monument to a man rather than a description of a valley. Every correction she publishes reads to the field as an attack on a dead man they were all rather fond of. She published once, at twenty-three, and was reviewed by three of his students. She does not discuss the reviews. I have read them, and she is right not to. The goose She was thrown out of the Slain Wyvern for saying that the wyvern over its mantel is a goose. It is a goose. Halloran Vance, the Forty-First, brought it home from the marshes in 1940 and made it into a wyvern with wire, in two days, because a whole town was waiting on the quay for a monster and he had nothing to give them. Mrs Dorcas Thrupp keeps the Wyvern, and would not take the wyvern down, or have it corrected, because the Forty-First was a good man and brought back what he could, and that is where the conversation ends. Miss Halloway was right, and she was right at length, and she was asked to leave for it. Of everything that happened to anybody in the company, it is the nearest thing to unfair. What came of it is a second plaque. It is beside the first. It does not correct the first, and does not repeat it. It says what the bird is, and where it was got, and by whom, and why. Mrs Thrupp read it twice, said nothing, and put it up herself. Both plaques are on the wall now. On the Quest The monograph. Publication at the Collegium Arcanum required a type specimen, intact, for every entry: eleven fights she objected to and conducted anyway, with a very bad grace and very good results. It required a subscription list, which she got, and three Fellows to review it, which she got, one of whom is the Collegium's duck. The Fauna of the Valley, by What They Are, by W. Halloway, is on the Collegium's shelf, in a gap exactly an inch wide that had been waiting for it. It has eleven type specimens and three reviewers. Page four hundred says goose. The Gloamwood Society. The Society had existed for forty years to prove that the Thing In The Woods is not there, with a newsletter, nine members and an annual walk. She proved it comprehensively. The Society was delighted. Its newsletter had its best ever issue. One member was quietly devastated, and was looked after very carefully by everybody else, and was fine by the end of the walk. The Fenmarch Collection. At Fenmarch Hall there is a gallery of impossible animals in glass cases, and she was engaged to authenticate them. They were composed by Mr Ottershaw, taxidermist, who is ninety and unrepentant and an artist: he did not forge them, he composed them, and the joins are magnificent. She wrote it up honestly, which required her to say that the workmanship is the finest she has seen, which she meant. Seventy-nine of the animals are composed. The family has never been prouder. Case forty was not examined. Bramus agricola. She named a new species after the Forty-Eighth: a small brown thing that lives in turnip fields, is of no consequence whatever, and is remarkable for one attribute, which is that it survives things it has no business surviving, by luck, repeatedly, in a manner she describes in print as "statistically indefensible". He was deeply touched until she explained why, and then deeply touched anyway, because it was accurate. The Prophecy does not read journals. It has read this one. Afterwards She is welcome in the Slain Wyvern, which she affects not to care about. She sits under the goose, by choice, most evenings, writing. Volume two of the monograph is in hand. It will contain a corrigendum about one specimen, which she will not name. I asked her whether case forty at Fenmarch had been left unexamined by accident. She said that a cataloguer does not examine a specimen she has not been engaged to examine, and that I should mind my own entries. I have looked at case forty myself, through the glass. I do not know what it is. That is not my field. See also The Bestiary , by W. Halloway The Goose Bramus agricola The Slain Wyvern The Obligatory Quest

title: Zephyrine Vance
text: Zephyrine Vance For the institution, see The Collegium Arcanum . For the duck, see the same, under Fellows . Zephyrine Vance Fine Known as Formerly of the College Of The Gilded Turnip , Thistlewick, "just passing through" since 1989 Trade Hedge mage; fire person Educated The Collegium Arcanum ; best in her year at Kindle Standing there Disputed by everybody, including her Good at Elemental damage, in quantity Bad at Being hit; budgeting Votes held One, by proxy, unused Fire, unsanctioned One quantity, 1989 Fire, sanctioned Nine hundred acres, 2000, in triplicate Zephyrine Vance is a hedge mage who has lived in Thistlewick since 1989, when she left the Collegium Arcanum after an incident involving the Dean, a duck, and what the enquiry called, twice, "an unsanctioned quantity of fire". The Dean is fine. The duck is fine. She would like it understood that everyone is fine. When Bram came to her table in the Gilded Turnip and began to speak, she said, "Don't. Whatever it is, don't." He said it was a quest. She asked what sort. He said a tower, with a Dark Lord in it. "That's the most fire-adjacent thing anyone has said to me in eleven years," she said. "Give me my hat." The incident The facts are these. In 1989, at a dinner at the Collegium, Miss Vance said aloud that a junior fellow's paper had gone out under somebody senior's name. She was told to let it go. She did not let it go. Some time later in the evening there was fire, in a quantity that had not been sanctioned, in the vicinity of the Dean and a duck. Nobody was hurt. The enquiry used the phrase twice. I have read the enquiry. I have also read the paper: On the Kindling of Damp Materials, by Dr Hapgood, which went out under the name of the Master, and the Master is a committee. The quantity of fire was unsanctioned. The point she was making was correct. Both of those have been true since 1989, and for eleven years only one of them was in the file. She was the best student of her year. Hedge magic is the discipline of doing the same work with worse equipment in somebody's garden, and she has been very good at it for a long time. It was not what she trained for, and she drank at the Gilded Turnip in the manner of somebody waiting for a letter. The letter It came. It bore the Collegium's crest, and it informed her that she was on study leave. "STUDY leave. I was EXPELLED. There was an ENQUIRY. It used the phrase TWICE." It turned out that the papers expelling her had been drafted and initialled and never filed, and she had therefore been on unpaid study leave for eleven years, in good standing, and owed eleven years of library fines. The fines were the largest sum of money anyone on the Quest ever saw written down. Sub-Librarian Prewitt was courteous, immovable and correct. How the matter ended depends on whom you ask, and I have asked her, and the answer I got was a look. The Collegium's register says she is a member of the Collegium in good standing, with her fines paid on the Library desk out of a purse. I have also seen a letter, in her hand, filing her own expulsion, eleven years after the event, at her own request. I have printed both, because one of them is true, and she has asked me to leave it that way. The duck The duck survived the incident, and the Collegium, not knowing what else to do with a bird that had given evidence at a formal enquiry, made it an Honorary Fellow. It has since sat in Congregation, held a chair, and acquired views on the endowment. In 2000 a vote was called and the quorum was short by one duck, which was on a pond four miles away. It had to be walked. It has four hit points and walks into everything. The party walked it. The Collegium has been quorate ever since. The duck's vote is held by proxy, permanently, by Zephyrine Vance. She has not yet used it. She is saving it. Other fires The Cinder Fen. Nine hundred acres of sodden fen had been drowning the road to Great Dunnage since the parish's last fire person retired in 1970. The remedy is fire, and in 2000 she was asked for it, in writing, with a form that asked her to state the quantity. "It's the first piece of paper about me and fire that I've liked." The fen was burnt, sanctioned, in triplicate; the road is dry; the form came back countersigned. Dean Fenwold. The Dean has made a second career of being the man who was fine, and does an after-dinner talk about it. He asked her to do the fire again, small, in a hall, with buckets. She refused, then agreed, on terms. It went wrong in exactly the way it had gone wrong the first time, for exactly the same reason, which is that the room was wrong. His talk now ends with the room being wrong, and Dr Hapgood's paper has Dr Hapgood's name on it. I take that to have been the terms. The lay-by. The hedge mages have an association. It meets in a lay-by on the west road, because none of them will host, and has been trying to agree a name for nine years. One of them taught himself out of a book with four pages missing, and is therefore better than the Collegium at exactly four things. It has four members now, and still no name. Item one is carried forward. Afterwards She is still in Thistlewick, now on purpose. She no longer drinks at the Gilded Turnip like somebody waiting for a letter, because the letter came. She still has the duck's vote, and still has not used it. I asked her what she was saving it for and she said she would know it when she saw it, and that it would not be soon, and that I was not to put that in. I have put it in. She is welcome to set fire to the page. Middle C on the Gilded Turnip's piano is a little warm. She tells me that is her, and has been since 1989. See also The Collegium Arcanum Dean Fenwold The Gilded Turnip The Obligatory Quest

title: Ashcombe
text: Ashcombe This article is about the village by the lake, and the one under it. For its best-known son, who took its name, see Corvin Ash . Ashcombe Known as Ashcombe; the village that is fine Where The east, on the shore of Ashcombe Lake Flooded 1989, on a Tuesday Lost Nobody. Not so much as a hen Dry by Teatime Rebuilt Only better Distance from the old village Eight miles, by the road. A stone's throw, as the crow flies Drains Fourteen hundred yards of culvert, a fall of one in two hundred Puddles since None Post Every letter answered. It's policy Ashcombe is a village on the shore of a lake in the east. Thirteen years ago the lake came up over the old village, on a Tuesday, and every soul in it walked up the hill with the kettles, and was dry by teatime, and by teatime had decided to build it again, only better. It did. The old village is under the lake. The new one has the best drains in the world, and is extremely cheerful about all of it. The village The plaque is polished stone, facing the lake, with the gilt still bright: HERE, ON THE DAY OF THE WATER, EVERY SOUL IN OLD ASHCOMBE CAME SAFE UP THE HILL, AND WAS DRY BY TEATIME. WE BUILT IT AGAIN, ONLY BETTER. And under that, smaller: MIND THE DRAINS. THEY ARE VERY GOOD. VISIT THE MUSEUM! (FREE.) Everything is new. The church is pale stone with a green roof and coloured glass in every window, and the bell is the old one, brought up the hill on a cart on the day of the water, because nobody saw why they shouldn't. It rings at six for dinner, and if you ring it at any other time a door flies open up the street and somebody shouts COMING! and then, rather put out, Oh. It isn't six. The church door's card says SERVICE AT SIX. KEY WITH THE BELL. The bell is at the top of the tower. The school has a brass plate, ASHCOMBE SCHOOL, polished, and under it, also polished, 'Very Good.' - H.M. Inspector of Schools. The blackboard has a history of Ashcombe on it: 1. IT WAS THERE. 2. IT WAS WET. 3. WE MOVED IT. On every desk there is a paper boat. Wilf, a small boy with another paper boat, is looking for somewhere to sail it, and there are no puddles, and Mr Weir says there will not ever be a puddle again, and says it like it's good. In one front room a line is painted on the wall at knee height, with a date beside it, and a smiley face. In another a family is at tea with every chair on little stilts. Old habits. The scarecrow wears waders and a life ring. The post office, kept by Mrs Dimmock, answers every letter that comes to Ashcombe. It's policy. ALL LETTERS ANSWERED, says the card in the window, and under it, WE MEAN IT. Years ago they had one addressed to THE RUINS OF ASHCOMBE, and so the Ruins wrote back, a lovely long letter, hoping he was keeping warm. The post box by the door is iron, painted red, with a slot like a polite smile, and is Hob Grumnir's, and he asked for it back, a while, and Mrs Dimmock asked where the letters would go, and said that box had had a letter from the Ruins of Ashcombe in it, and you cannot take a box back after that. Hob said no, you can't. The Drainage Museum The Ashcombe Drainage Museum is free, and so is the enthusiasm. Mr Hubert Weir, Curator, in a coat with gold frogging, stands in the middle of the room with his hands behind his back, the way a man stands in a room he is proud of. Fourteen hundred yards of culvert, a fall of one in two hundred, and not one puddle in Ashcombe since the day they went in. The flood, he says, was a tremendous success: everybody out by dinner, everybody dry by tea, and not so much as a hen lost. They have the Roll. The new village is eight miles from the old one, by the ROAD, sir. The road goes all the way round the lake. As the crow flies you could skim a stone on to the old church roof. The exhibits are worth an afternoon. The plan of the drains, on a great sheet of parchment, every culvert named in copperplate; the longest is called Hubert. Grown men have stood in front of that plan and gone quite quiet. Exhibit one is the stone that was set in the old high street over the only drain old Ashcombe had, carved DRAIN, and the card beside it says, kindly, It was not up to it. An empty plinth, beautifully polished: THE FLOOD (ON LOAN TO THE LAKE). Exhibits fourteen and fifteen are a plant (dry) and another plant (also dry). The painting, The Lake, at Evening, painted for the Flood Dinner, has the old church spire painted in under the water, very small, and it is the best bit of the picture, and they know it. The Roll was taken on the hill on the day of the water, in the schoolmistress's hand: every name in the old village, a tick by each, and after every tick one word, DRY. Two hundred and six ticks. Beside one name, in place of a tick, in the same careful hand: Away. (Written to.) That is Corvin's. Two hundred and six people stood on a hill in the rain and counted, and when they got to him they wrote down where he was, and then they wrote to him. He was in a corner of the Slain Wyvern, being away, on purpose. They counted him anyway. The Flood Dinner Every year there is a Flood Dinner at the church hall, with soup, a fish, a pudding and speeches, and the toast is TO THE WATER, WHICH WAS VERY GOOD ABOUT IT. The menus are pinned up in the museum, one for every year, and at the foot of each is the speaker: the Curator; the Curator; Mrs Ash, on knitting; the Curator; the Curator. The notice for the year 2000 read: SPEAKER: TO BE CONFIRMED, and under it, in pencil, Mr Weir has kindly offered. Again. It was confirmed: C. ASH. (CONFIRMED.) And under it, in pencil, Mr Weir has kindly offered. Next year. Two hundred and six people, and the old bell rung for six exactly. What Corvin Ash said is in his article, and I shall not shorten it here, except to say that he brought the name back, and that they may as well have it, because they were using it, and that the toast was to the water, which was very good about it. Mrs Ash cast off the last stitch in the front row, and stood, and held up a scarf that went most of the way down the aisle, bright yellow, the yellow of the new roofs, which is the wrong colour for everything Corvin owns. If she had done it in black, nobody would ever see him in it. He wears it everywhere. He was asked back to the Flood Dinner of 2001, and went, and was early. Mr Weir spoke that year, on culverts, for some time. Mrs Ash Mrs Ash has a kitchen so new the paint still smells of it, with a big window over the lake, and she knits something long and does not stop. Mind the step. It's new. It's all new. Isn't it lovely? The old kitchen was DARK; you couldn't see your potatoes. She can see every potato she owns. Her boy wrote to say that he had taken the name Ash, after the village, in its memory, and she thought, well, that's nice, and took it as well, to save the postman, and now they are all Ashes and the post comes lovely. He is very deep, her boy. She wrote to him at the Slain Wyvern, Wednesdays and Saturdays, for eleven years, and he wrote back once, to the Ruins of Ashcombe, and the Ruins wrote back. She thought he would like that. He did. His room upstairs is bigger now, and has the light, and is a study at the minute, where the papers of the Flood Dinner Committee are kept: Hon. Sec., Mrs Ash. Up the wall by the window are pencil marks with ages, C., 6; C., 9; C., 12; C., 16; C., 19. The old ones went under with the old wall. These were put back from memory, and every one of them is a little taller than a boy would have been, and the last is exactly the top of his head. She drew where he would be. Old Ashcombe Once a year, in the week of the Flood Dinner, they let the lake down for the sluices, and the old street comes up for air, at the bottom of a slope of wet mud below the shore. On a still day, they say, you can hear the old church bell ringing under the water. You cannot. It is up the road in the new Ashcombe, calling somebody in for their dinner. They took it with them. In sluice week the old street is mud and stones and lily pads. There is the sign of the Anchor, face up, where Corvin was not allowed in and sat outside and waited. There is a gatepost with a hinge on it that still turns. A rose has got through the gap where a gate was, and flowers on the lake side. A coot has built a nest on the old maypole stump and sits on it very seriously. Round a stump somebody has pressed a ring of shells into the mud; somebody who comes down here sometimes, and sits. At the edge of the old street there is a doorstep with nothing behind it, and cut into it are letters in the old script, the ones on the tang of Corvin's sword, and under them, in plain capitals, for visitors, MIND THE STEP. His grandfather cut that, and made the sword as well, and it stood there forty years holding the door open. That is its name. In the schoolroom next door a strongbox held a report for every child old Ashcombe ever had, dry, in oilcloth, in the schoolmistress's hand, and Corvin's was near the top, from the last year. It is a fair report. It is one fewer in the box now. At the end of the street the road goes on into the water, and just under the surface is a green roof: the old church, up to its eaves. You could skim a stone on to it. Corvin Ash showed me his report, which he carries in his coat, next to the scarf. I asked whether I might print it. He said no, and then he said that I might print the last line, and I do: Corvin could do anything he put his mind to, and has put it to waiting. He will go far, if he ever gets up. See also Corvin Ash The Slain Wyvern , and its corner The Sable Hart

title: Coldbarrow
text: Coldbarrow This article is about the Chapter House of the Order of the Errant. For the Order, see The Order of the Errant . For the knight with nine pins, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . Coldbarrow Known as The Chapter House Where In the snow of the far north, west of Frostwick Of The Order of the Errant Clerk Mordaunt System One knight, one pin Pins in Sir Aldric Nine, until 2000. Now one, carried Committee Sits on Thursdays. Quorate Daybook PINS REVIEWED. PINS REVIEWED (WITH TEA) Ceremonial armour Do not go on a quest in Coldbarrow is the Chapter House of the Order of the Errant, a hall in the snow of the far north where the Order keeps a great map of the island with a pin in it for every knight in the field. It is kept by the Order's clerk, Mordaunt, who reads the map the way other people read a will. One knight, one pin. That is the system. The map The great map is the island in the Order's own survey, four sheets wide. Each knight in the field is a white-headed pin, spread thin, standing where they were put. Until the year 2000 there were also nine red ones, all over it, for one knight, three of them labelled in the same hand: SAME WEEK. SEE COMMITTEE. The knight was Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Third. Six of his pins were correct, on different dates. Three of them were the same week: Frostwick, and Fenmarch, and a lay-by in the west. The Order had not lost his file. People said it had. It had nine of them, on the bottom shelf, nine fat volumes each labelled PEMBERTON-GORE, and each one certain that it was the real one. Mordaunt's ledger lay open at P, and every entry on the page had been crossed out and written in again somewhere else. He asked anybody who saw Sir Aldric to note the place, the date and the time, in ink. Not pencil. Pencil is how they got there. The committee A committee was formed to review the map, the pins and the week. It sat on Thursdays, at a table with two chairs and two stools, all of them empty, because the committee was Mordaunt, appointed to it four times, and quorate. In the year 2000 Sir Aldric came in, and Mordaunt put his pins down on the desk very carefully, as if they might go off, and said that it was Thursday, and the committee would see him now, and sat in each chair and on each stool in turn and then stood behind all of them. Its findings were three. Nine pins. All nine correct. Three of them the same week. The committee had been unable to fault the pins, and had therefore had to fault the knight, and Sir Aldric said that that was entirely fair. It recommended that he be requested to remain in one place for the duration of the review, and offered him Knight Commander of the Chapter, with a desk, there, and a pin that did not move, contingent on his remaining in one place. It was the one thing he could not do, and the one thing he had always wanted to be asked. He said that it was the finest thing he had been offered in nine years, and thanked Mordaunt, and said no. A knight who stays put is a post. He should be at that desk by nine every morning, and he should never once find it twice. But Mordaunt had asked, and nobody asks a man to stay, and he would like that put in the minutes. In ink. Mordaunt wrote for some time, and crossed nothing out, which the ledger on his desk would tell you was a first. Then he said that the committee had a data problem: the knight could not stay with the pin. Resolved, that the pin go with the knight. He took the nine red pins out of the map one at a time, and put eight of them in a heap on his desk, and held out the ninth. KNIGHT ERRANT, AT LARGE, a rank of the Order, created that Thursday. Wherever the knight is, the map is correct. That is the system now. The card on the committee's table reads: REVIEW OF PINS (PEMBERTON-GORE): CONCLUDED. SIR A. INFORMED. OFFERED THE CHAPTER. DECLINED. And under it, smaller, in ink: Beautifully. (Minuted at his request.) On the great map there are no red pins now, and in the margin a small card in Mordaunt's hand: PEMBERTON-GORE. AT LARGE. PIN CARRIED. I wrote to Mordaunt to ask for the Order's records of Sir Aldric since the review. He replied that Sir Aldric is wherever he is, and that the map is correct. He enclosed a note from Sir Aldric's squire, the Fourth, saying that his uncle was here, and the date, and the time, in ink. Mordaunt says that he has had one of these every week for a year and a half, and that he keeps them in a tenth volume, and that it is the only one of the ten that agrees with itself. The hall There is stained glass of a knight kneeling, with the Order's motto on a scroll above him, too small to read from the floor and, one suspects, too long to fit. There is a suit of armour, very bright, with a card: CEREMONIAL. DO NOT GO ON A QUEST IN. There is another, ISSUE PATTERN, KNIGHTS ERRANT, ONE, and under it, in pencil, SIZES RUN SMALL. The Order's daybook is open on a stand: PINS REVIEWED; PINS REVIEWED; PINS REVIEWED (WITH TEA). Of the Order's other knights in the field, one at least has a pin that has never once needed reviewing: Dame Winifred Cope, at Little Gore , who writes every quarter NOTHING TO REPORT, and is written back to, VERY GOOD. See also Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III The Order of the Errant Little Gore , and Dame Winifred Frostwick , one of the three in the same week

title: Fairholme
text: Fairholme This article is about the kingdom, its council, its princess and the dragon up the hill. For the knight with the empty chair, see Hithermost . Fairholme Known as The Kingdom of Fairholme Where The east, past the hills King HM King Aldous Princess Rosamund, frequently Reward Her hand, or half the kingdom Taken The half. Every time The King's share One two-thousand-and-forty-eighth Shareholders Nine heroes; Mr and Mrs Budge; Sir Dunstable (in a mountain); Mr Pilbeam (pending) Council business Drainage Tower door The fifteenth. The hinges are the original Dragon Mrs Emberthwaite, retired. Whist on Thursdays Fairholme is a small kingdom in the east whose princess has been kidnapped eleven times, twelve if you count the eagle, which the Palace does not, and whose king has posted the traditional reward every time: her hand, or half the kingdom. Every rescuer has taken the half. Very sensible. Nobody's fault. But there is only so much kingdom, and it is now governed by a council of its shareholders, round three tables pushed end to end, and its chief business is drainage. The council The council chamber is most of the palace. The table is three tables end to end in three different woods, a dark old one, the long pale royal one and, on the end, a plain kitchen table that still has a drawer for the spoons, and the council has outgrown each of them in turn. Through the tall window you can see the whole of Fairholme and every one of its eleven new fences. King Aldous sits at the middle, small, in a red robe and a crown, and will ask you whether you are here about the rescue. If you say you are only passing he says, oh dear, that is how Mr Pilbeam started. He has given away half the kingdom eleven times. Osric, who sits at the table, has done the arithmetic, and the King is down to a two-thousand-and-forty-eighth. His portrait on the wall shows him holding the kingdom, on a map, in both hands; the map has been cut into eleven pieces since, and nobody has told the portrait. He asks every visitor, if they do rescue her, to take the half. Everybody does. There is a form. The shareholders are the rescuers, and a deed in the chamber reads TO THE BEARER, ONE TWO-THOUSAND-AND-FORTY-EIGHTH PART OF THE KINGDOM OF FAIRHOLME, with a map; the part is mostly a ditch. Tamsin rescued her from a sorcerer, year before last, lovely girl, took the half, obviously. Brannoc had a wyrm, and has the eastern marshes. Aurel had a sorcerer; everybody had a sorcerer; she had packed a cardigan for the tower, and it was a cold tower. Hild got a turnip field and the north bridge, and the bridge is the troll's, and they take turns. Morwen was met at the door with a bag packed and a card, and says nobody has ever been so pleased to see her, or so ready. Kit got the bit with the orchard, and says it was worth it, and that she had brought sandwiches, for both of them. Leof's half came with a duck pond, and the ducks have been very good about it. Valen is a bit lost. Mr and Mrs Budge were only mucking out, when she came down the hill with a tin of cake, and they walked her home, and that was all. They got the half between them, and did not know what to do with it, and put most of it back into the orchard. There is an empty chair at the end with a place card: SIR DUNSTABLE OF THE VALE. ONE SHARE. BACK DIRECTLY. - D. And there is Mr Pilbeam, at the foot of the table, who was only passing. There was an eagle. That was six years ago. The council has not decided whether the eagle counts, and he cannot go until it does, and he looks at the door the way a man looks at a door he has been looking at for six years.
