A potted plant by the wall has a flag in it, SHARE TWELVE, pending a decision on the eagle. The minutes, as they stood when the Forty-Eighth called: MINUTES OF THE COUNCIL OF FAIRHOLME. Present: HM the King; nine heroes; Mr & Mrs Budge; Mr Pilbeam (passing). Apologies: Sir Dunstable (in a mountain). The table. To be lengthened again. Carried. Drainage. 3. Drainage, continued. 4. Drainage, continued. The eagle. The Palace does not count the eagle. Whether Mr Pilbeam, who rescued Her Highness from the eagle, therefore holds a share. Deferred. Mr Pilbeam asks whether he may go. Deferred. Thursdays. Her Highness has been walking up the hill on Thursdays, unaccompanied, and coming back. The Heroes' Guild has written to complain. Noted. Drainage. The council has two teapots, because the first is quite small, and that is why the meetings take all day; the second is for item six, which is always drainage, and always takes the afternoon. I have the minutes since from Mr Pilbeam, who writes. The eagle has been deferred eight times. Sir Dunstable's apologies have been recorded at every meeting, in a mountain, and the council has twice moved to consider whether a shareholder in a mountain is a shareholder, and has twice deferred it, on the grounds that he might be back directly. Hob Grumnir made the hinges on the tower door. In the year 2000 he asked whether he might have them back. The King said, oh dear, they were the only part that had held. Every rescuer kicks the door in, and the door goes, and the hinges are fine. They were on the fourteenth door. There is a drawing of the fifteenth on the council table now, and the hinges are not drawn, because they will not be needed. Rosamund The tower stairs go up from the chamber to Princess Rosamund's room, which is the one she is taken from. She will ask whether you are the rescue, and say lovely, and ask you to carry the cake tin, and mind the seventh stair, it's a trap; the eighth is also a trap; the ninth is fine. If you are only passing, she says that that is a relief, honestly, because it is Thursday. She goes up the hill on Thursdays. Mrs Emberthwaite does a lovely sponge, and cheats at whist. The first time Rosamund was carried up there, Mrs Emberthwaite made up the spare room, and said she had not had anybody to talk to since Mr Emberthwaite. So now Rosamund walks. It is quicker. Her room is a model of preparation. A travelling bag stands by the window, packed and buckled, with the look of a bag that is never quite unpacked: a book, a cardigan, sandwiches in greaseproof paper made that morning, and a second round labelled OTHERS. The wardrobe has eleven sensible travelling cloaks labelled 1ST, 2ND, 3RD and onwards, and one at the end marked EAGLE. There are two tiaras on the dresser, one FOR BALLS and one, a good deal sturdier, FOR KIDNAPPINGS. Under the pillow there is a rope ladder, which she has never used, because she thinks it would be unfair on the rescuers. Her memoir, Rescued Again, is in eleven volumes, and every chapter is named after a rescuer and written about very kindly. Her portrait downstairs shows her aged six in a ball gown, holding a small packed bag. Already. On the table beside the bag is a card, in a round, firm hand: FOR WHOEVER IT IS THIS TIME. No eels. No mushrooms. Nothing in aspic. Tea at four, and not stewed. I will not be carried unless there are stairs. I would like to be home by Thursday. Thank you so much for having me. She asks visitors to take something, if they like. Everybody who comes up takes something. Usually it is her. Mrs Emberthwaite Up the hill there is a cave, and by the way in a stone tablet carved deep, PLEASE WIPE YOUR FEET. NO RESCUES. Under it, in chalk, more recently: WHIST THURSDAYS. ALL WELCOME. Mrs Emberthwaite is a dragon, very large and very red, seventy-two this year by Rosamund's reckoning, with a pair of reading spectacles on a chain round her neck. She will ask you to come in, and to mind the gold, it gets everywhere, and whether you are a hero, only she is retired, she has had a letter. If you are passing, lovely. Do you play whist? She will win, by a margin that makes you check the deck. The deck is fine. It is you. Her hoard is dusted every morning, very gently, with a feather. A smaller heap has a flag in it, RAINY DAY, and another heap is for the card games, at a copper a hand on Thursdays, and Rosamund is ruthless; the score pad shows her winning by a mile. The best china has a small scorch mark on the rim of every cup, from being drunk out of by a dragon with a cold. The cuckoo clock's cuckoo is a very small dragon which comes out on the hour and sneezes. She keeps a pot of umbrellas for the knights who come up the hill in the rain meaning to slay her, so that they at least go home dry, and a bound volume of their letters, every one of which begins FOUL BEAST and ends YOURS FAITHFULLY. Her book of card games for two has TWO crossed out and AND ON THURSDAYS, THREE written in. There is a big wooden chair drawn up to the card table, much sat in, once, with a pipe on the seat. It was Mr Emberthwaite's. He did the roaring, mostly; she was always more of an indoor dragon. Rosamund asked whose it was, the first Thursday, and has never sat in it. She pulls up the stool. At the end of a short passage is the spare room: a bed made up with clean sheets, a washstand, a rag rug, and curtains hung neatly over no window at all, because a room ought to have curtains. On the pillow: ROSAMUND - THURSDAYS. AIRED WEDNESDAYS. NO EELS IN THE HOUSE. TEA AT FOUR, NOT STEWED. She has never once stayed the night. She walks home after the whist. There is a hot-water bottle in the bed all the same, and it is warm. Miss Halloway asked me to say that Mrs Emberthwaite is not in the Bestiary, at Mrs Emberthwaite's request, which Miss Halloway thinks is very proper. A tapestry in the cave shows two dragons asleep in the sun on a hillside, hung where the light catches it in the afternoon. I asked whether it was anybody. She said it was a very good likeness, and dealt. See also Hithermost , for Sir Dunstable The Wrong Dragon , who is somebody else

title: Fenmarch Hall
text: Fenmarch Hall This article is about the house of the Pemberton-Gores. For the knight who went out errant from it, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . For what is in the cases, see Miss Halloway's write-up, below, and her Bestiary , where none of them is. Fenmarch Hall Known as Fenmarch Where A headland in the far south-east, the sea on both sides Of The Pemberton-Gores Arms A knight rampant regardant: in armour, rearing up, looking back over his shoulder Motto Respice : look behind you Moat All the way round, and in places a little further Gate Found first time by the Fourth, aged ten. The first of the family Portraits Every one from behind, except the last Cases Eighty. Seventy-nine composed Case forty Not examined Fenmarch Hall is a grey house behind a low wall, with its roofs gone green and a moat all the way round it, on a headland in the far south-east with the sea on both sides. Everything about it is slightly wet. It is the seat of the Pemberton-Gores, a family which has always faced the wrong way. It is on the arms. The gate Two stone gateposts, green with damp, carry the family arms, a knight in armour rearing up and looking back over his shoulder at something behind him, and the motto, RESPICE. Look behind you. On the inside of the left-hand post, at about the height of a boy of ten, somebody has scratched FOUND IT. That was the Fourth, Sir Aldric's nephew, who found the gate first time when he was ten, and is the first of the family who ever has. His grandfather, Sir Aldric the Second, came over the wall until he was eighty, and said that it was quicker. It was not. He simply could not find the gate. The house is easy enough to find. It is the gate that the family has trouble with. The moat goes all the way round the house, and in places a little further than that: the lawn is wet for twenty yards in every direction, and so is the house. There are mushrooms on the lawn, which is also, in places, the moat, and a ring of them which the gardener has bordered with stones, as if they were meant. The gardener is Tom, of Little Gore, who walks over every day, four miles both ways, and says it is not a long way when you have somebody at the other end of it. He was married at Fenmarch, eleven years ago this summer. It rained. It always rains at Fenmarch. The gallery Most of the house is the long gallery. Mrs Puddifoot, the housekeeper, in a white cap with a duster in each hand, keeps house, what there is of it. Everything in the house is damp except the animals, because Mr Ottershaw won't have it. There are eighty of them. She starts dusting on a Friday and is done by the Wednesday after, and then it is Friday again. The cases in the gallery do not come to eighty; the rest are upstairs, one in every bedroom, and you get used to it. The portraits run down one wall, and every one of them is of somebody's back. Not one of them has ever followed anybody round a room with its eyes. Sir Aldric the First, in armour, from behind, looking back over his shoulder at something outside the frame. Dame Honoria Pemberton-Gore, 1811, from behind, looking out of a window; the painter was paid for a front, and waited three weeks for one. Rollo, a dog, 1840, from behind; she was the only one of the family who could find her way home, and she did it facing the right way. Sir Aldric the Third, from behind, in armour, walking out of the picture at a good pace, with a box of fresh flowers under it that Mrs Puddifoot has changed every morning for eleven years. And at the end, the Fourth, painted in the spring of 1999, the only portrait in the gallery facing out, pointing confidently at the gate. In the year 2000 Sir Aldric stood in front of his own portrait for some time, and said that he had been going to come back, and that he had, rather. Mrs Puddifoot changed the flowers anyway, because it was the morning, and nobody told her not to. She still does. The cases line the other side, thirty-two in the gallery, each with a brass plate. THE MARSH BEAR (Ursus fenmarchensis), taken in the moat by Sir Aldric the Second; it had come for the crayfish, and had been at them some time. THE FENMARCH PHOENIX, which rose from the kitchen fire, and was put out by Cook. A ROOK (Scaled), shot on the lawn by Sir Aldric the First, who had been looking for the gate at the time. THE GREATER MOAT BEAR, larger than the Marsh Bear, and wetter. A HORSE, and the plate says nothing else; there is room left on it where somebody meant to, and did not like to ask. A UNICORN, of the Home Farm, bred at Fenmarch; not a success as a unicorn; it kept the foxes down. The Latin names are Dr Rowbotham's. He named the bear. He named everything. That, Miss Halloway says, was the problem. Mr Ottershaw At the far end of the gallery, at a workbench among the cases, in green lenses, with a needle and a great deal of thread, sits Mr J. Ottershaw, who was ninety in March of 2000 and did the animals. Did he preserve them? Anybody can preserve. A cook can preserve. He COMPOSED them. Seventy years, three generations, and the family will tell you every one of them is rare, and the family are right: there is one of each. He will ask you to look at a shoulder and tell him where it stops, and you will look for a long time, at feathers and then scales, and find nowhere at all where the one becomes the other. In seventy years, he said, nobody had ever found a join. Not one of them had ever looked. In the year 2000 the family engaged Miss Wren Halloway, a naturalist, a proper one, with the jars, to look at them properly. The Fourth was across the gallery before Mrs Puddifoot had finished asking. Three generations they had been proud of them. Wren said she would tell them what they were, all eighty, and that they might not like it. The Fourth said they would love it; they love everything; ask anybody. Mr Ottershaw, when she told him she had been engaged to authenticate them, put down the needle, took off his lenses and put them on again to see her better, and said that in seventy years nobody had ever ASKED. He took her down the gallery at a pace you would not expect of a man of ninety, and showed her every join. The Marsh Bear is bear to the waist and crab below; the crab end came for the crayfish. The Phoenix is a salamander and the top of something that fell in Cook's fire. The Horse is crab and unicorn, and the plate is blank because nobody liked to ask what it was. She found each join only once he had put his finger on it, and wrote it down, and her hand was not quite steady. Then she read her write-up out to the household, standing, the way you would read a will: THE FENMARCH COLLECTION. EIGHTY CASES. Seventy-nine composed, each of two animals, by Mr J. Ottershaw, 1930 to the present. None is what its plate says. Not one of them ever lived. The joins are the finest work I have seen. I have looked for joins all my life. I could not find these without being shown, and then I could not stop looking at them. Case forty: not examined. W. Halloway. The Fourth said, None of them? and she said none of them, she was sorry, and he said COMPOSED, by Mr Ottershaw, nobody else in the county had a COMPOSER, and that was better than real; anybody could have real. Mrs Puddifoot paid the fee out of a tin on the mantelpiece and had the write-up framed before Wren had her coat on. It hangs over the fire, and Mrs Puddifoot dusts it first, before the cases. Mr Ottershaw has a copy over his bench, with finest underlined twice. Wren said that nobody had ever been pleased with a write-up of hers, and that she was not sure what to do with her face. Case forty is the Home Farm's unicorn. Mr Ottershaw went past it without looking at it, the way you go past a door you don't open. Miss Halloway stopped, and looked at the shoulder, and the horn, and the shoulder again, for a long time, and then at Mr Ottershaw, who was threading a needle, and closed her notebook, and wrote nothing, and walked on. She has not examined it since, and she will not discuss it, and I have not asked her to. It is in the write-up as she left it. I asked Mr Ottershaw, by letter, whether there was anything he wished to add to this article. He wrote back, in a very fine hand, that he would be ninety-two in March, that he was still composing, and that there were eighty-three now. He did not mention case forty. Nor do I. See also Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III Wren Halloway Little Gore , four miles off Coldbarrow

title: Firstfield Meadow
text: Firstfield Meadow This article is about the meadow at the foot of the rainbow. For the Guild that runs it, see The Guild of Guides . For tutorials in general, and why nobody finishes them, see the Glossary of Cliches . Firstfield Meadow Known as Where Every Journey Begins* Footnote *Journeys already in progress also welcome Where At the foot of the rainbow, north-west of Thistlewick Kept by The Guild of Guides, Firstfield Chapter Guide Fizz, Tutorial Sprite, Third Class Stations Four: items, treasure, quests, combat Chest restocked At nine Sheep Three, according to the Guild Tutorials completed One Firstfield Meadow is a small meadow at the foot of the rainbow, a short way north-west of Thistlewick , off the road, where the Guild of Guides explains things to Chosen Ones. Every journey begins there. Forty-seven Chosen Ones skipped it, by pressing the button really fast. The Forty-Eighth did not, and is the only graduate on record. The meadow It is a pleasant meadow, with flowers, a tent, a fence with a gap in it, and a great many signs. A long board by the path reads CONTROLS. UP IS UP. DOWN IS DOWN. LEFT AND RIGHT ARE ALSO AVAILABLE. THE GUILD OF GUIDES RECOMMENDS TRYING ALL FOUR. Another reminds the visitor that he may save his progress at any time. He always could. It is a great weight off the mind anyway. There is a barrel labelled BARREL (FOR PRACTICE), with a second label at the bottom: WELL DONE. YOU HAVE SEARCHED A BARREL. THERE WILL BE MANY MORE. There is a log labelled SIT HERE TO REST, and under it, RESTING DOES NOTHING. IT IS FOR THE ATMOSPHERE. There is another log labelled OBSTACLE (EASY), and when you walk round it a small voice somewhere in the meadow cheers. Fizz Fizz is the meadow's guide: Tutorial Sprite, Third Class, small, bright, and audible from the road. Her first words to the Forty-Eighth were HEY! LISTEN! Her second were that every journey begins here. He pointed out that his had begun some time before, in a turnip field, and that since then he had walked out of a village and down a road. She said every. Journey. Begins. HERE. Then she explained walking to him, because he had just done it, and told him he was doing so well. She explains everything once. The Guild is very firm on once. She is very firm on signs, and will tell you that a sign is a sign, and that signs are for reading, and that you should press the button to read it, and that she knows you already did, she knows. She does not cover lore. Asked what the Dark Lord's weakness was, where the Sacred Key was, or what the lever does, she said LORE, three times, and was right about the lever, which does not exist, and which there always is. Her ambition is to be a Boss Warning Sprite, First Class, and wait outside the last door and shout IT'S WEAK TO FIRE. She practises on the sheep. The sheep is not weak to fire. She asks you not to check. Since the Quest she has applied for the post, and has put the Forty-Eighth down as a reference. I wrote to the Guild to ask whether he had been consulted. The Guild wrote back to say that that was lore. The four stations Station One: Items. Old Hollis, by the tent, has been expecting you. He has been expecting everybody. He gives every hero a stick, with the words It's dangerous to go alone! Take this, adjusted for the size of the party; the Forty-Eighth's was a three, then a four. He had given eleven thousand, two hundred and six sticks in forty-one years, and not one of them had ever come back. They go into cupboards. Every hero's mother has a cupboard, and in it is a stick. His wife Nell cuts them, every evening, by the fire, and picks out the straight ones, because she says a hero deserves a straight stick. The Forty-Eighth gave his stick back. Hollis shouted NELL, NELL, ONE'S COME BACK at the tent, and a small, round, delighted woman came out, inspected it, went back in, and came out with a straighter one. The first is on their mantelpiece. It is the first thing on that mantelpiece in forty-one years that is not Hollis, and she dusts it twice a day. Station Two: Treasure. A chest in the flowers, with a Potion in it and a note: WELL DONE FOR OPENING THE CHEST. PLEASE CLOSE THE CHEST. The Guild restocks it at nine. It is the most-opened chest in the world, and the only one that has ever been expecting you. Nix checked it for a false bottom. There was one, and under it a second note, WELL DONE, NIX, and Nix said that they had met her, then. Station Three: Quests. The sign says that Mrs Fenwick's sheep are lost, and adds, in brackets, that they are not lost, and, in more brackets, that they are not sheep. Dilys Fenwick stands by the fence with three pigs, one of them leaning on her. The Guild ordered sheep and sent these, and the form says sheep, so they are sheep. The Guild said a meadow has to have a fetch quest, and she said her sheep were not lost, and they said, well, lose them a bit. So they are lost, a bit. They are very good about it, and have been practising their baa, and would like that noted. If you decline to find them she says But thou must, and then says sorry, the Guild gave her that line. She and her husband Tam were married in the meadow. Fizz explained the vows to them first, twice, in capitals, and Tam cried at the second one, and says it was the capitals. Station Four: Combat. AMBUSH IN PROGRESS. PLEASE QUEUE. THE AMBUSH IS CONTRACTED TO LOSE. THE AMBUSH WOULD LIKE YOU TO KNOW HE TRIES. The ambush is Norbert, who stands in the gap in the fence with a sandwich, and puts it down, and wipes his hands on his trousers, and says STAND AND DELIVER, and then, your best attack, if you'd be so kind. Then he falls over, quite convincingly, and has a lie down, which is in the contract and is the best part of the job. In the year 2000 he had lost three thousand, one hundred and five times. His wife has the first one framed, and packs his lunch, and puts a note in it every day: LOSE WELL, LOVE. She says he is the best loser in the county. She means it nicely. He asked. Corvin Ash asked Norbert whether he was his rival. Norbert said, sorry, no, he was booked up through the spring. Graduation At the top of the meadow is the graduation sign: TUTORIALS COMPLETED IN THIS MEADOW: ONE. The one is painted over a nought, very carefully, by somebody with small hands and no experience of paint. The Forty-Eighth received a Certificate of Completion, which goes in the accessory slot, next to the stick. Nobody knows why it goes there. It is in his house, in the cupboard, with the stick. I asked the Forty-Eighth why he had not skipped it, when forty-seven before him had. He said that nobody had told him you could. Then he said that Fizz had looked as if she had been waiting a long time, and that it had not taken very long, really, and that he had got a stick. See also Thistlewick , a short walk south The Guild of Guides Bram Thistle , the graduate

title: Frostwick
text: Frostwick This article is about the town. For the woman who keeps its winter, see Pargeter . For clause two, which she read, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick and Two Reckonings . Frostwick Known as Home of the Winter Festival Where The far north, east of the road Snow Guaranteed* * Under contract. Schedule of snowfalls available on request from the parish Tolerance Plus or minus one flake Governed by The Working Group on the Winter Chief asset The Winter (maintained). Depreciating at four per cent Not an asset Mr Stagg Festival The twelfth. Ribbon at noon Icicle Reginald Frostwick is a town in the far north where it snows because the town pays it to. Forty-two years ago a man walking north broke its winter, and it thawed, for eleven days. On the twelfth day the town held a meeting, and retained a practitioner to put the winter back on a sensible footing, and asked the man to cut a ribbon. It has done both every year since. The winter The sign at the town's edge reads FROSTWICK. HOME OF THE WINTER FESTIVAL. SNOW GUARANTEED*, and along the bottom, much smaller: *Under contract. Schedule of snowfalls available on request from the parish. It is available on request. I requested it. Contract for the Maintenance of a Winter, Appendix C: Schedule of Snowfalls. Ordinary snow: four inches, overnight, not on market days. Blizzard: at the committee's request, in writing, one week's notice, not during carols. Festival Day: a light dusting, commencing at the ribbon, to settle on Mr Stagg's hat. Tolerance: plus or minus one flake. Somebody measures the snow on the lamp-posts, and it is exactly the contracted four inches, and the grit barrel has a sign on it saying that it is not to be used during the Festival, because the snow has been paid for. The winter is kept by Miss Eudora Pargeter, retained practitioner, in the Cold Room on the square, in pale blue, with her gloves on indoors as a matter of course. She would like it known before you ask that she is not an ice witch. She does refrigeration: larders, dairies, the fishmonger's, and the winter, which is one client, and a good one. She does January in an afternoon and is home by four. Her contract is for nine years, and has been renewed on time, and she would sign it again tomorrow. Her own larder is a shelf of frosted jars, labelled JANUARY, and which week. Her box files read CONTRACT; CONTRACT (AMENDMENTS); CONTRACT (AMENDMENTS TO THE AMENDMENTS); and a slim one, COMPLIMENTS. She is the only person in the world, so far as I have been able to find, who has read the Prophecy of Thistlewick all the way through. She read it at her desk, when the Forty-Eighth showed it to her. She said there was no break clause, and no notice period, and that clause twelve renews itself, and that she would never sign a thing like that. Then she turned back to clause two, and read out that "a hundred years" is a defined term, meaning such period as the Committee shall find convenient, and then she mentioned that there would be a light dusting on Tuesday, for the look of the thing. She did not do the arithmetic for him. She does not do anybody's arithmetic for them. See Two Reckonings . The Working Group The town is governed by the Working Group on the Winter, which has never had apologies for absence, because nobody in Frostwick has ever missed a meeting. It is chaired by Mrs Wilhelmina Blagg. She will tell you that the curse is an asset. It is on page one of the register, depreciating at four per cent a year, towards spring, eventually, which has been budgeted for. The auditor called it forward-looking. He came in August. It was snowing. He was very impressed. The register of assets reads: 1. The Winter (maintained); value, considerable. 2. The Ribbon (one). 3. The Lanterns (212). 4. Mr Stagg, which is struck through, and in the margin: NOT AN ASSET. A PERSON. - W.B. The founding minutes are on the table, and I copy them as I found them: MINUTES OF THE WORKING GROUP ON THE WINTER. Extraordinary meeting, the twelfth day. Item 1. That the winter has stopped. Noted. Item 2. Takings, carols and lanterns, since: nil. Noted, with concern. Item 3. That a practitioner be retained to put it back, on a sensible footing. For, 41. Against, 3, who had planted peas. Carried. Item 4. That Mr Stagg be asked to open the first Festival. Carried unanimously, with one abstention: Mr Stagg. Item 5. Any other business. The peas. Deferred. The peas are still deferred. There is a crate of bunting in the room marked BUNTING (CONTESTED), and the carol sheets each have a verse crossed out by the Working Group, on the grounds that it promised snow on the twelfth without consulting them. Clem Blagg, who was seven in the year 2000 and does the lanterns, knows all the minutes off by heart: item three, the winter, CARRIED. Clem's view, given to the Forty-Eighth unprompted, is that Nan says Mrs Stagg has never once been cold, not in forty winters, and that it must be Mr Stagg's lanterns, because he does ever such good lanterns. I was told that, when this was said, the committee found the ceiling very interesting, and that Mrs Blagg found it most interesting of all. Perce and Ida Percival Stagg, Perce, is an old man in a red coat with a white fur collar who stands beside the ribbon post as though it might need him. He is the man who broke the winter. He was not, he will tell you, a Chosen One. Nobody chose him. Everybody went north that year, the year of the Forty-Fourth: farmers, tinkers, a man with a goat. He got as far as Frostwick, and the winter was in the way, so he saw to it. He has never mentioned that he was not chosen, because nobody has ever asked, and they were all so pleased, and it is a lovely Festival. When a lady with a basket goes by and says Our Chosen One! he does a face, warm and modest and very well practised. He does it again at noon on the twelfth, when he cuts the ribbon, and the whole town cheers, and he goes pink. The ribbon is in a gilt case at the Working Group's rooms, cut and tied so often it is mostly knots: THE RIBBON. 40 FESTIVALS. 1 RIBBON. There are forty-two now. Ida Stagg loves the Festival. She will tell you that he did one great thing forty years ago, and a great many things since, and none of those ever got a ribbon. She asks you not to tell him she said so, because he will only go pink again. Their house has its door shut, and a card in the window in two hands: AT THE RIBBON. - P. BACK FOR TEA. - I. Through the window there are two armchairs drawn up very close to the fire, and two pairs of slippers warming on the fender, toes touching. The ribbon post has an iron crown on top of it, worked like frost on a window. It is Hob Grumnir's work. In the year 2000 he asked whether he might have it back, for the spring, for a piece he had in mind at Great Dunnage. Perce said that everybody ties a ribbon to that crown, and that you cannot tie a ribbon to a bare post, you know. It slides down. Hob said that it did, aye. The crown is still on the post, and ribbons do not slide off it. The Eleven Days The inn is named for the thaw. Mrs Tibby Marchpane will tell you about it whether you ring the bell or not; the card on the bell says RING FOR SERVICE, OR FOR THE STORY OF THE THAW, and they are, in practice, the same thing. Eleven days it lasted. Asked what happened on the twelfth, she says: the meeting. A room is eleven crowns, three quilts and a hot brick, snow included. In the morning it has snowed four inches, exactly, and not on the path. She draws a little face in golden syrup on every guest's porridge regardless of age. She drew one on mine. By the fire is a brass plate over a line painted along the skirting: THE ELEVEN DAYS. SNOW DEPTH DURING: THIS HIGH. The line is on the floor. The visitors' book is open on the bar under a card, SIGNED BY THREE CHOSEN ONES. PLEASE ASK. It is ruled NAME, FROM, WHITHER, and a fourth column in a newer hand, CHOSEN ONE (Y/N). There are two very old entries a century apart, both bound north, both marked Y, the names faded out; one says Lovely weather, and the other says Cold. The third is P. Stagg, of nowhere in particular, bound north, and in the last column, in Mrs Marchpane's hand, a firm Y. Under the Y, rubbed out but not quite, smaller, in his own hand: N. The Forty-Eighth signed it too. The card has not been changed. I asked Mrs Marchpane whether it ought to say four. She said that it said three, and that it always had, and would I like the story of the thaw. The snowman on the green wears a Festival rosette: JUDGED - SNOW, ADEQUATE. The icicle on the tavern sign has been there so long it has a name, which is Reginald. A barrel by the Cold Room is labelled SPARE SNOW (CONTRACT), and is full, and I suspect is not, strictly, allowed. Spare Cotterill made a snowman here and wrote home that he was under contract. See also Pargeter Two Reckonings The Prophecy of Thistlewick , clause two Coldbarrow , the nearest neighbour, west along the snow

title: Gladhollow
text: Gladhollow This article is about the small town in the far south-west. For welcoming in general, and the people who do it at the gates of towns, see the Glossary of Cliches . Gladhollow Known as Gladhollow (welcome to it) Where The far south-west, a gate at each end Mayor A. Podmore Official Welcomer West gate. One copper a day Farewell Boy East gate. A copper and a half Arms Two crossed swords. (Welcome) The key Under the pot. Of course it is Best kept plant Eleven years running. The only entrant Heroes Please, no Gladhollow is a small town of one street in the far south-west, with a gate at either end. At the west gate a boy says Welcome to Gladhollow!, and nothing else, because it is in his duties. At the east gate another says Farewell from Gladhollow! and Mind how you go. In between, the town has had a great many heroes through it, and has learned to lock its doors. The Welcomer The council's notice at the west gate reads: OFFICIAL WELCOMER (WEST GATE). ONE COPPER A DAY. DUTIES: TO SAY "WELCOME TO GLADHOLLOW!" AND NOTHING ELSE. The paper has been read so often it has gone as soft as cloth. In the margin, in pencil, somebody has been keeping a count. The Welcomer in the year 2000 was Toby Wendle, ten, with a saucepan on his head, which rings like a bell when you walk into him. He does not fall over. He has had a great deal of practice. He straightens the saucepan, takes a deep breath, beams, and says Welcome to Gladhollow!, and there is no rest of it, and he is delighted. He is not allowed a second sentence, so he has worked on the first, and has fifteen ways of saying it. The list is on his kitchen table, headed FIFTEEN WAYS, and I have it from the Forty-Eighth, who heard all of them, in order: the Standard; the Formal, a bow so low the saucepan falls off, caught without looking; the Whisper, for people who look tired; the Song, on three notes going up, the last a little beyond him, and he goes anyway; the Salute, with the handle of the saucepan; the Surprised; the Slow One, one word at a time, for anybody from abroad, which the job description does not mention, and he checked; the Dramatic Pause; the Rainy Day, with the saucepan held over your head, for practice; the Very Loud, for people on horses; the Sorry, for people who have walked into him, with a touch of the plaster on his cheek; the Tour, turning slowly on the spot and pointing at every building, at the mayor's house rather longer than the others; the Evening, hushed and golden, which he could not wait for; the Classic, which is exactly the same as the first, and he is extremely pleased with it; and the fifteenth, which was not finished, and which he tried anyway, going up at the end, Welcome to Gladhollow?, and looked anxiously to see whether a question counted as a second sentence. It was decided that it did not. He wrote something on the back of his hand. Asked about the town, he will say Welcome to Gladhollow, with his eyes on the mayor's house, and both hands flat beside him, pushing, like somebody sliding a very heavy bookcase aside. His eyes then go to the well, and to the pot beside the well, and to the well, and to the pot, and then, very innocently, to the sky. Then he points at his granny's barrels, and at his granny, and puts a hand on his heart. He has said nothing. It is all in the duties. The town Granny Wendle's barrels stand outside her door, and every hero who comes through has the potions out of them. She does not mind. They are very good potions. She would like them back, though. They are for her knees. Each one is rolled up in a stocking in the straw, with a label sewn in, PLEASE RETURN TO MRS WENDLE, GLADHOLLOW. Her front door is locked, because there is nothing in there but her good china, and she has met heroes: every pot off the dresser and smashed on the floor before she had the kettle on, looking for coppers. There is never coppers in a pot. Ask anyone. The Forty-Eighth gave her a potion back, and she said that was Tuesday's knee sorted. The end house has a card in the window: NO HEROES, PLEASE. THERE IS NOTHING IN THE CUPBOARDS, NOTHING IN THE BARRELS AND NOTHING UNDER THE BED. WE HAVE CHECKED. SO HAVE THE LAST NINE OF YOU. Through the window every cupboard is open, and every one has a card in it saying NOTHING HERE. They have planned for you. The well has its lid padlocked shut, and beside it an old clay pot, and under the pot is the key. Of course it is. The water is cold and clear and tastes faintly of stone, and you put the key back. Through one window an old man is asleep in a chair with a newspaper over his face, and the headline says HERO PASSES THROUGH. It has been the headline for some time. By the road there is a log with WELCOME carved into one end and FAREWELL into the other, by two boys with one penknife. The Farewell Boy At the east gate the Farewell Boy in the year 2000 was Ned, Toby's brother, slightly bigger, with his hair brushed very flat for the job, and he had clearly been waiting for somebody to leave. His duties are two sentences, and he was paid a copper and a half. When the Forty-Eighth asked him about the boy at the west gate he said Farewell from Gladhollow! That's our Toby, and had spent his second sentence on his brother, and did not look as if he minded at all. Under the notice was pinned VACANCY SHORTLY. APPLICATIONS TO THE MAYOR, and under that an application, pinned up so that everybody could see it. It was one sentence long. The mayor's house The mayor's house has a bookcase full of the town council's minutes, going back a very long way, with one volume sticking out further than the rest. If you pull it the bookcase swings out on a hinge, and behind it there are steps down, and at the bottom there is a room. I describe what is in it because the town has asked me to, now. There is a ledger headed T. WENDLE, WELCOMER: a copper a day, in one column, going back years, and in the next column, in the mayor's hand, another copper from the council for every one he has saved. He has saved every one. At the bottom, underlined twice: DO NOT TELL TOBY. Under that, in pencil, in a much rounder hand: I havent. There is a bag of coppers tied at the neck, labelled FOR THE UNIFORM, a good deal heavier than a copper a day. There is a cap on a stand, blue with white piping, brand new and much too small for anybody but one person, and the label inside says FAREWELL BOY, and somebody has written TOBY under it, and somebody else has crossed that out because it was not official yet, and then written it in again, smaller. On the desk the mayor had left a note: GONE TO SEE ABOUT A FITTING. BACK AT FOUR. - A. PODMORE, MAYOR. The town map has a very small boy drawn in pencil at each gate. The council's minutes record that the Welcomer is to say Welcome to Gladhollow and nothing else: carried, nine to nil, with one abstention, in pencil, T. WENDLE (AGED SEVEN). Since the Quest Toby Wendle has been Farewell Boy since the spring of 2001, in the cap, which fits. He has two sentences now, and uses both of them with enormous care, and I am told that Mind how you go is said fifteen different ways. There is a new Welcomer at the west gate, a girl of eight, who has been given the saucepan, and has been told that she may say Welcome to Gladhollow! and nothing else, and has asked Toby how he managed, and he has not told her, because it is not in his duties. He has given her the list. The potted plant in the mayor's house has won BEST KEPT PLANT, GLADHOLLOW, eleven years running, and is the only entrant, and is very modest about it. It has won twice more since. The mayor says that this is a matter of record, and that I may print it. See also Olde Evermore , to the north Restwell

title: Great Dunnage
text: Great Dunnage This article is about the town inside its wall, its halls and its warehouse. For the works up the valley, which Great Dunnage would like you to know is only one works, see Upper Clanging . For the Smiths, see The Worshipful Company of Smiths . Great Dunnage Known as The Corporation of Great Dunnage Where In the west, inside its own wall, on the cut, eleven miles down the valley from Upper Clanging Arms An anvil, a bell and a key Motto Quis similis nobis? Who is like unto us? The Corporation has looked into it Works Nine, and the Other Nail Works Mayor Gristwood, in the most hat you have ever seen First Mayor Alderman Josiah Dunnage, in allegorical armour. He sold nails Counting House Sealed 1788. Opened informally 2000. Form L incomplete Anthem Nine verses, to be sung standing. Verse two is the same, but more Haulage Plummer & Partner. The partner is the grey Great Dunnage is the largest town in the west, a walled works town on the canal with nine works inside its wall and a Corporation that is very proud of every one of them. It has never heard of you. Nobody is too busy for Great Dunnage; they only think they are. The gate Over the gate, on a gilded board, are the arms of the Corporation: an anvil, a bell and a key, done so small and so gold that from the road they look like a flourish. The key is the key to the Counting House. It is the only one the town still has, and it is painted on a board. Under the arms is the motto, QUIS SIMILIS NOBIS? Who is like unto us? The Corporation has looked into it. In the gateway, in the Corporation's blue coat, stands a watchman who has been asked to be impressive and is doing his best. He asked the Forty-Eighth his name and business. Bram, of Thistlewick, Chosen One number forty-eight. Forty-eight what? Thistlewick: that's the Prophecy people, down south. Charming. He wrote in his ledger BRAM (THISTLEWICK) - PROPHECY, SOME SORT, and let him in, and told him to mind the carts, mind the canal, and mind the Mayor. He is the only person I have found in the whole of this history who had never heard of the Forty-Eighth, and the Forty-Eighth says that it was the most restful conversation of the year. The town In the square stands a statue of a knight in full armour with a sword and a shield: ALDERMAN JOSIAH DUNNAGE, FIRST MAYOR. ERECTED BY THE CORPORATION, TO THE CORPORATION'S OWN DESIGN, AT THE CORPORATION'S EXPENSE, IN HONOUR OF THE CORPORATION. Under it, smaller: THE ARMOUR IS ALLEGORICAL. ALDERMAN DUNNAGE SOLD NAILS. The Nine Works of the Corporation are listed on a board: the Dunnage Iron Company, the Bell Foundry, the Nail Works, the Chain Works, the Wire Works, the Anchor Works, the Screw Works, the Brass Works, and the Other Nail Works. Along the bottom, smaller: SEE ALSO UPPER CLANGING - A WORKS, UP THE VALLEY. The anthem is posted beside it, to be sung standing, all nine verses, on the Mayor's Day: Great Dunnage! Great Dunnage! Nine chimneys, and more! We make what they make up at Clanging, but more. Verse two is the same, but more. Mrs Poskitt went up to Upper Clanging for the day once, and says you would love it: only the one works, and they all know each other, which she thought was ever so sweet. Great Dunnage is like that, but nine times. The foundry gate has a board wired to it: NO VISITORS. THE CRUCIBLES ARE NOT MIMICS. THE MOULDS ARE NOT MIMICS. NOTHING IN HERE IS A MIMIC. PLEASE STOP HITTING THINGS TO CHECK. The Iron Company's gate says NO ADMITTANCE EXCEPT ON BUSINESS, and under it, newer, HEROES ARE NOT BUSINESS. Somebody has had a hero in, once. On the quay the crates are stencilled GREAT DUNNAGE - TO ALL PARTS, and smaller, (MOSTLY SUMP). A barrel with the Corporation's seal on it is dated 1788 and says EMPTY, like everything else in Great Dunnage that was sealed in 1788. At the Iron Company's gate, in the year 2000, was Cotter Cotterill, eldest of the Cotterills of Upper Clanging, on the big furnace till the spring and then home for good. He went home every Saturday, off at six, eleven miles up the valley, and back down for the Monday. Twenty-two miles, for one night. He is always very glad to get home. He has been home since the spring of 2000, for good, and the heel-irons Hob made him are on his boots still. Plummer & Partner In the haulage yard in the north-west corner, Mr Plummer, a broad man with a moustache, does anything, anywhere, by Tuesday, with his partner, who is the grey. She walked in off the west road one winter, on her own, with a good saddle on and nobody in it. Nobody came for her, so she stayed. She is the best worker in the yard, knows every road in the valley, has a stall with her name on it and a say in the routes, and plans the Tuesdays. Her name is Duchess; there was a crest on the saddle, and it seemed to suit her. The crest was a knight in a field, looking back over his shoulder. It was Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore's saddle, and she was his horse, whom he had tied up in a village with a sign six years before, and gone to find the gate. He only ever called her Horse. He crossed the yard to her, slowly, and she put her nose into the front of his tabard, where it always went, and breathed out. Mr Plummer said that she would be his, of course, saddle and all, only she did the canal run, and the Tuesdays. Sir Aldric looked at her, and said, Oh, no. No, no. Look at her. She is doing so well. The cart's tailboard now reads PLUMMER & PARTNER. HAULAGE. (THE PARTNER IS THE GREY.) And under that, newer, very neat: (HER KNIGHT CALLS. NOT TUESDAYS.) The Counting House The Counting House is mostly door: bronze, a good deal taller than a man, with a lock in the middle the size of a cartwheel. It was sealed in 1788, when the key was lost, and the town has been run since on a memorandum, framed beside it: THAT, the Counting House being sealed, the accounts of the Corporation be taken as read; and THAT the Corporation be assumed to have enough. Carried unanimously. It was to be opened formally, by a licensed person, with the preamble read in full. A licence is issued on completion of Form L, An Application by a Licensed Person to Open the Counting House, to be completed by the licensed person and countersigned by a licensed person. There are no licensed persons. The Town Clerk's book of applications to open the Counting House goes back two hundred and twelve years, and every one is marked DECLINED - FORM L INCOMPLETE, and the clerk who wrote the first one also designed Form L. Mayor Gristwood had the preamble ready. It took forty minutes, and he was down to thirty-eight. In the year 2000 Nix, who locates things, and says that doors are things, put an ear to the lock and did something small with two fingers, and it took nine seconds, and the Door stood open while the Mayor was still on mindful. That was not the Opening. The Counting House is opened informally; the Opening proper will follow on completion of Form L. Form L is still blank, and in law the Counting House has never been opened. Behind the Door there was one room, and one chair in it, and on the chair a note, and under the note, very neatly stacked, a little money: WE SPENT IT. J. POCKLINGTON, CLERK TO THE CORPORATION. 1788. Two hundred and twelve years the Corporation had been assumed to have enough, on the strength of a chair. It is, to be fair, a very good chair. The Mayor sat down on it, as the first Mayor to do so. The money came, when counted, to one thousand seven hundred and eighty-eight crowns, which nobody can explain, and the Mayor said it was not the Corporation's, because the memorandum says they have enough. Nix asked its provenance, and was told none whatever, and wrote that down. The Mayor read the preamble to the chair, in full, twice. He has since been composing a shorter one. The Smiths' Hall The Worshipful Company of Smiths of Great Dunnage holds its Assize of Hammers every three years, at which every smith in the land may submit one piece, to be judged by the Wardens against the Schedule. Very few manage to submit one. It is a very good Schedule. Prime Warden Stannard, a tall woman in black with iron-grey hair and gold at her collar, stands at the Company's table as if it might try something. Warden Crabbe, Junior Warden, reads the Schedule out at the Assize, all forty-one clauses, and it takes most of the day. People ask why they don't just pin it up. They do. He reads it out as well. Miss Fettle, Appraiser, in round spectacles, looks at swords the way other people look at sunsets, and always asks after the tang. She does not charge for tangs. She also does curses, elective, on Form C-1, in triplicate, the economy one lasting till you next sleep in a proper bed. They are mostly paperwork. The Schedule's first two clauses are that a piece shall be the entrant's own work, from the ore up, and the entrant's own property. Hob Grumnir has never owned anything he made; somebody wants a thing, and he says take it, and there is a shelf for the invoicing. In the year 2000 he asked eleven people for one thing back, for the spring, and every one of them said no, with a better reason than his. He laid Beatrice on the Company's table instead. She was disqualified, under clause one, not being his own work, and passed clauses two to forty-one, and the Wardens' notes are pinned up beside the prize piece of the last Assize, which is a very good hinge: BEATRICE. A hammer. From H. Grumnir, Thistlewick. Clause one: not satisfied. Two to forty-one: satisfied. DISQUALIFIED. Remarks: in the Wardens' opinion, right about everything. Hob said that she would be unbearable, and that he would not bother entering again, because he had had what he came for. The hall is worth seeing for itself. The Company's shield reads STRIKE WHILE IT IS HOT, and under it, AND THEN LET IT COOL. WE ARE NOT ANIMALS. The banners read BY HAMMER AND HAND, and under that, in chalk, AND BY SCHEDULE. An apprentice's examination armour has a note pinned to it: PASSED. ONE ELBOW BACKWARDS. The prize shield of 1987 is Bryd Ollerenshaw's, BEST IN HALL; Hob did not enter in eighty-seven, because he had a cold, and would have won. Another suit of armour has a card in Warden Crabbe's handwriting: ENTERED FOR THE PRIZE BY A SMITH WHO WISHES TO REMAIN ANONYMOUS. The Bell The Bell is an inn where the panel for the Contest at the Sign of the Bell eat, and they cannot help it; they mark the soup. Mrs Dewhirst keeps it, a room is fifteen crowns, and you will be judged at breakfast. Breakfast, the morning the Forty-Eighth stayed, got a seven. Mrs Harbottle, in gold lace, chairs the panel, which practises on everything between contests: the fire was a six; the door was a four, because it creaks in the wrong key. Mr Ambler gives everything a nine, and cannot hear, and nobody has ever had the heart. Miss Quayle gives everything a two. It averages out. The Contest is always tonight; it has simply not had the entries. In the year 2000 it had four: Mr Septimus Dray, Instrumental (Other Wind), on the serpent, for eleven minutes, very like a drain that has had bad news; Miss Lettice Moon, Ballad (Sad), fourteen verses, everybody dies, including the narrator, who comes back for the chorus; Mr Tweddle, Birdsong (Open), whose thrush that had lost its keys went looking for them all round the room and found them, and drew a three from Miss Quayle, at which the room gasped; and Piper Quill, Ballad (Not Sad), which nobody had ever entered. She came second, by one point, to the thrush. Her article has it. There is also a snug at the Bell, which in the year 2000 was booked in the name of Mr Fairweather, for eleven minutes, as a standing appointment. What was said in it is not mine to print, and I have not. The Bonded Warehouse On the quay is the Bonded Warehouse, kept by Mr Tibbs, wharfinger, in half-rimmed spectacles. Nothing out without the ticket, and the duty, and him. Brandy, iron, cloth, and a piano from abroad, the wrong way up in a crate marked THIS WAY UP, on which the duty is more than the piano. The bonds are numbered, and are a history of the town in themselves. No. 2, one statue of the First Mayor, actual size, duty on the hat. No. 7, ten thousand buttons, all different, declared as one button, repeated. No. 9, a ship in a bottle; the ship is full size; the bottle is not described. No. 11, fog, one barrel, from Nether Sopping, duty paid in advance by Nether Sopping, to be rid of it. No. 23, spare keys for the Counting House; the crate is empty, which explains a great deal. No. 31, rain, one barrel, returned by Upper Clanging as second-hand. No. 40, one cabbage, very large, for the show. The show was in 1802. Nobody has been brave enough to check on the cabbage. Bond No. 1 was a tall wardrobe, locked, the only thing in the warehouse that was: ONE COAT. HELD. RENT PAID TO DATE. The Bond Book had a date for it, and the word coat, and nothing else, and for eleven years the rent came by post every quarter, never late, no name. The coat was collected in the year 2000, by the party of the second part, and it fits. The Bond Book's first entry has a name now. It is in Nix's article , as much of it as she will allow, and Nix walked a long way round to avoid that door before she went through it. The rent has stopped coming. Mr Tibbs says he misses it, a little, every quarter day. The Bottom Lock At the end of the basin, where the cut goes out under the road, is the bottom lock. In the spring of 2000 it jammed, with thirty of the Iron Company's boats sat on the cut, because something was on the paddle down in the culvert, and the Canal Company sent in their smallest man, and he did not come out. A man does not fit. Spare Cotterill fits. He checked that his jumper was on, because those are the terms, and gave the Forty-Eighth his bag to hold, and asked whether they would be there, and was told yes, and went down a ladder into a square black hole in the brickwork about the size of a nine-year-old. He was not frightened of the dark. He came out, and the man came out, and the paddle was cleared, and everybody was there. Spare's article has it, as he tells it, which is to say very briefly. I asked the watchman at the gate, when I wrote for this article, whether he had heard of the Forty-Eighth now. He wrote back that he had looked in his ledger, and that he had a BRAM (THISTLEWICK) - PROPHECY, SOME SORT, in the spring of 2000, and that he was very welcome to come again, and to mind the Mayor. See also Upper Clanging , eleven miles up the valley The Worshipful Company of Smiths Nix , for the coat Hob Grumnir , for Beatrice Carn Drey , east of the town

title: Hithermost
text: Hithermost This article is about the village under the mountain, and its chapel. For what is through the Door, see The Stair . For the knight, see Sir Dunstable of the Vale . Hithermost Known as The last village before the mountain And For some, the first one after it Where The far north-west, at the foot of the mountain Chapel The Chapel of Continuance Services Continuous Keeper of the Record Brother Quillon Teas Kettle permitting The village lamp Borrowed. Back directly Saved Four times in the one year, by one account. Please stop Hithermost is a village at the foot of the mountain in the far north-west, the last before it and, for some, the first after it. People go into the mountain through a door at the top of the village, and most of them come back, and quite a few come back in through the porch of the chapel, looking puzzled, and the village gives them tea. The village The sign says HITHERMOST. THE LAST VILLAGE BEFORE THE MOUNTAIN, and under it, added later and in smaller letters, AND, FOR SOME, THE FIRST ONE AFTER IT. The well says LAST WATER BEFORE THE MOUNTAIN, and under it, FIRST WATER AFTER (SEE CHAPEL). Asked what is after the mountain, a villager will say Hithermost, mostly. They come back down, you see. We do teas. The tea room's card says TEAS. HOT FOOD. KETTLE PERMITTING, and it is frequently not permitting, because the kettle is at the chapel again. Brother Quillon makes a great deal of tea, and most of it has been made in that kettle. The teapot stands, when it is in, on an iron trivet worked like a sprig of holly. It is Hob Grumnir's work. In the year 2000 he asked whether he might have it back, for a bit. The villager asked where they were to stand the pot, then; on the cloth? They come down off that mountain cold to the bone, every one of them, and the first thing they get is a pot of tea off that trivet. Hob said keep it. The village has been saved a great deal. A house near the bottom answers a knock with Not today, thank you, in the tone of a house that has been saved four times this year and is still finding the bits, and you hear a cupboard being locked. Through its window a family sits in its front room, braced. A rain barrel has its lid weighted down with a very large stone and a card: THE BARREL HAS ALSO BEEN SAVED. PLEASE STOP. Another house has pots by the door, and under one of them a note: THERE IS NO KEY UNDER ANY OF THE POTS. PLEASE PUT THE POTS BACK. Under another: STILL NO. There is a mountaineer, whose door is locked with a card on the knocker, GONE UP THE MOUNTAIN. BACK SHORTLY, and eleven more cards pinned under it in the same hand, all saying the same thing. He always does come back. Usually in through the chapel porch, looking puzzled. His calendar has GONE UP written on every Tuesday. The Chapel of Continuance The board outside reads: CHAPEL OF CONTINUANCE. KEEPER OF THE RECORD: BR. QUILLON. SERVICES: CONTINUOUS. Travellers are asked to sign the Book before proceeding into the mountain, and again on the way back, if applicable, and again after that. The glass is worth looking at. In one panel a saint goes into a mountain; in the next, the same saint comes out of a chapel porch, looking puzzled. In another a saint writes her name in a book, and again, and again, smaller, to make it fit. In another a saint with a candle stands at the door of a mountain, looking back over her shoulder, the way people do when they have done this before. And in the last a monk stands at a lectern with a cup of tea, and a very expressive silence, and the glazier has managed to get the silence in. You can see it. The Book lies open on the lectern and glows, softly and evenly, with nothing to account for it. Those going into the mountain write their names in it, in case of misfortune. In case of misfortune they come back in through the porch, and write their names again. The page is in a great many hands. Most of them are the same hand. The old volumes are stacked beside the lectern, every one of them full, and the spine of each says CONTINUED. The porch has a plant in it which has been knocked over and stood up again so many times that it has grown a little to one side, to be ready. Brother Quillon keeps the Record. Asked whether he remembers the people who sign it, he says that the Order forbids it, and that it is the only thing the Order forbids. He smiles, serenely, with his eyes shut. It is a very expressive smile. It has had forty years. He says that every soul deserves a second chance, and does not look at Sir Dunstable, very clearly indeed, and says something under his breath that sounds like a number in the low two hundreds. Every afternoon at ten past four he pours a cup of tea and puts it on the lectern. It is still warm. It is always still warm. Sir Dunstable Sir Dunstable of the Vale is a knight in armour that has been polished a great many times and scorched very slightly more, who comes in through the chapel porch at a quarter past four, every day, to the minute, and signs the Book, just in case, and finds his tea waiting, and is delighted. "Oh, how kind. Every time! The fellow's a mind-reader." Brother Quillon says nothing, with enormous tact. Sir Dunstable explains, with some warmth, that nothing happened. He has been through the Door once or twice. Went in, had a look round, came out. Grand day. There are, in the village and well beyond it, competing theories about Sir Dunstable, and I set out the evidence on both sides as fairly as I am able. I have not decided between them, and I am not going to. That he is alive. He takes the tea, and is delighted by it, every time. He borrowed the village's lamp ("Back directly. - D."), and after the Quest he lent it to the Forty-Eighth, in person, handle first, with lovely manners, and it was a perfectly solid lamp, and the Forty-Eighth carried it down the Stair and has it still. He is a shareholder in the Kingdom of Fairholme , with a chair and a place card, and the council minutes list him under apologies (in a mountain), not under deceased, and the council minutes everything. He is very slightly more singed each time, and the singeing is cumulative, which is a living thing's habit. And the Forty-Eighth's party came back in through the porch too, and nobody suggests that the Forty-Eighth is dead. That he is not. The Book is his name all the way down the page, Just in case, and Brother Quillon's number is in the low two hundreds. He comes in through the porch, the way people come back who went through the Door and did not come out of it. His chalk marks down the Stair, each a D. and a number and each a little deeper than the last, stop at D. 212, and nobody had been past it. Something on the Stair is always on its way up, in the dark, and nobody has seen who. And a quarter past four, every day, to the minute. The village has its own evidence, and every piece of it has an answer. His laundry is done on Mondays by the woman at the tea room, who says that it is always a little singed, and always dry, and that she has never once seen him bring it or fetch it; it is simply there in the basket at a quarter past four. He receives post: the Fairholme minutes, every quarter, and a seed catalogue. He has never been seen to read either, and both are gone by the morning. Whether he casts a shadow by lamplight has been argued in the tea room for years, and is not settled, because the lamp he would cast it by is the village's, and he has had it, and lately the Forty-Eighth has had it. The tea does not go cold. Brother Quillon will not say whether that is the tea. I asked Sir Dunstable directly, on my visit, in the chapel, at a quarter past four. He said that it was very good of me to come so far, and that nothing had happened, and signed the Book. I asked why he signed it every time. He said: "Just in case." My own view is that the knight is a man of excellent manners, and that the question is none of my business. At the Slain Wyvern there is a book on it. It is held by Sops. The odds have not moved in two years, which Sops says has never happened before on anything, and which he declines to interpret. The Door into the Mountain At the top of the village, a timbered mouth in the rock, and past it a stair going down into a dark that does not stop. A board is nailed to the frame: NO ADMITTANCE WITHOUT A LAMP. BY ORDER. LAMP ON HOOK. There is a hook under the board, and no lamp on it, and chalked beside it, in a cheerful hand, Borrowed lamp. Back directly. - D. Until the Quest was over the Forty-Eighth had no lamp, and did not go in. Sir Dunstable would not have dreamt of lending it before. A man with an appointment. Not done. Afterwards he had a free afternoon, and Sir Dunstable said that he would want the lamp, then, and unhooked it from his belt, and asked for it back directly, because he goes in at a quarter past four. He did not say which quarter past four. He has not asked for it back. See The Stair . See also The Stair Sir Dunstable of the Vale Brother Quillon

title: Places
text: Places The world is about a hundred and twenty days' walk across in either direction, by the reckoning of anyone who has tried it, and most of those days are spent in a field. What follows are the parts that are not field. The road north Place What it is Thistlewick The village that sends the Chosen Ones, and believes itself the middle of the world. Prophecy Hall The gold one, up the road. The Committee, in session. The Gilded Turnip The inn, named after the problem. Rooms twenty crowns. Nix's Emporium Everything previously owned. By whom, we don't ask. Firstfield Meadow A meadow at the foot of a rainbow, where things are explained to you. The Gloamwood A wood, with a Thing in it, and a man on a log. The Obligatory Tower Where the Dark Lord lives. Ground floor. Door at the bottom. The south Place What it is Nether Sopping Where the Chosen Ones go afterwards. The sea is right there. The Slain Wyvern A tavern, with a goose over the mantel. Also, my table. The Lighthouse of Saint Bother A light for a sea nobody sails. The Bottomless Pit Approximately. The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth A hero's grave, with a bench on it. The north Place What it is Upper Clanging Engineers, rain, and a ship two hundred years in the making. The Long Field Where Upper Clanging keeps its attempts. Frostwick Snow, a working group, and the only person who has read clause two. Further out The rest of the world is being written up as I am able to visit it, or as people come in out of the rain and tell me about it. It includes Great Dunnage , Olde Evermore and a great many villages with fewer than one inn.

title: Little Gore
text: Little Gore For the elegy on the fingerpost, see Piper Quill . For the invitation, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . For the big house four miles off, see Fenmarch Hall . Little Gore Known as Little Gore Where The south-east, four miles from Fenmarch, which round here is the same as a long way from anywhere Population Eleven, and a cat, and some more since Knight in the field Dame Winifred Cope, of the Order of the Errant Reports Nothing to report. Quarterly Banns Hester Plumb and Thomas Vane. Third time of asking Invitations Followed Carrier Abel Thrush, 1941 - 1991. He walks it still Little Gore is a hamlet of a few houses round a green in the south-east, on a sandy road four miles from Fenmarch . Eleven years ago its whole population walked to Fenmarch in the rain for a wedding nobody had invited them to, because nobody had told them not to. The invitation arrived in the year 2000. It is on the mantelpiece. The green Mrs Hester Vane, in the front garden of the nearest house, is plainly delighted to see anybody. She has been to Fenmarch, and that is the furthest; she was married there, eleven years ago this summer. The whole of Little Gore walked over for it, all eleven of them, in their best, and it rained the whole way, and nobody minded at all. Her husband Tom is in the gardens at Fenmarch, and walks it every day, four miles there and four back, and says it is the best part. On the green, three children play weddings. Bess, with a daisy chain on her head, is the bride, or Mum; it is the same thing. Alfie, with his hair wetted flat, is Dad, and has to stand there and look pleased, and Dad says that is the whole job. Nell is everybody else: the whole of Little Gore, half of Fenmarch, the vicar, the rain and the cake. Mrs Vane asks visitors to mind them, because they will marry you if you stand still. A log by the green has a row of daisies laid along it very carefully; they are the pews. A barrel of confetti is labelled FOR THE NEXT ONE, and there is confetti on the barrel, the step, the cat and the vicar. The banns are on the board by the post, older than all the other notices and very carefully kept out of the rain: BANNS OF MARRIAGE between HESTER PLUMB, of this parish, and THOMAS VANE, of the parish of Fenmarch. Third time of asking. Pinned under them, on a card gone brown at the edges: INVITATIONS TO FOLLOW. Round them, newer, are three notices of births, a year or two apart, each with a drawing of a very round baby in the corner. The invitation The invitation was in Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore's tabard. His father gave it to him the morning he rode out from Fenmarch in 1991, to carry four miles to Little Gore as his first errand: deliver this, and then you may go errant. He went errant for nine years, and did not deliver it. In the year 2000 he read the banns over the Forty-Eighth's shoulder, and the card under them, and went a colour, and said Invitations to follow. I am the invitations. Whether he then set out for Little Gore the long way, by the coast and a lay-by in the far west and Frostwick and the Fenmarch road twice, in different directions, both times on purpose, and came over a rise on the third evening and said THERE, told you I knew the way, or whether somebody pointed at the fingerpost, which said LITTLE GORE, is a matter on which the company differ, and I have not tried to settle it. Either way it was a very good way, and nobody would change a mile of it. He took off his helmet, which nobody had seen him do, and held out the letter in both hands. SIR ALDRIC PEMBERTON-GORE THE SECOND REQUESTS THE PLEASURE OF THE PARISH OF LITTLE GORE AT THE WEDDING OF HESTER PLUMB AND THOMAS VANE, AT FENMARCH. Mrs Vane opened it on the doorstep, with the children round her, and said It's my wedding, and he said that it was, and that he did apologise, it was his first errand. She said that they had all come anyway, and that now they were invited properly, and it was going on the mantelpiece, and Bess was to fetch the good pin. It is there now, propped against the clock, where you can see it through the window from the road. Under INVITATIONS TO FOLLOW, in a fresh hand, very neat: FOLLOWED. (P-G.) He stopped for tea. He said that he might not find his way out afterwards. Mrs Vane said that then he would stop for supper. His nephew, the Fourth, came up the sandy road at a run that afternoon, and has been three paces behind him ever since. See the article on Sir Aldric . Dame Winifred Dame Winifred Cope of the Order of the Errant stands outside her own front door as if it were a post. She is the Chapter's knight in the field at Little Gore, and has been since 1989, and there is a pin in her at Coldbarrow , just the one. She is here; that is the whole of it. Somebody has to be where the pin is, or what is the map for? She writes every quarter, NOTHING TO REPORT, and they write back, VERY GOOD, and she says it is the nicest correspondence she has ever had. Her door has a card in the Order's lettering, KNIGHT IN THE FIELD. DO NOT DISTURB, and she is standing four feet from it, and as far as the Chapter is concerned that is the field. Her helmet is good and plain, with a small G stamped inside the brim, and is Hob Grumnir's. He asked whether he might borrow it back, for the spring. She said that she was in it. That turned out to be the whole of her reason, and it was a very good one. Sir Aldric has called her a very fine post, and has said that she is happy, and that he honours her. She says that is very kind, and that there is still nothing to report. Abel Thrush The fingerpost on the green points one arm at the houses, LITTLE GORE, and the other back down the road, FENMARCH 4 MILES, and there are a great many initials carved into it, and a heart round two of them, eleven years deep. On the back of it, from 1991 until the year 2000, there was a card, gone soft with weather: WANTED: AN ELEGY. For ABEL THRUSH, carrier, who walked this road fifty years and never had one. Something with a bit of a tune. The parish will pay. Ask anybody. Piper Quill asked anybody, eleven of them, in Little Gore, Fenmarch and Sump, and every one described a different man, and she wrote the elegy out of all of them, and pinned it under the Fenmarch arm. It is there now, under a little roof somebody has made for it, and people stop and read it on their way past. It is printed whole in her article . Little Gore's own contributions to it were that he never spoke a word, that he read no letter and knew them all, that he carried a cow to Fenmarch once because it would not walk, that he could whistle with two fingers so that you could hear it at Sump, and that he brought the letter round the green. I have not been to Little Gore. Mrs Vane wrote to me, when she heard I was writing this, to say that I should be very welcome, and that it was only four miles from Fenmarch, and to mind the children, who would marry me if I stood still. She enclosed a drawing by Nell, of the wedding, with all the hats much bigger, and a man in armour at the back, holding a letter, very late. See also Fenmarch Hall Sump , the other end of the carrier's road Coldbarrow , where Dame Winifred's pin is

title: Nether Sopping
text: Nether Sopping This article is about the town. For the tavern, which is most of it, see The Slain Wyvern . For the clause that sends people here, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick , clause nineteen. Nether Sopping Known as The coast; the seaside; "somewhere with sea air" Where The south coast, at the east end of the coast road from Thistlewick Distance Four leagues, by the signpost; forty miles, by Mr Quy Motto The sea is right there Confirmed It is. We checked Weather Rain. Painted on Tides High when it feels like it. Low, see above Speed limit A brisk walk In Bloom Highly commended (damp category) Names on the memorial One hundred and eighty-one Population Mostly people who went north, and came back, and were sent here Home of The compiler of this volume Nether Sopping is a fishing town on the south coast: roofs, rigging, and a great deal of weather arriving off the sea. It is where Thistlewick's heroes went afterwards. For most of a century, clause nineteen of the Prophecy sent every Chosen One who came home, and a good many of the people who went with him, to a cottage "at such distance from the village as is mutually agreeable", and the distance was always here. Nobody in Thistlewick mentions that it exists. It is my home, and I have been mentioning it for forty years, to anybody who would sit still. The town sign says NETHER SOPPING, THE SEA IS RIGHT THERE, and under it, in a different hand, IT IS. WE CHECKED. I have checked as well. It goes out, and then it comes back. The memorial On the harbour front there is a standing stone with names cut into it. Not forty-seven names. A hundred and eighty-one. The Chosen Ones are on it, but so is everybody who went with them: healers, hired swords, cousins, a cook, somebody listed only as the lad who carried the rope. Thistlewick's Wall of the Forty-Seven has forty-seven portraits on it. Nobody in Thistlewick has ever counted the difference. There is room underneath for more. There is always room underneath for more. I am asked, by visitors, whether the stone is a memorial to the dead. It is not. Most of the hundred and eighty-one were alive when their names were cut, and a good many of them drink in the Wyvern, and some of them will show you where they are on it. It is a memorial to having gone. The town The harbour. A pier, two bollards worn smooth by a hundred years of rope and a hundred years of people sitting on them to look at the sea (one has a little brass plate: THIS BOLLARD IS FOR BOATS, and under that, worn almost away, AND FOR GRANDAD), and the Harbour Rules: No adventuring on the pier. The crab on the west beach is nobody's fault and is not to be provoked. Rule 2 is not a challenge. There is a crab in the well as well. It looks up. Rule two applies. The Ferryman will take you anywhere at all: islands, the far shore, that bit on the map with the writing you can't read. The tide was wrong. It had been wrong since he bought the boat. Nix returned to him, in the year 2000, a printed tide table with his boat drawn in the margin, which he had owned for one week and she had owned since, and he read it, and looked at the water, and read it again, and said that the tide was right today. He has it open on his knee, and is giving it a few more days. The market. SEA POTATOES, which are potatoes; SEA CARROTS, which are, as far as anybody can tell, carrots. In Nether Sopping everything is sea something. We have a sea cat. The fish stall sells fish under a card that says FISH, which is the only thing on the market that is exactly what it says it is, and the stallholder is very proud of it; and Sopping biscuit, which is older than the fish and will outlive the both of us. The stall's stamped scales go up to twenty stone and have never once lied, and were lent, in the year 2000, for a medical examination, of which more in Sister Merribell's article . There is a tub of eels sold by the yard, and a tub with an octopus in it, which is very relaxed, and has arranged itself so as to be holding the fishmonger's pencil. A big crate on the market is stencilled RETURN TO SENDER, and under that, SENDER UNKNOWN, and under that, RETURN. It has been waiting to be returned for some years. The boards. NETHER SOPPING IN BLOOM - HIGHLY COMMENDED, DAMP CATEGORY. SPEED LIMIT - A BRISK WALK; ADVENTURERS ARE NOT TO RUN THROUGH THE TOWN, HOWEVER URGENT THE PROPHECY. YES, YOU. WE CAN SEE YOU. TODAY'S WEATHER - RAIN, which is not chalked, but painted on. The beach. Driftwood bleached silver, with K + M, WED 1972, and a small heart carved into it, and under it, in newer, deeper letters, STILL. A gull on a log that has opinions about you. The net loft, with a card on the door: IF YOU ARE HERE ABOUT THE ROPE, THE ROPE IS SPOKEN FOR. It is spoken for by whoever asks properly. Nobody ever had; they read the card and went off. Nix asked properly, and the rope came out of the window, and the voice said, "Properly." The boat shed. Locked. Through the window, eleven boats, all upside down, all belonging to somebody who went north. Nobody has rowed them since. One of them gave an oar, in the year 2000, which was asked for and offered, and is a sword now; "she'd like being a sword". The receipt is in the Ferryman's hat. The Chandler's keeps the hours on the card in its window, which are when the light is on at the point. For one spring and the summer after, the light at the point was out, and the Chandler's was shut. The card is turned round now, OPEN, because the light is lit; see The Lighthouse of Saint Bother . Inside, everything was dusted, twice. The people Sops, the potboy at the Wyvern, and his friend Tibb, who play Chosen One on the front. The rules are that one of them walks north and the other has to be the Dark Lord and lose, and neither of them wanted to be the Dark Lord, and they settled it by both being the Chosen One and agreeing that the Dark Lord had stayed at home today. Which, as solutions go, was well ahead of anything the Prophecy Committee had managed. In the afternoons now the Dark Lord comes down the street, in a teal hood, under protest, and loses. Cobb Lorrimer, a thief, registered with the Guild under T, who challenged Nix to a contest of fetching and lost it on paperwork, and signed for the post of Dark Lord (afternoons), and read what he had signed a moment too late. He has come back every day since, and is getting very good at losing. He would like a receipt for his tools. A man having a day off, asleep against a stack of crates with a very good sword across his knees. He has done this for thirty-one years, and today, every day, he is having a day off. There is a lad in the Wyvern who will go with anyone. Ask him. Let him sleep. The sword is one of Hob Grumnir's. Neither of them is working today. The Courier, a man in a red coat and a flat cap, with a satchel on a strap, who is always already here when you arrive, and whose boots are dry. Nobody asks him how any more. He carried Spare Cotterill's letters home from eight towns, this one among them. He is on his rounds. He does not say whose. Wick & Barrow, Outfitters Across from the Guild: EVERYTHING FOR THE ROAD NORTH, and chalked under it, ALSO THE ROAD BACK (ASK). A painted breastplate, ARMOUR REPAIRED, DRAGONS QUOTED FOR. A painted teapot: A HERO RUNS ON TEA AND BOOTS. MOSTLY BOOTS. In the window, boots WALKED NORTH AND BACK, ONE CAREFUL OWNER, which look as though they would rather not talk about it, and a display of rucksack, rope, lantern and a tin of biscuits with a card, YOU WILL NEED A BIGGER RUCKSACK. Mrs Barrow has been in the trade thirty-nine years. "Everything an adventurer needs, and four things nobody does." She sells the hat that the Guild's Form A-1 requires, for thirty, and is not related to the Registrar. She sells lamp oil, and a bottle of DRAGON REPELLENT, whose small print says IT IS LAMP OIL. THROW IT HARD. She sells chalk for marking the walls of dungeons, one crown, FINDING YOUR WAY OUT - NOT INCLUDED. She sells ten-foot poles, which every adventurer needs, and nobody has ever said what for, and everybody buys one. A crate of returned compasses all point at the Gilded Turnip in Thistlewick; she says it is a known fault. In the year 2000 she supplied forty bolts of oilskin to the Hoyle Works at Upper Clanging, and wrote on account for the first time in thirty-nine years, three times, and propped the card against the till where it could be seen from the door. "Well. Something's going the right way up that road for once." Wick's peg is at the end of the row of pegs on the wall, with nothing on it, dusted. Wick went north, the same as they all do, forty-one years ago this spring, by her count; forty-three, now, by mine. "The sign says Wick and Barrow. That's two names, and one of them's still walking about, and the other one went north, and both belong on a sign." The bench. For many years Wick & Barrow had a bench in eleven pieces leaning against the wall under a card: BENCH. 400. NOBODY HAS EVER BOUGHT THIS. Somebody bought it. It is on the top of a mound in the eastern hills now, facing the sea. See The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth .
