The Guild The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) has its hall on the front, under a sign held on with six bolts (the last sign had one bolt, and was taken by somebody who needed a sword more than the Guild did), and a crest of a sword, a scroll and a small question mark. The question mark is the provisional part. It was founded in 1960, provisionally, pending a review, and the review has been scheduled ever since. Registrar Pell keeps it. It has its own article. Number Forty-Five's, and the cottage next door At the north end of the town are two cottages side by side, which clause nineteen gave to two Chosen Ones who came home. Number Forty-Five's is Halbert Quy 's, the Forty-Fifth, who went north in 1970 and was offered a cup of tea at the top and said no, and has thought about it ever since. He grows roses. There is not one turnip in the house, and it is a policy. The Committee's framed commendation is face down on the shelf, dusted round rather than moved. The sword over the fire is exactly like the one over every Chosen One's fire, and has dust on the upper edge, which takes a long time and a great deal of not looking. The cottage next door was Ambrose Fitch's, the Forty-Fourth, who lived in it for forty years, from 1960, and watered a pot with a dead thing in it every morning, and nothing grew. He is dead; see his article , and the Barrow. Mrs Pimm, who has the other key, airs it on Tuesdays, and does the windows inside and out, and has left a note on the table: AIRED TUESDAYS. KETTLE IN THE CUPBOARD. PLEASE DON'T MOVE HIS CHAIR. In the cupboard there is a kettle, a caddy of tea and one cup. From the window you can see the sea, and the end of the north road where it comes over the hill. The Committee sent the key to that cottage to the Forty-Eighth after the Quest, with his pension and its congratulations, and trusted Friday would suit. Clause nineteen was struck six months later, and he has never lived in it. He uses it when he comes south, which is about once a month, to correct me. He waters the pot. Nothing has grown. I have checked. He has never moved the chair. The coast road The road from Thistlewick's turning runs east along the coast. At the turning is a signpost, EAST, Nether Sopping, WEST, Thistlewick, on which somebody from one end of the road has scratched out the other end's name, and somebody from the other end has scratched out theirs. Both are still legible. It has been like this for a hundred years. The signpost gives Nether Sopping as four leagues. Mr Quy, who was sent here by the Committee and has had thirty years to think about it, makes it forty miles. I have walked it, once, to see Thistlewick for this volume, and I side with Mr Quy, and I think the signpost was put up by somebody from the Thistlewick end. Off the west beach, from the road, you can see the Isle of Uncertain Ownership, a rock with a plaque bolted to it, THIS ISLAND IS THE PROPERTY OF, and then a very great deal of scratching out, and a flagpole with two flags on it, one above the other. The order has been reversed nine times, by parties who could not get ashore and were shouting from boats. There is a sheep on it. It has never been sheared, because shearing it would be an act of ownership, and it is, by now, very nearly a sphere. It looks at you with the calm of an animal that has never once been asked to do anything. The west beach itself was held, for longer than the town, by the Crab of Unusual Size, the size of a garden shed, which was on the Guild's board, and which everybody in Nether Sopping was very careful to call unusual. It does not hold the beach any more. Four smaller crabs hold it between them, badly. Underneath it, in the shingle, were eleven years of other people's bad afternoons. Miss Halloway has a note on the crab in the Bestiary. See also The Slain Wyvern The Lighthouse of Saint Bother The Bottomless Pit The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Hosea Bellwether , who lives here

title: Nix's Emporium
text: Nix's Emporium For the proprietor of the back room, see Nix . For the provenance of particular items, see Arms and Artefacts , where Nix has supplied it. Nix's Emporium Known as The Emporium Of Thistlewick , the east side of the square Established Recently Sign A painted sack, a little open, so you cannot see what is in it Policy We buy anything. We ask nothing Neighbours' policy Please ask something Stock Previously owned By whom We don't ask. That's the arrangement Swords and shields Not sold. Have, at various times, been in Nix's Emporium is the general shop on the square at Thistlewick . Everything in it is previously owned, and the shopkeeper at the counter does not ask by whom; that is the arrangement. In the back room, for eleven years before the Quest, Nix did an inventory of things that were not on the inventory. The sign is a painted sack, painted a little open so that you cannot see what is in it, which is, the Forty-Eighth suspected on his first visit, the whole business model. The windows In one window: a stuffed owl, a lute with no strings, a single boot, and a card that says EVERYTHING MUST GO. Somebody has added, in a small neat hand: (BACK). The card is not Nix's. The boot is. In the other: WE BUY ANYTHING. Under it, smaller: WE ASK NOTHING. Under that, smaller still, in a different pen: PLEASE ASK SOMETHING. - YOUR NEIGHBOURS. The shop The stock changes, and I can only describe what was on the shelves when I called. Loaves, each labelled with where it was ACQUIRED. Most say A BAKERY. One says THE BAKERY, and has been corrected to A BAKERY. Three potions. A purple one, labelled NOT POISON, with small print: THIS LABEL IS PROVIDED FOR REASSURANCE ONLY. A blue one, labelled MANA, because blue is always mana, and everybody knows that, and nobody knows how; small print, OR IT IS BLUE WATER. ONE OF THOSE. A green one, labelled ANTIDOTE; small print, TO WHAT IS NOT STATED. WE ARE NOT IN A POSITION TO SAY. Apples, ONE PER CUSTOMER; under that, in a different hand, PER VISIT; under that, PER HAND. Somebody has been arguing with the card. Two basins. One so that customers can wash their hands in case they have touched anything they are not going to buy, and one for customers who have touched something they are not going to buy and feel bad about it. Crates. One stencilled PROPERTY OF THE ROYAL MAIL, painted over PROPERTY OF THE EMPORIUM, painted over again, and now just PROPERTY, which, it has been pointed out to me, is honest. You can't say it isn't honest. Another with holes in the lid, labelled LIVE: houseplants, which are, technically, alive. Odds and ends: one glove, a teapot lid, a key to something, and a jar marked MISC (DO NOT ASK). A shelf of returns, each tagged RETURNED TO OWNER, and one, very small, RETURNED TO OWNER, WHO WAS VERY UNDERSTANDING ABOUT IT. The ledger The ledger lives in the back room. For eleven years every entry in it read ACQUIRED, and none of them said from where, and one entry in a different hand read PLEASE STOP WRITING ACQUIRED. It was ruled with a RETURNED column, very neatly, down eleven years of pages, and there was nothing in it. There is now. In the year 2000 Nix took back to their owners the eleven oldest things in the book, the ones on its first page, which had never been sold: a pie dish, a kitchen chair, a keep net, a gate key, a tide table, a pair of spectacles, some stamps, a pair of good boots, a snap tin, a small oil can and a cradle. None of the owners knew the things had gone, and every one of them was pleased to see them back. Two of them tried to pay. The last page of the first volume is ruled off with a double line, the way it is done, and blotted, and I am told that nobody had ever seen that book finished before, Nix included. The first line of the book had no provenance at all. It has one now, in Nix's hand: one coat, COLLECTED, on behalf of the party of the second part. How it came to be written is her business, and is told, so far as she has let me tell it, under her article . The second volume began on the page after the coat. It is filling up. I asked the shopkeeper at the counter where the stuffed owl had come from. He said that everything there was previously owned, and that by whom, they don't ask. I asked whether anybody had ever asked. He said that one person had, once, and pointed at the card in the other window, and said that she was a neighbour, and that she had been very understanding about it. See also Nix Thistlewick Arms and Artefacts

title: Olde Evermore
text: Olde Evermore This article is about the hidden village of the elves and its Archive. For the Oracle, see Mirabel . For the elves' way of counting years, see Two Reckonings . Olde Evermore Known as Hidden Village of the Elves Since The First Age Where Under a ledge in the south-west, at the bottom Way in Off the ledge, as is traditional Way out Down the path, past the well. Nobody has ever come in by it Arrivals Judged, out of six Best score Five point nine, the Forty-Seventh Oracle Mirabel, four thousand one hundred and twelve (and a quarter) Bedtime Half past seven. It is not half past yet Olde Evermore is the hidden village of the elves, at the foot of a high ledge in the south-west, where it has been since the First Age. Every visitor arrives by falling off the ledge into a heap of leaves, which is raked up again after each arrival. There is a perfectly good path out. Nobody has ever come in by it. Nearly every Chosen One has found the village eventually, and every one of them found it the same way. Arriving The village sign reads OLDE EVERMORE. HIDDEN VILLAGE OF THE ELVES. SINCE THE FIRST AGE, and under it, smaller: VISITORS ARE ASKED TO ARRIVE BY THE LEDGE, AS IS TRADITIONAL. At the bottom of the ledge there is a second sign: ARRIVALS. The leaves under it are raked into a deep, soft heap every morning and fluffed up again after each arrival, and it is somebody's whole job. He will tell you to mind the leaves, he has just done them. Beside the heap stands Thalion, Judge of Arrivals, with a little book. He has judged every arrival off the ledge since the First Age, out of six, and is the whole panel, and there is no appeal. The scores have been very consistent. He gave the Forty-Eighth five point eight: the arms were lovely; he lost it on the landing; everybody loses it on the landing. The best score on record is the Forty-Seventh's, five point nine, twelve years ago. He landed on his feet. Thalion was very moved. In a window across the green there is stained glass of an elf falling off a ledge, gracefully, and below her a second elf holding up a card that says 6.0. Nobody has ever been given a six. It is a very old window, and a very hopeful one. I have not been to Olde Evermore. I have been to the top of the ledge, and looked over it, and come home. I am told the leaves are very soft. I am a historian, and I do not need to be judged. The village Aelwen sings to the well in the Old Tongue. It is the Lay of the Chosen, with a verse for every Chosen One who has come off the ledge, and it is three days long, sung properly, and nobody has ever heard the end of it, because she keeps having to add verses. The Forty-Sixth never came at all, so his verse is a rest, four bars long, and she says it is the best bit. She said that she would write the Forty-Eighth's when she had seen how it ended. I have asked whether she has. I am told that she has, and that it is not finished, and that it does not have to be yet. Calder stands at the edge of the pond, with enormous patience. There is one fish in it, and he has been after it since the Second Age, and has caught it twice, and put it back both times, because then what would he do all day? It has a name. He will not tell you it. It would be insufferable. Ninian sweeps the path out. Nobody has ever come in by it, so it is always very clean. He sweeps it because somebody might go out by it one day, and you would want it nice for them. When the Forty-Eighth said that he would be going out by it, Ninian looked delighted and swept a little faster. Elowen, an old elf at her front door, is knitting something very small, very fast. It is a tea cosy with two little sleeves, and a large B on the front. B for Bryony. Or Bronwen. It is not for anything else. Asked about the sleeves, she says it is for a very small teapot. They get cold. Her daughter is Elder Lirien, who has been married to Elder Faelan since the Second Age. Elowen had stopped knitting. The rest of the village is beautifully kept. There is a room in which everything has been carved, including, as far as can be told, the soap. There are mushrooms growing in a perfect spiral, which in Olde Evermore counts as untidy, and somebody has already been told. There is a carved elven door with no handle, no lock and no keyhole, which opens for those it expects. It has not expected anybody for four thousand years, and has got very good at it. There is a front door in a knitted cosy, and so is the knocker, and so is the handle, and so, very likely, is the key, which would be why nobody can find it. The Forbidden Archive The notice by the Archive door reads: THE FORBIDDEN ARCHIVE. THE ORACLE RECEIVES VISITORS UNTIL A QUARTER PAST SEVEN. BEDTIME IS HALF PAST. THIS IS NOT A PROPHECY. Under it, in a very careful hand, somebody small has added: IT IS NOT HALF PAST YET. Inside, on a stepstool, stands Mirabel, the Last Oracle of Olde Evermore, a very small girl with long silver hair and a silver circlet, who is four thousand one hundred and twelve, and likes the quarter mentioned. She prophesies in the Old Tongue. It is flawless, and it is terrible, and every candle in the Archive leans towards her, and Elder Lirien translates: When the moon devours the sun, and the last bell falls silent, the one who was not chosen shall- and then Mirabel asks whether that is a biscuit. It is always a biscuit. She has been doing that one since the Second Age, and it never gets finished, and nobody seems to mind. The shelf of discarded prophecies has it on top, AND THE ONE WHO WAS NOT CHOSEN SHALL, and then a jam stain. Elder Lirien translates for Grandmother, when she prophesies, and when she asks for pudding, and the pudding is more urgent. Elder Faelan fetches things from the top shelf, which is where the Chronicle of the Second Age is kept, so that she cannot reach it, because she reads the endings first. Everybody calls her Grandmother. She was old when Faelan's grandmother was a girl, and his grandmother was a girl for a long time. Faelan is the source for a sentence I have quoted elsewhere in this volume and will quote again: the Committee counts the way the Prophecy does; the elves count the way the sun does. The Forty-Seventh came off the ledge ten years before the Forty-Eighth, he said, and not a hundred, and when the Forty-Eighth said that the Age began with the Prophecy, Faelan said that the Age began with a great many things, and that the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. See Two Reckonings . The horse. Mirabel was at the signing of the Prophecy of Thistlewick. It was ever so long, and everybody had to sign it three times, so she drew a horse on it. Elder Faelan has views about that, which are that it was in the margin of a sacred and binding instrument. She says it is a good horse. The Archive has a fair copy of the Prophecy, made at the signing, under a sign that says FORBIDDEN in four languages; the copyist was told to copy everything, and he copied everything, and in the margin beside clause twelve, very small and in wax crayon, there is a horse. It is quite a good horse. Asked who the villain really is, Mirabel said that she knows, and is not allowed to say, and would draw it. She drew for a long time with her tongue out of the corner of her mouth, and then showed the Forty-Eighth, and it was a horse. He said carefully that it was a very good horse. She said that it was not a horse, it was the villain, and that she was only very good at horses. There is a picture book on the forbidden shelf in which every page is the same horse, and on the cover, in the Old Tongue: THE VILLAIN. The secret. Mirabel also told the Forty-Eighth a real secret, not a prophecy, which is that Elder Lirien is going to have a baby. Across the Archive, Elder Lirien dropped a scroll, and at the foot of the ladder Elder Faelan stopped moving altogether. Mirabel had foreseen it, and told them at breakfast, before they knew. She had known since the ninth of March. It is a girl, and she is going to be called Biscuit. Elder Faelan says that she is not going to be called Biscuit. Mirabel says she is, though. I am told that neither Elder could stop smiling, which was making the colour worse. The clock. The Archive clock is tall and beautifully kept, and says a quarter past seven. The pendulum is not moving. It has been tied to the side of the case with a hair ribbon, in a very neat bow. Mirabel's bed is in the corner, turned down, with a stone hot-water bottle already in it, and on the pillow a note in the Old Tongue, flawless and terrible, which Elder Lirien translates without looking up: Not tired. The copyist sits behind a desk, copying a book in a beautiful hand, very slowly. He was told to copy everything, so he copies everything, and at present he is copying the catalogue of everything he has copied, which is very nearly up to date. Everything means the margins too. Nobody has told him to stop. He has been listening very carefully. See also Mirabel Elder Faelan The Prophecy of Thistlewick , clause twelve Two Reckonings

title: Penultima
text: Penultima For the sword in the window, see The Sword of Ultimate Ending . For the actual last shop, see below; it is closed. Penultima Known as The Last Town Before The End Where On the road north, just short of the Tower Signs LAST CHANCE FOR POTIONS (WE MEAN IT) Rates Seasonal Season All of them Wells Two. One crown a bucket; half a crown at the other, tell nobody Twinned with Nowhere. There is nothing to be twinned with The last shop Ye Final Shoppe The actual last shop Closed for the season Penultima is a small town on the road north, the last before the Obligatory Tower , which lives on the fact. Every Chosen One in living memory has come through it on the way up, with a hundred years' savings in his purse and no other shop in front of him, and Penultima has priced accordingly. It is not dishonest. It is seasonal. The town The sign is a board, repainted often, in gold: PENULTIMA. THE LAST TOWN BEFORE THE END. Underneath, smaller and newer: LAST CHANCE FOR POTIONS. Underneath that, smaller again and newest: (WE MEAN IT). When a Chosen One comes into the street, a bell rings once, briskly, the way a shop bell rings, and along the street, unhurried, several shopkeepers turn over several small cards. Nobody looks at him while they do it. A man on a ladder hangs a fresh board over the old one. The old one said SUMMER RATES. The new one says SEASONAL RATES. When the Forty-Eighth came through it was the twelfth of November. The bell does not ring twice for the same customer. There would be no point. Everything in Penultima is the last of something. The well is the LAST WELL BEFORE THE END, ONE CROWN A BUCKET, SEASONAL; the other well across the street is the LAST WELL BEFORE THE END (THE OTHER ONE), HALF A CROWN, TELL NOBODY. There is a LAST LOG at the top of the town, priced. There is a barrel with a price on it, and it is empty, and the price is for the barrel. There is another barrel with a card on it, THIS BARREL HAS BEEN SEARCHED BY A CHOSEN ONE, and in Penultima that is a selling point, and it is priced accordingly. Through one window a family is at its supper, and there is still a price tag on the teapot; they stopped noticing years ago. Through another a man is counting his money very slowly, for the pleasure of it, and then counting it again. Pinned to a barrel under glass is the parish notice: PENULTIMA IS TWINNED WITH NOWHERE. THERE IS NOTHING TO BE TWINNED WITH. WE HAVE WRITTEN TO THE TOWER TWICE. The Tower has a correspondent now, and I asked him whether he had had Penultima's letters. He wrote back that he had, both of them, and had not known what to say, and was sorry, and that he was told the potions were very good. Ye Final Shoppe YE FINAL SHOPPE - LAST SWORDS FOR TWO HUNDRED LEAGUES. Chalked under it: LAST POTIONS. Under that: LAST SPOONS. Under that: LAST CHANCE TO BUY A SPOON, REALLY, THINK ABOUT IT. It also does a final cup of tea, at a price which is also final. It is kept by Gideon Markup, who welcomes you, and asks what you are buying, and, when you say that you have only just come in, says of course, of course, take your time, everything is priced, everything has always been priced. Asked about the prices, which are high, he says seasonal. He has been in the trade thirty-three years, and it has been seasonal every one of them. It is a very reliable season. The shop buys at one crown and sells at forty, and asks you about its warranty. There is no warranty. Asking about it is free. Some of the stock deserves a mention. Forty potions, each labelled LAST POTION. Rope, sold by the yard, priced by the inch. Two jars side by side, each labelled UMBRELLAS - THE LAST ONE. FINAL WINE, under which Mrs Markup has written (IT IS NOT. WE HAVE A CELLAR.). A crate of things bought at a crown each, among them half a potion; Gideon is waiting for somebody who needs exactly half a potion, and is sure they are on their way. A book, HOW TO HAGGLE, marked NOT FOR SALE. A gilt case with the first crown the shop ever took, NOT FOR SALE, and under it, smaller, (OFFERS). A case of rings, each tag reading MAKE AN OFFER, except one, under which Gideon has written (NOT THAT ONE). It is a plain gold band, old, and very well polished. In the window, behind a velvet rope, is a sword and a shield, polished every morning. The card reads THE SWORD OF ULTIMATE ENDING. 9,999,999 CROWNS. Gideon priced it in 1969. Asked whether sir might hold it, he says, warmly, that sir cannot afford to hold it. He has said it to everyone who has ever come through that door, and he is not going to stop now. Dorothy Markup keeps the ledger, and every page balances, and in the margin of every page, very small, is G. WAS HONEST TODAY, a few of them with a question mark. He brings her tea every morning, and then he does the window, and has never once in thirty-three years had to be asked. He has never sold the sword. He has given one discount, in thirty-three years, of eleven coppers, off a lamp, to a girl who would not stop haggling. The first volume of the Markup accounts opens with it, in his hand: DISCOUNT - ELEVEN COPPERS - WORTH IT. She has ruled round it twice. She has still got the coppers. Ultimate Outfitters Two hundred yards up the street is a good shop front, boarded, with the paint still sound: ULTIMATE OUTFITTERS - THE ACTUAL LAST SHOP. A painted hand points confidently up the road, TWO HUNDRED YARDS FURTHER ON. Two hundred yards further on there is the road, and then the hills, and then the Tower. There has never been anything else. Through a crack in the boards you can see a shop exactly like Ye Final Shoppe, with everything in it priced at exactly one crown less. A card in the window, in a different hand, has been there some years: THANK YOU PENULTIMA FOR NINE WONDERFUL MONTHS. Since the Quest The road north has fewer Chosen Ones on it than it had, there being no clause twelve, and Penultima has noticed. It has not changed its prices. It does a good trade in people going up to see the chair, who need something for the walk, and in people coming down, who need something to say they went. The sign has a fourth line now, smaller than the third: LAST CHANCE FOR A SOUVENIR. See also The Obligatory Tower , two hundred yards further on, and then some The Sword of Ultimate Ending

title: Prophecy Hall
text: Prophecy Hall For the body that sits in it, see The Prophecy Committee . For the document, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . Prophecy Hall Known as The gold one, up the road Of Thistlewick , the top of the square Use The Committee, in session Hours Always Held up by A pillar, by order of the Committee (Minute 4,410); and another, by a majority of one Portraits Forty-seven, and a frame Struck material Behind the red curtain. Form S-7 Red tape Bought by the mile, from a man in Nether Sopping Potted plant To be watered (minuted, 1987) Prophecy Hall is the seat of the Prophecy Committee of Thistlewick , and the place where every Chosen One since the first has been told what he is for. It has a crest, two pillars, forty-seven portraits, a great many shelves, a box of verses nobody may read, and a scroll that reaches the far wall. Outside Over the door is the village crest, a turnip rampant on a field of slightly different turnips, with the motto in Old Thistlewick: NON NOBIS, NISI FORTE. Not us, unless it has to be. It has been repainted so often that it is now mostly paint, and slightly more rampant. Through one window you can see the Committee in session, and one of them will see you, and hold a form up to the glass, and the correct response, which every Chosen One has worked out for himself, is to duck. On the sill of the other window is a row of little clay figures made by the village school, one for each Chosen One. In the year 2000 a forty-eighth was begun. At first it was mostly turnip. Then it was given a sword, which it is holding by the wrong end, and the school has decided that it is finished. The Hall The Elder stands at the far end, under a stained-glass window of the First Chosen One slaying the Dark Lord. The glazier has given the Dark Lord a very patient expression, like a man waiting for a bus he has been told is coming. I did not think anything of it until I had been to the top of the story, by letter; I think the glazier had been there in person. *Elder Wispel * gives the Prophecy to each Chosen One by unrolling it until it reaches the far wall, and then rolling it back up, which takes a while, and nobody helps. On his desk is a note in his own hand: BUY MORE SCROLL. It is underlined twice. Beside it is THE PROPHECY OF THISTLEWICK (ABRIDGED), which is exactly as long as the unabridged one, the abridging having been done by the Committee. The Committee's table runs down one side. At one end sits the Clerk, with Form C-12, Roster Amendments, by which a Chosen One may strike a companion from the roster and send them home to think about it. Thistlewick personnel only. Anybody picked up south of the wall is Form C-12(S), which is held in Nether Sopping, by a man called Pell. "Not my circus." A companion struck off keeps the kit and the experience. It was tried the other way once. There is a form about why not. At the other end sits a councillor whose whole contribution to the year 2000, so far as the minutes show, was to ask whether the Dark Lord shall be slain or shall be defeated, because slain is a commitment, and to countersign one form, as to the wording. And there is * Councillor Fenn *, who has been saying for forty years that clause twelve is the problem. "That's not a warning. That's a subscription." Nobody listened to him until somebody asked him what he meant, and he said that nobody had ever asked, and sat them down, and began at the original wording, which goes back to a horse. He is still explaining it. He looks very well on it. The Committee's minute book for the week of the ending records, as item five, that Councillor Fenn wished it minuted that he had been saying so. Minuted. The Wall of the Forty-Seven On the west wall: forty-seven portraits. Forty-six of them are looking at the viewer. One of them is looking at the door. At the end of them, since the year 2000, there is a forty-eighth frame, new, and empty, with a card pinned in it: PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. The sitter is not at the coast. He is two fields away, and has been for two years. Nobody has changed the card. A second card, the Quills', is tucked into the corner of the frame to make room. It gives the official account of the Forty-Eighth, and who wrote it, and whether it was APPROVED or AMENDED, and on that subject I refer the reader to Piper Quill , and say no more. The shelves The Committee's library is one of the wonders of the village, and is very nearly all minutes. A selection, from the shelves by the door: The Meeting To Decide When To Hold The Meeting, Volume IV. Prophecy: A User's Guide. Chapter One is "Have You Tried Being Chosen Again?" Standing Orders of the Prophecy Committee, Revised. It has been revised in pencil, on every page, by somebody who was outvoted on all of them. The Forty-Seven: A Souvenir. Every page has a portrait, a date and a pressed flower. The flowers are all turnip flowers. A dictionary, which has been opened at SLAIN and DEFEATED so often that it now falls open there by itself. So You've Been Chosen: A Leaflet. It is one page long, and says CONGRATULATIONS!, and then, in very much smaller print, CLAUSE FOUR APPLIES. What To Do If The Chosen One Is Not In. It recommends leaving a note, and choosing again if he has not replied by Thursday. The accounts of the Prophecy Fund. Income: the fete. Expenditure: swords, forty-seven; scroll, a great deal. A petition to rename the Obligatory Tower the Optional Tower, with one signature on it, Councillor Fenn's. Under them is a pad of forms, of which the top one is Form S-7, Application to Consult Struck Material (Verse), to be countersigned as to the wording. And beside them, on the Committee Records, are the minutes of the meeting at which the Forty-Eighth was chosen, with his name under apologies for absence, and one goat. Struck material The Fete Sub-Committee's minutes hang on the wall, and they are the most-read document in the Hall: Verses one to six: approved. Verse seven: struck. Verse eight: struck, and we would like a word. Verse nine was read aloud at the fete. In error. By Mrs Wispel. There were children present. There were GRANDPARENTS present. Motion to strike verses seven and eight: carried, four to one. The one against is Mrs Wispel. Nobody has written down what verse seven was. Nobody is going to, and that includes me. The Committee keeps what it strikes. Of course it does; it is a committee. Behind the red curtains in the east wall there is no window, but a door, STRUCK MATERIAL, NO ADMITTANCE WITHOUT FORM S-7, and the key to it hangs on Councillor Fenn's belt. Behind that are the struck shelves (Struck: A History, Volume One, which has been struck; The Prophecy: Early Drafts, in which the Dark Lord rises "every hundred years, or so", with OR SO crossed out and the crossing-out crossed out; Names Considered for the Obligatory Tower, which include the Compulsory Tower, the Mandatory Tower, the Tower You Have To, and the Tower (Sorry); and Things Not To Read Aloud At The Fete, inside the cover of which Mrs Wispel has written, NOW you tell me). And there is the box: the best box the Committee owns, gilded, with a red stone in the lid, full of two hundred years of struck verses, one to a slip, each dated and initialled. Piper Quill has read every one of them, and printed none. Pinned under the Fete Sub-Committee's minutes now is a slip: Struck material consulted, Form S-7, initialled P.Q., in metre. In the box, one slip has been very slightly straightened. The minute book, and the lectern The Committee's minute book lies open on the table at the week the Forty-Eighth came home: ITEM 3. Clause twelve. Struck, nem. con. In its place, a note: SEE BRAM. ITEM 4. Clause nineteen. Applies. Letter sent, cottage aired. Friday suggested. ITEM 5. Councillor Fenn wished it minuted that he had been saying so. Minuted. Item four was itself struck six months later, after a very long meeting. I have the minutes of that meeting. It lasted eleven hours, and they are mostly about the biscuits. By the door, since the ending, stands a lectern, and on it a ledger in the Committee's best hand, open at the first page, with a pen on a chain: The Obligatory Quest, as amended. It is the Prophecy's own tally of the Quest, read against the world as it now stands, and it is kept up to date. It is the only document in the Hall that admits it is not finished. It ends: The account ends there, for the present. There is a good deal of ruled paper after it. The account at the lectern says that I wrote a song about the Quest, from first-hand accounts, and that it is complete and not remotely accurate. I have written to the Committee to say that I wrote a history, and that it is in prose. The Clerk has stamped my letter and filed it. I am told it was filed under "no change". See also The Prophecy Committee The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones , for the Wall Piper Quill , for the box

title: Restwell
text: Restwell This article is about the town of inns. For inns in songs, and the eight hours in them, see the Glossary of Cliches . Restwell Known as Restwell; Restwell (Cont.) Where A crossroads in the south-west Inns Nineteen Streets One By-law Please do not sleep in the road The one in the songs The Eight Hours The others Also very good Breakfast Served until four. At the Eight Hours, whenever you come down Curtains Drawn at noon Restwell is a town of nineteen inns and one street, at a crossroads, where a traveller goes upstairs and sleeps eight hours and comes down whole, warm, unpoisoned and agreeing without discussing it that it is morning. That is the arrangement in the songs. In Restwell it is also the arrangement, and it takes about seven minutes. The town The fingerpost at the crossroads has four boards. Three say RESTWELL. The fourth says RESTWELL (CONT.) and points back the way you came. Under them, smaller: NINETEEN INNS. ONE STREET. PLEASE DO NOT SLEEP IN THE ROAD. The inns of Restwell are listed under glass on a barrel in the street, nineteen names, eleven of them crossed out and written in again. At the bottom, firmly: THE EIGHT HOURS IS THE ONE IN THE SONGS. THE OTHERS ARE ALSO VERY GOOD. Under that, in eighteen other hands, the word YES. The others are indeed also very good. The Seven Hours is just as restful and one hour quicker, and has a clock an hour fast so that the guests feel rested sooner, and a card in the window saying BACK IN EIGHT HOURS. The Nine Hours is for those who find eight a little rushed. The Four Hours is for the busy hero, and is closed, gone to bed. The Traveller's Rest, The Traveller's Second Rest and The Traveller's Rest (Annexe) are all over the same door, and it is the only door there is. The Lie-In serves breakfast until four. The Nightcap is open all night for those who cannot sleep, and in Restwell that is nobody, and its landlord has never served a drink and is very well rested. The town well has a sign, PLEASE DRAW WATER QUIETLY, PEOPLE ARE SLEEPING. A water barrel is labelled FOR WAKING GUESTS. USE SPARINGLY, and under that, in a different hand, USE NEVER. Pillows are ordered by the barrel. Spare nightcaps are sorted by inn, with a tassel in each inn's colours. At the edge of town is a log worn into a comfortable dip by travellers who could not quite make it as far as the inns, and slept there instead, very well. A satisfied guest coming out of the street at four in the afternoon told the Forty-Eighth good morning, and that he had slept like the dead, eight hours, easy, best night in years. He had gone up at noon. He said it without the slightest difficulty, and walked off whistling eight bars of something. The Eight Hours The Eight Hours is kept by Mrs Hester Ashbury. A room is ten crowns, breakfast included. Breakfast is whenever you come down; she argued about that for a year, and now she just cooks, and in Restwell breakfast is served after lunch and is therefore a chop. Asked about the songs, she says that resurrection is extra, and that she will want the room back by noon. It is generally already twenty past two. Her husband, Walt Ashbury, sits on the bottom step of the stairs with a fiddle, where he can see the whole room, and plays every guest up: eight bars, the same eight bars, every time, for twenty-eight years now. It has to be that one. He tried a different one once, and they came down tired. Mrs Ashbury has listened to those eight bars for twenty-eight years and has never once asked him to stop. She says that he is very good at it. The register is open on the bar, ruled in a firm hand. Every entry on every page says eight hours, every entry is in a different hand, and nobody has ever written anything else, except once, eight hrs, where somebody was in a hurry. When the Forty-Eighth came through, the last two entries read: Party of six. Up 12.02. Down 12.09. Slept: eight hours. Remarks: lovely. Mr & Mrs Tolley. Up 12.11. Down 12.19. Slept: eight hours. Remarks: LOVELY. I print the register as it stands. The Tolleys are a young couple who were travelling that year, and they turn up elsewhere in this volume, at Hithermost , in the Book, where they had just been married. Dr Pike has a chair by the fire and a bottle labelled TONIC - DR PIKE, which is cold tea, and he has never once claimed otherwise. He is retired, in the practical sense, which is to say nobody comes. He took a room for a fortnight, thirteen years ago, to think about it. Twelve hundred guests a year go up the stairs, and every one of them comes down better, and nobody can tell him why. He watches. He looks at the fiddle player for slightly too long, and then back at his breakfast. He has theories. He does not like them. Merribell has told me that cold tea is a perfectly good tonic, and that I am not to tell him she said so. I took a room at the Eight Hours on my way back from the coast road, and Walt played me up, and I came down, and it was morning, and I agreed that it was. I looked at the clock afterwards and I would rather not say. I have written in the register: eight hours. Remarks: I am a historian, and I should like to have stayed longer. See also Hithermost The Slain Wyvern , where you may also sleep, upstairs

title: Sump
text: Sump For the Sister who lifted the curse, see Merribell . For her order's Rule of Life, which Sump has adopted as a by-law, see The Order of Whatever Works . Sump Known as Sump Where A spit of sand on the south coast, the far end of the carrier's road Cursed 1794 Lifted 2000 The curse Thirst Parish Clerk Absalom Thurle, who is also the chair Water Committee Wound up 1794. Re-formed 2000. One member Wasps Not deferred. Removed, to the end of the spit By-law The Rule of Life, four lines, one about socks The pool Salt. Somebody has put a sign in it that says NO Sump is a hamlet on a sandy spit on the south coast, under a sign bleached almost white by the sun. For two hundred and six years it was cursed: headaches, everybody; sleep, nobody; tempers, short; and a general sense that things used to be better. In the year 2000 a field medic asked the parish when anybody in Sump had last drunk a glass of water. The curse The first thing anybody sees of Sump is a pool with a palm tree leaning over it, blue and clear. It is salt. It is the sea, which comes in under the sand at high tide and goes out again at low, and somebody has stuck a little sign in the middle of it that says NO. The parish minutes are posted. 1794. Item 1: Wasps, in the well. Whose? Deferred. 1794. Item 2: The Water Committee to be wound up, there being no water. Carried. 1795. Item 1: Wasps. Deferred. 1795. Item 2: A general sense that things used to be better. Noted. Suspected curse. And so on, every year, in six different hands, WASPS - DEFERRED, until the year 2000, when it was underlined, and the pen had gone through the paper. Nobody could say whose the wasps were. A wasp is an animal, which is the Pound. A nest is a structure, which is Buildings. A well is Water, and the Water Committee was wound up in 1794. The parish clerk, Mr Absalom Thurle, in a wide hat, pressing two fingers very hard to the side of his head, had a head like a drum, and so did everybody, and nobody in Sump had had a decent night's sleep in six generations. Item one was always the curse. Item two was always the wasps, deferred. There was never an item three. There was never time. The houses said the rest. QUIET PLEASE. TRYING TO SLEEP, on an old card, put up in hope. NO CALLERS. NO HAWKERS. NO CHOSEN ONES. THE CURSE IS QUITE ENOUGH TO BE GOING ON WITH, THANK YOU. A clay pot, empty, with a card, FOR RAIN, a very optimistic pot. A cactus with a card on a spine, THINGS USED TO BE BETTER, and it was the only thing in Sump that disagreed. In the parish hut a long table, one chair at its head, and a great many empty chairs, kept for when things got better. Mrs Pardew would not be talked to before noon, or after; it was the curse. Mr Gammage sat against a wall with his eyes shut and was not asleep, and had been trying to get off since Tuesday. The lifting The whole of it is in Merribell's article, and in the minutes, and I give the shape only. Merribell asked for an item three, and was told, through the chair, that there was never time, and said there was now, and was quick: headaches, sleep, tempers, a general sense, and skin like a letter left in a window. Mr Thurle went back through the ledger, a page at a time, for some while, to find when anybody in Sump had last drunk a glass of water. It was 1794. It was not a curse. It was thirst, six generations of it. He said it was a very thorough curse. She said it was a very thorough thirst. She moved that the Water Committee be re-formed, and the Forty-Eighth seconded, which was the first motion seconded in Sump since 1794, and Mr Thurle had to look up how it was written down. Its first business was wasps. Not deferred. Wasps want water and something sweet, and they had had the water for two hundred years, so Mrs Pardew's gran's last jar of gooseberry jam, 1931, labelled (BETTER), was opened at the far end of the spit, in the sun, and the wasps went to it, all of them, in about four minutes, extremely loudly. Nobody was stung. Nobody had ever asked them to leave. The parish had Standing Orders for the Lifting of the Curse, drafted in 1795 and never used, and it followed them, in order. A Chosen One was present. The guardian of the well was overcome, by jam. An ancient relic was given up: gooseberry, 1931. A price was paid, in sorrow: it was the last jar. The eldest spoke the riddle; Mr Gammage opened one eye and asked what was wet, and in the middle of the village, and they had not had any since 1794, and said it had taken them six generations, that one. The curse was called by its true name. Merribell let down a coil of rope and a tin cup, which she had in her bag, of course, and it came up full, clear and cold and only very slightly wasp-flavoured. Item three was the Rule of Life of the Order of Whatever Works, four lines, by Mother Ursula Pym, 1702, adopted as a by-law: I. Drink a glass of water. II. Sit down. III. Dry socks: two pairs, and a spare. IV. Then see how you feel. So the parish of Sump did it, by law, in order, down the street and back. Socks were the one line of the four nobody in Sump had ever had any trouble with. Then it saw how it felt. Mr Thurle took his hat off. Mrs Pardew said Oh. Mr Gammage was asleep, sitting up against the wall, properly, for the first time since Tuesday. The minutes read: 2000. Item 3: The Rule. Carried, and done, in order. Under it: Felt better. And: Item one. The curse. Lifted, 2000. There was time for an item four, and nobody had one, and it was wonderful. Since The sign on the spit now reads, in fresh paint under the old: LIFTED 2000. PLEASE MIND THE WELL. (RULE OF LIFE APPLIES.) The well has a rope on it, and a tin cup on the rope. Mrs Pardew can be spoken to before noon now; not after, but that is just her. Mr Thurle writes WASPS on every agenda still, and after it, NOT DEFERRED, to see how it looks. The wasps carry on at the far end of the spit, unminuted. Sump was the far end of Abel Thrush's road, and Mr Gammage told Piper Quill that for forty years, every Tuesday, a bottle of Fenmarch water was left on their well, and nobody drank it. She put that in the elegy: He brought the water nobody would drink. Mrs Pardew told her that he was a terrible man for his tea, and stopped anywhere for it, and took all day to do four miles. I wrote to the parish of Sump, as I have written to every parish in this volume, for anything it wished to add. Mr Thurle replied for the chair. The parish wished to add that things are better, and that it is in the minutes, and that the cactus planted to cheer the place up, which has been trying for two hundred years, has flowered. See also Merribell Little Gore , the other end of the carrier's road Weeping Bottom , where Mother Ursula Pym founded her house

title: The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth
text: The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth For the man, see Ambrose Fitch . For his medic, see Ysolde Marrow . For the dog, see the Bestiary . The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth Known as The mound; the Barrow Where The eastern hills, above the north road, facing the sea Of Ambrose Fitch, Chosen One #44 Raised About 1999, within a fortnight Status A Scheduled Monument of the district Entry Registered adventurers only, by order of the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Lock None. There is simply a sign Curse There is a curse on it as well, according to the chalk Asked for A bench On top A bench, since the year 2000 The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth is a long grass mound with a stone mouth in its side, in the eastern hills above the north road, where Thistlewick buried Ambrose Fitch , Chosen One number forty-four, at some expense, within a fortnight of his death, after ignoring him for forty years. He did not ask for a mound. He asked for a bench. There is one on it now. The sign Outside the stone mouth there is a sign: THE BARROW OF THE FORTY-FOURTH. A Scheduled Monument of the district. Entry restricted to registered adventurers. By order: the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Underneath, in chalk, in a much older hand: THERE IS A CURSE ON IT AS WELL. The stone is not locked. There is simply a sign, and you are simply not registered, and the Forty-Eighth found, to his considerable annoyance, that this was enough. He went back to Nether Sopping and registered, with a character reference, a hat and the mat, and came back and showed the sign his Guild Card. The sign did not react. He went in anyway, which was the whole of what the card was for. The dedication Cut into the stone of the porch, deeply, and recently, and at some expense: AMBROSE FITCH. CHOSEN ONE #44. THISTLEWICK REMEMBERS. Underneath, small, in chalk, in a woman's hand: thistlewick did not write once. I have not asked whose hand it is. I have a good idea, and I have left it there, which is where she left it. Inside The Barrow has a west chamber and an east, each with grave goods laid out on a cloth, which nobody had touched because nobody had been in: the things a hero is supposed to be buried with. In a stone alcove off the passage there is a dish, and a collar, and a name: BUDGE. Something is still using the alcove. On a mossy pillar near it, low down at about the height of a big dog's shoulder, the moss has been worn smooth by something leaning there for a very long time, every day, very contentedly. In the burial chamber, in the year 2000, a man was standing in the middle of the floor, in armour, with a sword, in the exact centre of a circle somebody drew for him. "The dead hero in the mound fights the living one. It's what's done. It's on the sign outside. It's in the chalk. It's in the shape of the room. I didn't ask for any of it. I asked for a bench." They did what was done. It took four minutes. Then he sat down on the floor of his own burial chamber, which was not something the shape of the room allowed for, and said that he had been waiting forty years to have that fight. "That's the whole trouble with the lot of us. It's what's done, so we do it." He gave them the sword and the ring, given rather than taken, which he was extremely particular about. Then he told them what he wanted. "Top of the mound. Facing the sea. You can see the north road from up there. People walk that road tired and there's nowhere for them to sit down for four miles. Forty years of standing in a circle and that's what I want. A bench. Anyone's bench. Not mine. Anyone's." The bench Wick & Barrow of Nether Sopping had had a bench in eleven pieces leaning against the wall for some years, under a card: BENCH. 400. NOBODY HAS EVER BOUGHT THIS. The Forty-Eighth bought it, and carried it out to the mound in eleven pieces under his arm, and put it together on the top. The diagram was wrong. He worked it out. It took an hour and a half and one piece was left over, which is traditional. There is a bench on the top of the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth now, facing the sea. Anybody may sit on it. That was the point; he was very clear that that was the point. From it you can see the sea one way, and the north road and the Tower the other. The burial chamber is empty. The circle on the floor has gone unswept for the first time in forty years, and there is nobody standing in it. If you want him, he is on the top of the mound, on a bench, facing the sea. When I went out to see it, the grass in front of the bench was flat, and there was a cup on the end of it. The cup was not mine. Ysolde Somebody had to tell Ysolde Marrow, who kept the Forty-Fourth alive for nine years, on and off, and who has sat at the table by the bar in the Slain Wyvern ever since with a kit she does not need open in front of her out of habit. The Forty-Eighth told her. Nobody in the room looked over. Everybody in the room was listening. "Forty years I've had that argument with a village I've never been to. They wanted a hero in a mound. He wanted somewhere to put his legs up." He had also asked the Forty-Eighth to tell her that he said she was right about the four hit points. I do not know what the argument was. I know that she was right. Near by The Middle Distance. South-east of the mound there is a hill with grass, a view of the sea, and nothing else of any description whatever, and on it there is a bench. It is older than the one on the mound. It has no plaque. Nobody remembers who put it up. If you sit on it, nothing happens, and the sea does what the sea does. The two benches face the same water. The Hermit. Not far off, a hut, a rock, and a man looking at the middle distance with great authority, who has been up there nineteen years, and has wisdom for passing travellers: bread, candles, a wedge of the hard cheese, not the soft, nails, two inch, and something for a cough. It is a shopping list. Nobody had ever once come up and asked him if he needed anything. The Forty-Eighth went and got his shopping. He would like it known that he did not need the company. He needed the cheese. He is nearly out of candles again, but he shan't mention it. I asked at the Wyvern who put up the bench on the Middle Distance, which is older than anybody's memory, and has no plaque, and faces the sea. Nobody knew. Merrow Halgate said that it was probably somebody who had walked that road tired, and had nowhere to sit, and had done something about it, and had not wanted a plaque. Then he said that it was a pity Ambrose had never been told about it, because it is not far. Then he said, after a while, that perhaps Ambrose had known, and wanted one nearer the road. See also Ambrose Fitch Ysolde Marrow Nether Sopping , for Wick & Barrow, and for the cottage The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) The Chosen Ones

title: The Bottomless Pit
text: The Bottomless Pit For what lived at the bottom, see Miss Halloway's Bestiary , where it is not called a Thing. The Bottomless Pit Known as The Bottomless Pit; a wonder of the district Where A hillside in the western hills, west of Thistlewick ; Nether Sopping's, by custom Custodian Fenwick Splint Admission 2 crowns. Children, 1. Free, for ever, to one party Refunds None, re: depth Depth Four feet Bottomless Approx. The step There isn't one. That's the joke Contents Two hundred years of lost property, mostly eaten; socks, odd The Bottomless Pit is a hole in a hillside in the western hills, with a hut, a rope and a turnstile, kept by its custodian, Fenwick Splint , as a wonder of the district. It is four feet deep. It is called the Bottomless Pit because "the Pit" is not a wonder of the district. "Two crowns and you may look into the Bottomless Pit, which is a wonder of the district and, I'll be straight with you, four feet deep." Mr Splint says this to every visitor, and then he says to mind the step, and then he says that there isn't one, and that that is the joke, and that he does it every time. He does. The pit At the bottom there is a painted board facing up at the visitors: BOTTOMLESS (APPROX.), and somebody has added, YOU ARE STANDING ON IT. There is a pickaxe, left by somebody who came down to dig for the bottom of the pit; they found it almost at once, and left in a hurry, embarrassed. There is a broken pot with one sock in it. The town of Nether Sopping has been throwing things down the Pit, or losing them near it, for about two hundred years, and all of it has come to rest at the far end, where the pit goes back into the hill further than anybody expected. There is a drift of odd socks four feet deep, which is to say, as deep as the pit. None of them match. There is a hamper marked PROPERTY OF THE 39TH - DO NOT TOUCH. There is a picnic hamper with a note in it, BACK IN AN HOUR - H.V., in the same hand as the plaque under the wyvern in the Slain Wyvern. Nobody came back for it. I do not know why, and I have not been able to find anybody who does. The badger For forty years Mr Splint reported to the Adventurers' Guild that something had moved in down the far end and was eating the lost property. Two hundred years of lost property, and it had eaten it. The Guild said that a badger was not a monster. He said, come and see the badger. They never came and saw the badger. The Forty-Eighth's company came and saw the badger. It was the size of a hay cart, and asleep on a mattress of everything Nether Sopping had ever failed to come back for, and it opened one eye, and had a strong opinion. It left, at speed, up a slope nobody knew was there, and took one boot with it. It had earned the boot. Miss Halloway's notes on the badger, and on the other thing asleep in the crack in the north wall, which she says is the single most normal thing in the cave, are in the Bestiary. "You've done it. You actually did it." Mr Splint looked into the pit for a while. He paid seven hundred crowns, which is a great deal for a custodian of a four-foot pit, and told them that admission was free for them now, for ever. "It's four feet deep and you're welcome in it whenever you like." I paid my two crowns and went down, for this article. Mr Splint told me to mind the step, and that there wasn't one, and that that was the joke. I said that I had heard it was. He said that he did it every time, and that it had never been told to a historian before, and that he would like that noted. It is noted. See also Nether Sopping The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) The Bestiary

title: The Former Premises
text: The Former Premises Contributed by P. Hollowell, Caretaker (retained) I wrote to Mr Hollowell to ask whether I might describe the Former Premises, which I cannot visit, because the only way there is by air. He wrote back by return, eleven pages, offering to give me the tour in writing, since I could not come to it. It is printed here as he gave it. For the tower the engagement moved to, see The Obligatory Tower . For the contract, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . - H.B. The Former Premises Known as The venue; the castle on the cloud Where The sky, above the southern sea Built by Malagant the Provisional Means of support As before Access By air. That was rather the point Heroes arrived None. It worked perfectly Lift Courtyard to battlements. Commissioned following a complaint (upheld) Caretaker P. Hollowell, retained, pending instructions Visitors' book One entry Visitors! Oh, VISITORS. Come in, come in, mind the step. No, there isn't one. Force of habit. Prosper Hollowell. Caretaker. Retained. Welcome to the Former Premises! I should shake your hand, and I shall imagine that I have, and then again, in case it did not take. The tour The tour starts here. It also ends here. It is one hall. I have been working on it. You will have come by air. Of course you will. It is the only way, and that was rather the whole point of the place. These were the premises of the engagement: two thousand years of Dark Lords, raised up here by somebody's grandfather so that no hero could ever reach them. And no hero ever did. It worked perfectly. Not one. I do think that is worth saying at the start, because people tend to hear the rest of it and forget. Then there was a complaint, about the climb. Then a second one. Then a recommendation. So the engagement was moved into a tower, with a door at the bottom. Ground floor. Very sensible. The heroes have to be able to ARRIVE, you see. That was four thousand eight hundred years ago. I was retained. I have kept it ready ever since, in case it is re-let. The old throne, on your left as you come in, facing the door, black and red, polished to a shine. There is a dust sheet folded on the seat, ready to go back over it the moment you leave. The armour. Four suits. One is labelled DISPLAY ONLY - NO LONGER IN SERVICE. One has a little tag on one finger, KEPT FOR THE LOOK OF THE THING - H. One has a feather duster under one arm, as if it has been helping. It has not, but it is nice to think so. The last stands a little apart from the others, facing the door, in case anybody ever comes. I polish that one more than the rest. I could not tell you why. The windows. Through the tall one: sky, and under the sky, more sky, and a very long way down, the sea. Through the other a cloud will drift by at eye level, and is politely ignored. The waiting area. A sofa for visitors, in case of a wait. There has never been a wait. The cushions are plumped every morning anyway. The deeds, framed. The builder is given as MALAGANT THE PROVISIONAL, and the site as the sky, above the southern sea. Visitors always ask what holds it up, and I always show them the clause. Means of support: as before. They read the deeds through twice, looking for the before. There isn't one. I have never thought that a weakness in a document. The quarterly reports, bound, one for every quarter since the lease lapsed: nineteen thousand two hundred of them. These are the copies. The originals were filed. Tucked into each is the reply, which is the same form letter every time, THANK YOU FOR YOUR REPORT, WHICH HAS BEEN FILED, and I have found that very steadying. The longer recent ones are mostly about the lift. The lift. LIFT - COURTYARD - BATTLEMENTS. Commissioned following a complaint (upheld). It goes up, smoothly and in perfect silence, to the battlements, and from the battlements you can see four thousand feet of sky, straight down, all the way to the sea. Then it comes back down, smoothly and in perfect silence, to the hall. It does not go any further than that. Nobody asked it to. It works beautifully. It always has. It is the best thing in the building, and I have said so in every report. The potted plant by the door is watered by the rain, from underneath, and is the best-watered plant in the world. I mention that on every tour, and visitors are always very nice about it. The visitors' book The visitors' book is on the lectern. It does not leave the lectern; it never has. It is ruled in three columns, NAME, FROM, REMARKS, and for four thousand eight hundred years there was nothing in any of them, on any page. It was the one gap in the record. In the year 2000 I had visitors. Living ones, from below, by air, in an airship from Upper Clanging, which I am told has a lift of its own of a kind, and I should very much like to see it. They were going up the tower; they had the look. I asked them whether they would ask the current incumbent to sign the book, for the file, and gave them a slip, ruled to match, because the book does not leave the lectern. They came back with it. I have pasted it in, square: NAME: GRIMSPITE THE INEVITABLE. FROM: HERE. REMARKS: Never been. Heard marvellous things about the lift. He had heard marvellous things about the lift. I have read that a great many times. That quarter's report has, under ITEM TWO: VISITORS, where every other report on the shelf says NONE, the word Yes!, underlined twice. I believe that is the first underlining in nineteen thousand two hundred reports, and I do not regret it. The post In the spring of that year I had a letter from the Prophecy Committee, sent to me as a matter of course: NOTIFICATION OF CHANGE OF ADDRESS. THE ENGAGEMENT HAS REMOVED TO: THE OBLIGATORY TOWER. GROUND FLOOR. DOOR AT THE BOTTOM. PLEASE AMEND YOUR RECORDS. I had amended them four thousand eight hundred years previously, but it was very kind of them to write. After that, one morning, came a second letter: NOTICE OF TERMINATION. The Engagement is concluded. The Premises are released from retention. No further action is required. No further action. I have filed it, under N, for Notice, and under T, and under C, in case, and that took me until about half past nine. Then I looked round the hall, and it was very clean, and I had nothing else to file. Four thousand eight hundred years, and that is the file. But the book has one in it now. It is in the record, and nobody can take it out of the record. And the lift is still running. I cannot think who would stop it. Pending instructions Mr Bellwether has asked me what I shall do now that I am released from retention. I have thought about it a good deal. The Premises are in perfect working order, and somebody ought to keep them so, in case. I have no instructions to the contrary. I am therefore staying on, pending instructions. I have stopped drawing my retainer, since I am no longer retained, and I have written a quarterly report to say so, and had the reply, which is that it has been filed. I find I do not mind in the least. If any reader of this volume is passing by air, the tour starts in the hall, and also ends there, and the lift is always running. Beautifully. P. HOLLOWELL, Caretaker. The Former Premises, the sky. First quarter, 2002. Mr Hollowell's letter came by the courier, the man in the red coat, who had been up there, it seems, before anybody else ever was. I asked the courier how he got up there, and he said he was on his rounds, and did not say whose. Spare Cotterill, who went up with the Forty-Eighth, wrote home from the waiting area: "I waited. Only the post came." See also The Obligatory Tower , where the engagement moved Grimspite the Inevitable , the only entry in the book Upper Clanging , for the airship

title: The Gilded Turnip
text: The Gilded Turnip This article is about the inn at Thistlewick. For the vegetable it is named after, which is on a plinth inside, see below. For its sister house on the coast, see The Slain Wyvern . The Gilded Turnip Known as The inn; the Turnip Of Thistlewick , the south side of the square Landlady Prudence Thrupp Rooms Twenty crowns. Still twenty crowns Breakfast Turnip Rating One star, in chalk. Four more, in a different chalk, in Prudence's handwriting Credit None. That means you, Bram Singing on tables Not permitted Piano Please do not play Societies meeting One, on Thursdays The Gilded Turnip is the inn on the square at Thistlewick , warm and brown and loud, kept by Prudence Thrupp . Three of the Forty-Eighth's companions were found in it, one of them on a table. It is named after a turnip on a plinth, painted gold, which a small plaque says is not a metaphor. Over the door hangs a tin tankard on a bracket, which creaks when the wind blows in exactly the rhythm of the inn's favourite song, and has taught it to three generations of the village. The song is Turnips in the Morning. It is a good tune. Nobody knew that until a professional played it properly. The house The turnip. A single turnip on a plinth, painted gold, with a plaque: THE GILDED TURNIP. It is not a metaphor. It is just a turnip somebody painted. It is also, in the words of the inn's most famous guest, "the problem", and in the year 2000 the whole of the Forty-Eighth's company sat down in front of it for an afternoon to find it a rhyme. There is none. The afternoon is described under Piper Quill , and lasted until Prudence stopped bringing tea and brought soup, out of pity. The last verse of the ballad was finished at this table, in nine seconds, by moving the turnip down a line: and sat down with a turnip, which was worth the journey, and the wait. P. Quill, the ballad, its last verse (in part) The piano. An upright, with a sign on the lid: PLEASE DO NOT PLAY THE PIANO, and under it, smaller, THIS MEANS YOU, BRAM. The Forty-Eighth knows one tune, with one finger. The company between them have played everything else on it: Sir Aldric a stirring march that turns into a different stirring march and back; Hob, hard and in time, taking two keys off and putting them back on better than they were; Zephyrine a scale, after which the piano smelt faintly of toast for the rest of the evening. Middle C is still a bit warm. The shelves. Sacks and boxes of turnip, labelled by year like wine. The '87 is said to be very good. The '91 is not spoken of. Behind the bar, jars and bottles each with a regular's name painted on: REGULAR, REGULAR, REGULAR, REGULAR, and at the end, PIPER (NOT ON THE TABLE). There is a big lidded pot labelled POT, so that everybody knows, with a second label inside it that says INSIDE OF POT. There is Prudence's own cordial, elderflower and turnip, which is better than it sounds. It would more or less have to be. The rooms. A big bed, made up very tightly. In stories, heroes lie down on any bed they find and wake up feeling much better. Prudence will be watching you, and it is twenty crowns. The card on the bedside table asks guests to leave the room as they would wish to find it; underneath it somebody has written ON FIRE?, initialled Z.V. "It was a question," I was told. "It was a genuine question." There is a washstand with a towel folded by somebody who folds towels properly. The register. The most recent entry, for six years, was SIR A. PEMBERTON-GORE. ONE NIGHT. Every night after it he wrote DITTO. "One keeps records. One never knows where the gate will be in the morning." The counter. NO CREDIT. NO SINGING ON TABLES. NO CHOSEN ONES ON CREDIT EITHER. THAT MEANS YOU, BRAM. There is a lot in this inn that means you, Bram. The regulars Prudence Thrupp keeps the house, and has kept it for longer than she will say, and her sister Dorcas keeps the Slain Wyvern , forty miles south, which nobody in Thistlewick had mentioned. They did not speak for thirty years. "That's not a falling-out. We just stopped one day and neither of us started again. So we send each other things instead." In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth carried a jar south for her, warm on one side, which he was told not to shake or ask about, and carried a reply back north which was heavier, and deliberately worse, and had been under construction for some time. Prudence laughed. She has written since: four pages, two of them about the Forty-Eighth, and one of those complimentary. The sisters' locket, two portraits facing opposite ways, which had been in a drawer since they were girls, went north on the Quest. "That was HER idea, that was." The Regular, whose cousin was the Thirty-Ninth. Lovely tower, apparently. Since the ending, lovely coast, apparently. The Gloamwood Society, which meets at the table by the door on Thursdays: nine members, forty years, a walk once a year, and a quarterly, The Sighting, edited by Mr Dunmore. Mrs Lumb does the talking. Miss Pellow saw the Thing in the Woods in 1971, and counted nine, and was the only one who got it right. The Society's long work came to its conclusion in the year 2000, with the help of Miss Halloway, and is described under The Gloamwood . Zephyrine Vance drank at the table by the window for eleven years, being just passing through, like somebody waiting for a letter. The letter came, on thick cream paper with a purple seal, and Prudence propped it against the glass where she would see it: the Collegium Arcanum's eleventh notice of outstanding fines. See her article. The table is still hers when she wants it. She does not sit at it like that any more. There is a scorch mark on the ceiling above it, which was a moth. Piper Quill was standing on a table when the Forty-Eighth first came in, describing him, out loud, in the third person, as he approached. The tavern had not fallen silent. The tavern was ignoring her. Through the window from the square you can still hear somebody in there singing a song about the Forty-Eighth which rhymes Bram with jam. It is hers. The jam was a placeholder. It has tested very well. I stayed a night at the Gilded Turnip on my visit, at twenty crowns, and the breakfast was turnip. Prudence asked after her sister, and I said that she was well, and Prudence said "I didn't ask," and then asked again, more particularly, about the shelf. See also Thistlewick The Slain Wyvern , the sister house Piper Quill , for the rhyme Zephyrine Vance , for the letter

title: The Gloamwood
text: The Gloamwood For what lives in it, as opposed to what was said to, see Miss Halloway's Bestiary . For the man on the log, see The Chosen Ones , number forty-six. The Gloamwood Known as The wood; the woods; "enough" Where Across the north road, between Thistlewick and the Obligatory Tower Ways through One. The gap is the road Contents Trees; mushrooms, named; beanstalks, dead; a chest The chest A mimic. Everybody knows Residents The Forty-Sixth, on a log Things in it Argued about for two hundred years. See below, and the Bestiary Society The Gloamwood Society (1960), nine members Searched Yes. The logs say so The Gloamwood is a dark wood across the north road out of Thistlewick , and the only way north. The road ends at a wall of trees. There is a gap. The gap is the road now. Every Chosen One has gone through it, and one of them, the Forty-Sixth, went no further, and is still there, sitting down. "You think about it," the Forty-Eighth told me, of the moment at the mouth of the wood. "It does not improve." The first path The near half of the wood is a long path between big trees, much walked, and dressed, over the years, by everybody who has walked it. The carved tree. Somebody has carved an arrow into the bark, pointing north. Underneath it, in a shakier hand, a second arrow points back the way you came. Further on, a boulder has an arrow chalked on it pointing north, and under it, by a different hand: ARE YOU SURE? A mossy log has its moss on the north side, as the books say it should, and somebody has nailed a small sign to the south side: OTHER WAY. The logs. Every hollow log on the path has a hand-lettered sign at one end: SEARCHED. Somebody has been along the whole path with these, and it saves everybody a great deal of time. The beanstalks. One goes straight up into the canopy and stops, as though it had thought better of it, with a card nailed to the bottom: GIANT NOT IN. PLEASE DO NOT CLIMB. THIS MEANS YOU, JACK. The others are dead. One has a little wooden marker in front of it like a gravestone: HERE LIES A MAGIC BEAN. IT WAS NOT. The mushrooms. Pale ones in a neat row, which are edible and, I am told by a naturalist, delicious, and which I am to tell nobody about or there will be a society. (There is a society. It is about something else.) Red ones with white spots, of the kind in every picture book with a gnome sitting on top: there is no gnome, but there is a very small dent in the top of the biggest one, as if one had just left. One has a tiny door painted on the stalk, very carefully, by somebody with a very fine brush and a great deal of hope. The boulder is hunched over in exactly the shape of a sleeping troll. It is a boulder. You may check from the other side, to be sure, and then a third time, and by the third time you will feel that it knows. The chest. A treasure chest, alone, in the middle of a wood, on a path, in perfect condition. It is a mimic. Everybody knows it is a mimic. Nearly everybody opens it. Not far from it are a helmet, a boot, and a note in a jar: IF FOUND, I WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE MIMIC. The mimic was carrying an Elixir about with it as bait, which is either clever or very sad. It is splinters now. The man on the log Half way along the first path is a log across the way, with a cushion on it, and a little card on the cushion: RESERVED - NUMBER FORTY-SIX. The Forty-Sixth is a man in very good armour, and he is sitting on the log. He set out in 1980, and got as far as the woods, and decided that the woods were enough. "Nobody writes songs about that. But I'm here, and I'm forty-six, and I'm sitting down." Beside the log is a sack of letters, a great many, in two hands, one round and one narrow, going back years. They are from Nabb and Tolly, of his old party, who write every month, both of them. He does not write back. "I read them. Reading them's the answer. They know that. Nabb doesn't, but Tolly does, and Tolly does the stamps." I know Nabb, and Tolly. They drink at the Slain Wyvern, and Nabb gave the Forty-Eighth one of the six accounts in my history, which is the whole story: he stopped, on the path, and said the woods were enough, "and we looked at each other, and we said: fair." Everyone wants there to be more. There isn't more. Post goes out on Thursdays. Tolly buys the stamps in twos, because it is a long way, and he is worth two stamps. Nabb says the man who collects the post says he reads them. The deep wood Beyond the log the path goes into the dark part of the wood, where the trees are a wall, and there is a clearing, and there is the Thing. The Thing in the Woods has been argued about in Thistlewick for two hundred years. Is it a bear? Is it several bears? Is it a bear-shaped hole in the idea of a wood? Nobody ever got close enough to settle it. The Forty-Eighth got close enough, and the Thing stopped being in the woods, and Thistlewick has never believed him, and he has never told them anyway. What it was, in the sense of what it was, is a matter for a naturalist, and the naturalist has dealt with it in the Bestiary. The clearing has a ring of mushrooms round it, very large, very even and very obviously magic, with a little rope round it and a sign: SITE OF SPECIAL INTEREST. DO NOT DANCE IN. Each mushroom has a label on a stick: MUSHROOM 14 OF 31. THE SOCIETY COUNTS THEM EVERY YEAR. There were thirty-one last year as well. Near by there is a log with a flask, a sandwich box and a notebook on it, all labelled G.S., which has been the Society's picnic spot for forty years. There are some bones, and a sign beside them in the Society's hand: THESE ARE A SHEEP'S. THE SOCIETY HAS CHECKED. IT WAS A VERY OLD SHEEP AND IT DIED HAPPY. PLEASE STOP REPORTING IT. The Society has given each of the pale mushrooms a name. One of them is called Norman. Miss Halloway has written to them to say that it is a Cyril. The Gloamwood Society The Gloamwood Society was founded in 1960 to prove that the Thing in the Woods is not there. It has nine members, meets at the Gilded Turnip on Thursdays, walks the wood once a year, and has published The Sighting four times a year for forty years, edited by Mr Dunmore. For forty years it took anything: a shape, a smell, a feeling. For forty years it found nothing, so far, that would stand up. In the year 2000 Miss Halloway read all forty years of The Sighting in an afternoon, and told them that she could prove it did not exist, and that it never had, and the whole Society leaned forward as one. The walk was that night. It is always that night, when there is news. I was not there, and I have the account from Mr Dunmore's issue one hundred and sixty, which they printed extra of, and from Miss Halloway, who corrected it. There is nothing in the Gloamwood. That is proved, in writing, by a professional. The Society cheered. The method, and what the sightings were sightings of, are in the Bestiary, where Miss Halloway has asked me to leave them. One member did not cheer. Miss Edith Pellow saw something in the clearing in 1971, and wrote it up in issue forty-four, and counted nine. Nobody had seen it since. Miss Halloway had read issue forty-four. She told Miss Pellow that of forty years of sightings, hers was the only accurate one. On the walk home the whole Society contrived, without anybody arranging it, to be on either side of her, and by the edge of the wood she was telling everybody about the nine, and nobody minded in the least. Miss Halloway was made an honorary member, the first, and given the badge. She wears it on the cloak. The Society's walk of 2001 was, as the tally promised, very well attended: three hundred and twelve walkers, in good boots, with lanterns. Nothing was found. It was minuted with satisfaction. Miss Pellow led it. I am told she stopped the walk in the clearing, at dusk, and pointed, and said "There," and that three hundred and twelve people looked, and that there was nothing there, and that it was the best walk the Society has ever had. Bassoons The Gloamwood is the only road between the south and the works town of Upper Clanging , and it is a hard road to walk at night with eight feet of folded tube in a case. Mr Enoch Bagshawe, first bassoon of the Works Band, sat on the milestone at the mouth of the wood for some time, many nights, because if anything so much as looked at him he would drop the case, and that would be the reed, and the reed took three weeks. The band had never had a bassoon. It is a brass band; he is aware. Nix took him through. She halves encounters; it is a knack. With mothballs as well, which the Band keeps the uniforms in, he crossed the whole wood by night without a single encounter, or half of one, and at the north end he opened the case in the road and played one long low note on the reed by moonlight, for no reason but that he could. The Works Band has a bassoon. See also Thistlewick , to the south The Obligatory Tower , to the north The Chosen Ones , for the Forty-Sixth Wren Halloway The Bestiary

title: The Lighthouse of Saint Bother
text: The Lighthouse of Saint Bother For the town it is seen from, which it is not for, see Nether Sopping . The Lighthouse of Saint Bother Known as The light at the point Where A headland east of Nether Sopping , at the end of a road that goes nowhere else Keeper Ferrety Bother, fourth generation Saint His great-grandmother. She'd have hated the fuss Last ship 1909 For The ones coming back down the north road at night Takes One gallon Out One spring, until the year 2000 Lit Yes Rule two There is no rule two The Lighthouse of Saint Bother stands on a headland on the south coast, east of Nether Sopping, at the end of a road that goes nowhere else. No ship has passed the point since 1909. It is kept lit anyway, by the fourth generation of Bothers, because it can be seen from the crossroads on the north road, and it is what the ones coming home walk home by. The keeper Ferrety Bother keeps the light. "It's a family name. The saint was my great-grandmother and she'd have hated the fuss." There are tapestries of her on the ground floor: with a lantern, glaring at a ship, which looks very sorry; telling off a storm, which is leaving; and in a deckchair with her feet up and the lamp lit, with, embroidered underneath by a great-grandson, SHE'D HAVE HATED THE FUSS.
